<p><strong>Corporate adjustments</strong></p>
<p>From 2027, embedded currency hedging results on participation investments will no longer qualify for the participation exemption.</p>
<p><strong>Tax changes for entrepreneurs and businesses</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Carbon and waste tax timelines pushed back:</strong> The Netherlands has postponed its industrial CO2 levy target from 2030 to 2035 (EUR 304 per ton for waste incineration plants) and cut the waste tax increase to EUR 23.75 per ton in 2028, down from EUR 53.25 per ton.</li>
<li><strong>Forestry exemption abolished:</strong> The forestry profit exemption ends on 1 January 2029, generating EUR 34 million that year and EUR 35 million annually after.</li>
<li><strong>Pillar Two safe harbours introduced:</strong> Pillar 2 safe harbour rules (including Side-by-Side, UPE, and Simplified ETR provisions) take effect retroactively from 2026 under the Wetsvoorstel Wet aanvullende veiligehavenregels Wet minimumbelasting 2024.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Innovation and sustainability measures</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Expansion of innovation Box SME lump-sum cap: </strong>The lump-sum threshold for the SME innovation box increases from EUR 25,000 to EUR 100,000 per year starting 1 January 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Real estate transfer tax reduction for investors:</strong> The transfer tax rate for residential properties not used as a primary residence (investors/landlords) is reduced from 8% to 7% from 1 January 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Transfer tax exemption for social housing corporations:</strong> A targeted transfer tax exemption is created for social housing (DAEB) property transfers between housing associations effective 1 January 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Energy investment allowance:</strong> EIA deduction increases from 40% to 45.5% from 1 January 2027 to encourage business energy efficiency.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Measures for start-up entrepreneurs</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Employee stock options:</strong> Tax rules will be simplified and deferred from 2027 under measures for startups and scale-ups.</li>
<li><strong>Start-up deduction: </strong>The deduction falls to EUR 10 in 2027 and will be abolished from 1 January 2028.</li>
<li><strong>Accelerated depreciation: </strong>The special accelerated depreciation scheme for startups will end on 1 January 2028.</li>
<li><strong>Disability start-up deduction: </strong>The deduction for disabled entrepreneurs will be abolished from 1 January 2029 due to low use and high administrative costs.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Tax changes for products and services </strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Fuel excise duty: </strong>Temporary petrol excise relief is extended to 31 December 2027.</li>
<li>Flight tax: Distance-based rates begin in 2027, with the highest rate reduced to EUR 59.43 per passenger from 1 January 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Alcohol excise duty: </strong>Inflation indexation starts from 1 January 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Small breweries: </strong>The 7.5% excise duty discount for small independent breweries will end from 1 January 2028.</li>
<li><strong>Tap water tax: </strong>The tax will rise by EUR 0.10 per m³ from 1 January 2027 to EUR 0.537 per m³.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>VAT rate alignments</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Floriculture VAT:</strong> VAT on flowers and plants will increase from 9% to 21% from 1 January 2028.</li>
<li><strong>Hot air ballooning VAT:</strong> Balloon flights will move from 9% to 21% VAT from 1 January 2028.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Motor vehicle &amp; transport taxes</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Youngtimer scheme:</strong> Existing users retain current tax treatment for one additional year in 2027, while the eligibility age threshold will be reduced to 20 years from 2029.</li>
<li><strong>Motor vehicle tax relief: </strong>Entrepreneur delivery vans receive a 50% MRB reduction, while heavy goods vehicles receive a zero rate for the second half of 2026.</li>
<li><strong>Truck charge: </strong>Truck charge rates are reduced by 22.3% from 1 September to 31 December 2026 to offset higher fuel costs.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Individual income tax measures </strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Higher tax-free travel allowance: </strong>The maximum tax-free travel allowance will rise from EUR 0.23 to EUR 0.25 per kilometre, retroactive to 1 January 2026.</li>
<li><strong>Pension accrual cap frozen: </strong>The EUR 137,800 income cap for tax-favoured pension and annuity accrual will remain unchanged from 2027 through 2032.</li>
<li><strong>Staff discount exemption abolished: </strong>The EUR 500 annual tax-free exemption for employee discounts on employer-produced goods will be abolished from 1 January 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Healthcare cost deduction abolished:</strong> The income tax deduction for specific healthcare expenses will be fully abolished from 1 January 2028, reducing compliance burdens and raising additional revenue.</li>
</ul>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Dominican Republic’s Tax Authority (DGII) clarified the inheritance tax treatment of estates of foreign pensioners or rentiers covered by Law 171-07 on Special Incentives for Pensioners and Rentiers of Foreign Source. The ruling, <a href="https://dgii.gov.do/legislacion/consultas/Consultas%20Tecnicas%202026/Febrero/Consulta%2011-Sucesi%C3%B3n%20de%20pensionados%20y%20rentistas%20acogidos%20a%20la%20Ley%20N%C3%BAm.171-07.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">G.L. <p>Under Law 2569 on Successions and Donations, the taxable base of the inheritance tax (impuesto sobre sucesiones) is the total estate left by the deceased, including movable and immovable property and duly documented rights and obligations. The tax is charged at 3% of the net hereditary mass after permitted deductions under articles 4 and 6.</p>
<p>The DGII confirmed that Law 171-07 benefits apply during the lifetime of the principal pensioner or rentier. These include an exemption from transfer tax on the first property acquired, 50% relief from mortgage tax and real estate property tax (IPI) where applicable, an exemption from tax on dividends and interest of any source, and 50% capital gains relief subject to specified conditions.</p>
<p>The benefits do not exempt the deceased’s estate from inheritance tax. However, certain incentives may continue after the death of the principal beneficiary for the spouse and dependants defined in article 5 of Law 171-07, provided they also meet the qualifying conditions under article 17.</p>
<p>The eligible dependants can include unmarried minor children, disabled adult children, university-enrolled adult children who remain economically dependent on the deceased, and qualifying minors under legal guardianship. The DGII stated that beneficiaries seeking continued incentives must satisfy the documentation and compliance requirements applicable under Law 171-07.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan’s Southern Area National Taxation Bureau had <a href="https://www.mof.gov.tw/singlehtml/384fb3077bb349ea973e7fc6f13b6974?cntId=708e376e505d4b128a64fa8696070162" target="_blank" rel="noopener">reminded</a> businesses on 16 September 2026, that travel expenses claimed for tax purposes must be supported by evidence showing that the trips were related to business operations.</p>
<p>Under Article 38 of the Income Tax Act and Article 62 of the Guidelines for the Examination of Corporate Income Tax Returns, expenses unrelated to a company’s principal or ancillary business activities cannot be recognised as deductible expenses or losses. Paragraph 1 of Article 74 further requires businesses to provide business trip reports detailing daily destinations, parties contacted and the nature of business activities, along with relevant supporting documents.</p>
<p>The bureau said transportation and accommodation receipts alone may not be sufficient. Businesses should also retain evidence such as invitation letters, email correspondence, meeting notices and exhibition photographs to establish the business purpose of trips.</p>
<p>In a recent examination of a company’s 2023 corporate income tax return, the bureau found that approximately TWD 800,000 in travel expenses had been claimed for a Europe trip by the company’s responsible person and shareholders. Although air ticket stubs and hotel receipts had been provided, the business trip report only stated “market research”.</p>
<p>The company was unable to provide details of the parties visited, business negotiation records, correspondence with potential local customers or relevant contracts. As it could not demonstrate that the trip was connected to its business operations, the bureau disallowed the claimed travel expenses and assessed additional tax.</p>
<p>The bureau advised businesses to strengthen internal controls by requiring employees to record their daily business activities during trips and retain business discussion records, emails and other supporting documents together with accounting vouchers.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Dominican Republic’s Executive Power had submitted the draft Application Regulation for Law No. 30-26 for <a href="https://www.consultoria.gov.do/consultas/publicas/consulta-publica-borrador-reglamento-de-aplicacion-de-la-ley-num-30-26-sobre-medidas-pro-crecimiento-economico-simplificacion-fiscal-y-mitigacion-de-la-crisis-internacional-3068" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation</a>, setting out rules on tax procedures, incentive regimes, withholding taxes and other administrative measures.</p>
<p>The consultation was open from 7 September to 8 October 2026. Questions and comments could be submitted through the “submit comments” form accompanying the publication.</p>
<p><strong>Tax incentives</strong></p>
<p>The draft regulation provided that a single tax-generating event, economic activity, investment or operation could not benefit from more than one special tax incentive regime.</p>
<p>Taxpayers conducting separate economic activities or investments could access different incentive regimes if they maintained separate accounting identifying the revenues, costs, expenses, assets and liabilities of each activity.</p>
<p>The Ministry of Finance and Economy could request the Executive Power to object to a taxpayer’s incentive classification where a technical report showed that the investment:</p>
<ul>
<li>Failed to meet the objectives of the law;</li>
<li>Generated tax expenditure exceeding its social benefit;</li>
<li>Created unfair competition or market distortions;</li>
<li>Was profitable without the incentive; or</li>
<li>Failed to generate wider economic effects.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Tax appeals and debt consignment</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers challenging a tax debt administratively or judicially could consign the disputed amount with the tax administration, DGII.</p>
<p>DGII would be required to accept the consignment and could not apply precautionary collection measures. Consignment would immediately suspend late-payment surcharges and indemnity interest.</p>
<p>If the debt became res judicata, the consigned amount would extinguish the tax obligation. If the debt were annulled or reduced, the taxpayer could initiate a refund procedure for an undue or excess payment.</p>
<p><strong>Payment agreements and audit discounts</strong></p>
<p>DGII would assess payment agreement requests based on the taxpayer’s payment capacity, the amount of debt, tax compliance history and the sufficiency of guarantees offered.</p>
<p>The draft also proposed:</p>
<ul>
<li>90% reduction: For voluntary tax return rectifications made without a prior tax authority determination or requirement.</li>
<li>70% discount: Where the taxpayer requested the discount within 20 business days of receiving a potential debt notice and accepted the identified tax determinations.</li>
</ul>
<p>Payment under the latter procedure would complete the audit and result in a “no fiscal interest” certificate.</p>
<p>The statute of limitations would also be suspended for delinquent debt where a return was filed without timely payment, or where an audit debt became res judicata and remained unpaid.</p>
<p><strong>Income tax rules</strong></p>
<p>Residents would remain subject to tax on Dominican-source income and foreign-source income derived from investments, financial gains and technical assistance.</p>
<p>The draft regulation defined technical assistance as independent services provided locally or from abroad that supplied specialised knowledge, experience or skills through non-patentable procedures or techniques, including associated training.</p>
<p>Excluded services would include teaching, employee services, foreign trade or customs-transparent costs, travel reimbursements, intellectual property or equipment transfers, administrative execution without knowledge transfer, technical opinions without ongoing training and standardised mass digital services such as streaming, digital advertising and marketplaces.</p>
<p><strong>Digital assets and software</strong></p>
<p>Digital assets and cryptoassets would be defined as digital representations of value or rights based on Distributed Ledger Technology or similar cryptographic mechanisms. The definition would include stablecoins, non-fungible tokens (NFTs) and crypto derivatives.</p>
<p>The draft distinguished royalties from software transactions. Payments for the use of patentable intangible assets or industrial or scientific equipment would constitute royalties, while software licences would be excluded.</p>
<p>Software licences would cover rights to use or exploit software where the licensor retained copyright. Periodic fees, subscriptions and usage-based payments would be presumed to constitute licences.</p>
<p>A software acquisition would instead involve a full, permanent and irrevocable transfer of the economic rights to the copyright.</p>
<p><strong>Foreign tax credits</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers claiming credits for foreign tax withholdings would need to substantiate the claim by providing evidence of actual tax payment abroad, contracts or DGII-compliant invoices and proof of payment through reliable financial channels.</p>
<p>Withholding tax measures</p>
<p>The draft established several withholding rules, including a 15% withholding on a presumed net income equal to 20% of gross value, resulting in an effective 3% withholding, for:</p>
<ul>
<li>Cargo and passenger transportation services;</li>
<li>Certain non-personal services, including cleaning, fumigation, electrical and mechanical repairs, masonry, carpentry, painting and plumbing;</li>
<li>Civil construction contractors covering roads, aqueducts and buildings; and</li>
<li>Transfers of registrable movable property.</li>
</ul>
<p>A 15% ISR withholding on rental income would apply only where the tenant was a legal entity or organisation and the landlord was an individual receiving rent directly.</p>
<p>State suppliers authorised as electronic issuers and invoicing through E-CF would be exempt from the standard 5% ISR withholding.</p>
<p>A temporary 30% withholding rate would apply during fiscal years 2026, 2027 and 2028 to Dominican-source income payments of at least DOP 1,000,000,000.00 made to non-residents.</p>
<p><strong>Primary residence and capital gains</strong></p>
<p>The draft defined a primary residence as an individual’s physical, continuous main home.</p>
<p>The property would generally need to correspond to the seller’s RNC address, have a Title Certificate and active basic utility contracts, and have been continuously occupied for at least three years before the transfer.</p>
<p>Commercial, rental and vacation properties would be excluded.</p>
<p>For capital gains reinvestment into a new primary residence to qualify for exemption, the transaction would need to satisfy three conditions:</p>
<ol>
<li>Full or partial payment in accordance with the contract, supported by evidence;</li>
<li>Payment of the 3% Real Estate Transfer Tax to DGII; and</li>
<li>Formal deposit and registration of the title transfer with the Title Registry.</li>
</ol>
<p>Pre-sale contracts, purchase options and unregistered private acts would not qualify.</p>
<p><strong>Advance tax payments</strong></p>
<p>Companies exceeding MSME revenue limits during a fiscal year would retain their existing advance payment schedule until the end of that year. The new classification would apply from the following fiscal year.</p>
<p>DGII could authorise full or partial reductions in advance payments where taxpayers demonstrated force majeure or exceptional circumstances.</p>
<p><strong>ITBIS and other tax measures</strong></p>
<p>Manufacturers of ITBIS-exempt goods could choose, for each purchase, either exemption through approval of a proforma invoice or payment of ITBIS followed by a tax credit. Both mechanisms could not be used for the same purchase.</p>
<p>Tax benefits and exemptions for life insurance would apply only to the life portion of premiums. Combined policies would therefore need to separately identify premiums attributable to life coverage.</p>
<p>The LPG contribution rate would be fixed at USD 174.50 per metric ton based on import parity pricing formulas.</p>
<p><strong>Accelerated depreciation</strong></p>
<p>The proposed regulation would expand the definition of “industrial use” for accelerated depreciation.</p>
<p>The definition would cover assets directly, habitually and necessarily used in production, transformation or technical service activities in sectors including commercial, healthcare, agro-industrial, shopping centre and power generation operations.</p>
<p>Medical, surgical, optical, measuring and precision instruments under Customs Tariff Chapter 90 could qualify where they complemented machinery under Chapters 84 or 85 or served as primary operational equipment.</p>
<p>Taxpayers would need to provide technical descriptions, customs tariff classifications, purchase invoices, payment evidence and written justification of industrial use.</p>
<p><strong>Inheritance and asset valuation</strong></p>
<p>The proposed rules would establish specific valuation methods for inherited assets.</p>
<p>Real estate would be valued at the higher of the cadastral value or DGII reference value. Vehicles and movable goods would use the DGII reference price or an official expert appraisal.</p>
<p>Bank accounts and publicly traded securities would be valued using certified balances or the stock exchange closing price on the date of death.</p>
<p>Private shares would be valued using the net book value or equity balance from the last closed fiscal year.</p>
<p><strong>Donations and property transfers</strong></p>
<p>Transfers of property between relatives would be assessed based on evidence including payment, third-party financing and market price references.</p>
<p>Where such indicators existed, the transaction could be treated as a taxable sale rather than a tax-exempt donation. Transfers between spouses would generally receive neutral tax treatment unless they arose from divorce.</p>
<p><strong>Transit passengers</strong></p>
<p>Passengers in transit who remained in the Dominican Republic for less than 24 hours without formally entering through immigration would be exempt from airport departure contributions.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Romania’s Ministry of Finance has confirmed a 25% reduction in excise duty on diesel for the period 16 September to 30 September 2026 in an <a href="https://mfinante.gov.ro/presa-comunicate-de-presa/-/asset_publisher/vMeOfqIFpa30/content/ministerul-finan-c8-9belor-men-c8-9bine-reducerea-de-25-a-accizei-la-motorin-c4-83-pentru-16-30-septembrie-2026?_com_liferay_asset_publisher_web_portlet_AssetPublisherPortlet_INSTANCE_vMeOfqIFpa30_assetEntryId=20187709&amp;_com_liferay_asset_publisher_web_portlet_AssetPublisherPortlet_INSTANCE_vMeOfqIFpa30_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmfinante.gov.ro%2Fpresa-comunicate-de-presa%3Fp_p_id%3Dcom_liferay_asset_publisher_web_portlet_AssetPublisherPortlet_INSTANCE_vMeOfqIFpa30%26p_p_lifecycle%3D0%26p_p_state%3Dnormal%26p_p_mode%3Dview%26_com_liferay_asset_publisher_web_portlet_AssetPublisherPortlet_INSTANCE_vMeOfqIFpa30_cur%3D0%26p_r_p_resetCur%3Dfalse%26_com_liferay_asset_publisher_web_portlet_AssetPublisherPortlet_INSTANCE_vMeOfqIFpa30_assetEntryId%3D20187709" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announcement</a> on 15 September 2026. This decision follows the bimonthly assessment process set out in Law no. 162/2026.</p>
<p><strong>Ongoing market pressures</strong></p>
<p>International diesel prices have climbed sharply in recent weeks. Platts diesel quotations rose 51.19% during the assessment period, while pump prices for standard diesel fuel increased 27.47%. The formula established by law determined that the 25% excise duty cut should remain in place based on these figures.</p>
<p><strong>What the reduction means</strong></p>
<p>The 25% cut removes RON 701.07 per 1,000 litres or RON 829.69 per ton from the excise tax. This brings the effective excise duty level on standard diesel to RON 2,103.22 per 1,000 litres or RON 2,489.05 per ton during this period.</p>
<p><strong>How the mechanism works</strong></p>
<p>Law no. 162/2026 created a dynamic system that reviews fuel market indicators every two weeks. The Ministry adjusts the excise duty reduction based on international quotations and domestic pump prices. This approach aims to shield transport and logistics sectors from sudden cost spikes and prevent fuel costs from pushing consumer prices higher across the broader economy.</p>
<p>The Ministry of Finance will continue tracking international prices and domestic market conditions.</p>

Calculation method and rate Taxpayers apply a rate of 2% to the total volume of sales of goods and services...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Angola’s taxation authority, the General Tax Administration (AGT) has <a href="https://portaldocontribuinte.minfin.gov.ao/noticia?id=985597" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced </a>on 27 August 2026 that taxpayers under the general regime must settle their provisional industrial tax for the 2026 fiscal year by 31 August 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Calculation method and rate</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers apply a rate of 2% to the total volume of sales of goods and services not subject to withholding tax during the first six months of 2026. This calculation follows Article 66 of the Industrial Tax Code, established under Law No. 19/14 (22 October 2014) and amended by Law No. 26/20 (20 July 2020).</p>
<p>Sales already subject to withholding obligations are excluded from this calculation, as withholding payments already contribute to the taxpayer&#8217;s annual tax obligation. The taxable amount must be reported in the &#8220;Taxable Value&#8221; field when filing the settlement.</p>
<p><strong>Special cases and exemptions</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers who reported losses in the previous tax year remain exempt from the provisional settlement requirement. However, the AGT requires them to submit a declaration through the Taxpayer Portal to formally report this status and maintain compliance records.</p>
<p><strong>Supervised financial and insurance entities</strong></p>
<p>Entities regulated by the BNA (banking sector), ARSEG (insurance sector), ISJ (financial services), or CMC (gaming sector) follow a different calculation method. These organisations apply the same 2% rate to the total result from financial intermediation operations, insurance and reinsurance premiums, or gaming activities generated during the first six months of the prior financial year. Capital gains income is excluded from this calculation to prevent double taxation.</p>
<p><strong>Filing requirements</strong></p>
<p>The AGT directs all submissions through the Taxpayer Portal at<a href="https://portaldocontribuinte.minfin.gov.ao" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> https://portaldocontribuinte.minfin.gov.ao</a>.  Filers log in with their credentials and navigate to Declarations, then Industrial Tax, then Provisional Settlement.</p>
<p>Once the voluntary deadline passes, the AGT will identify taxpayers in default or those with inconsistencies in their submitted information and issue notifications accordingly.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Philippines’ Bureau of Internal Revenue released <a href="https://bir-cdn.bir.gov.ph/BIR/pdf/RMC%20No.%2096-2026_redacted.pdf?fbclid=IwY2xjawUXN2xwZG9mBWV4dG4DYWVtAjEwAGJyaWQRMW5SNGV3c05wTnRxZk5jNjFzcnRjBmFwcF9pZBAyMjIwMzkxNzg4MjAwODkyAAEeHB6g2cRdg2nSz7lrt1FHH2vY94Ur2E-xEkdphqDAN-DQQsqmErUm7wAnwhM_aem_lqgFASQ5gMr2mbfkPmCHkg" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Revenue Memorandum Circular (RMC) No. 96-2026 </a>on 7 September 2026. BIR Commissioner Charlito Martin R. Mendoza issued the circular to provide guidance on how qualified Export-Oriented Enterprises (EOEs) handle Value-Added Tax refund claims during a defined transition period.</p>
<p>The circular addresses a specific gap in Section III(1)(a) of RMC No. 37-2025. It clarifies which input taxes EOEs may recover as the government shifted EOE certification authority to the Department of Trade and Industry-Export Marketing Bureau.</p>
<p><strong>New refund window for transitional period</strong></p>
<p>The transitory period runs from 28 November 2024 through 31 December 2025. This window aligns with the effective date of Republic Act No. 12066, commonly known as the CREATE MORE Act.</p>
<p>EOEs that obtained their DTI-EMB zero-rating certificates during this timeframe may claim VAT refunds for passed-on taxes. The refund period extends from 28 November 2024 until the specific date each enterprise received its certification certificate.</p>
<p>The DTI-EMB issued these certificates on varying dates. Records show certificates were issued from as early as 14 May 2025 to as late as 26 December 2025. This variance prompted the need for clearer refund parameters.</p>
<p><strong>Documentary requirements separate by filing date</strong></p>
<p>The BIR revised its supporting document checklist requirements to account for different filing periods. The revision splits compliance obligations based on when claims are submitted.</p>
<p>Enterprises that filed refund claims before 1 April 2025 must submit documentation under Annex A.1.1 of the amended circular. Those filing from 1 April 2025 onwards follow Annex A.1.2. This separation reflects regulatory changes that took effect on 10 April 2025, when the BIR originally issued RMC No. 37-2025.</p>
<p>The DTI published its own Department Administrative Order No. 25-03 on 28 March 2025 to establish the certification framework for these enterprises.</p>
<p><strong>Consequences of missing the certification deadline</strong></p>
<p>Enterprises that reached the 70% export sales threshold but failed to secure DTI-EMB certification by 31 December 2025 face restrictions. These entities cannot claim a cash VAT refund in the immediately following taxable year.</p>
<p>However, the regulation does not eliminate their input tax entitlement. Unused input VAT balances may carry forward to subsequent quarters. Enterprises may apply these carried-forward amounts against future VAT liabilities under standard tax provisions.</p>
<p>The circular reinforces that all refund claims must meet Section 112 requirements of the Philippine Tax Code. Only input taxes directly attributable to zero-rated export sales qualify for recovery. The BIR will not process refunds where the input tax has already been reimbursed, credited, or used elsewhere.</p>
<p>The circular took effect immediately upon publication on 7 September 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Brazil&#8217;s government announced fresh fuel relief measures on 9 September 2026, expanding diesel subsidies and cutting taxes on gasoline and ethanol. The move comes as crude oil prices remain elevated near USD 100 per barrel, driven by regional tensions in the Middle East.</p>
<p>The Planning and Budget Minister Bruno Moretti confirmed that total fuel-relief spending will reach approximately BRL 40 billion between March and the end of September.</p>
<p><strong>Tax reductions on gasoline and ethanol</strong></p>
<p>Federal taxes on gasoline will drop by BRL 0.63 per litre over the next 30 days, up from the previous BRL 0.44 per litre subsidy. Ethanol taxes fell by BRL 0.19 per litre, eliminating all federal levies on the biofuel.</p>

<p>The government added a fresh BRL 1 per litre subsidy to diesel, layered on top of the existing BRL 1.12 per litre subsidy running through at least the end of September. The new scheme requires fuel producers and importers to deduct subsidy amounts from sale prices and record them on invoices. State oil regulator ANP then reimburses participating companies.</p>
<p>The diesel subsidy carries a monthly fiscal cost of BRL 5 billion.</p>
<p><strong>Offsetting costs with oil revenue</strong></p>
<p>Government officials stated that higher oil prices generate roughly BRL 10 billion in extra monthly revenue through increased tax receipts and royalties. This windfall covers most of the subsidy expenses. An executive order authorised BRL 6.6 billion in extraordinary spending, with BRL 5.6 billion directed to diesel subsidies and BRL 998 million supporting domestic gasoline production and imports.</p>

Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced on 15 September 2026 that the government intends to impose a 60% levy on revenue generated above normal levels by oil firms between 1 March 2026 and 31 December 2026. The...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Poland&#8217;s government has <a href="https://www.gov.pl/web/finanse/rzad-przyjal-projekt-ustawy-o-podatku-od-nadzwyczajnych-zyskow-osiagnietych-w-okresie-od-marca-do-grudnia-2026-r-ze-zbycia-paliw-cieklych" target="_blank" rel="noopener">moved</a> forward with plans for a windfall tax (excess profit tax) on oil companies&#8217; excess profits. Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced on 15 September 2026 that the government intends to impose a 60% levy on revenue generated above normal levels by oil firms between 1 March 2026 and 31 December 2026.</p>
<p>The tax will be paid through monthly advance payments, followed by a final annual tax return. The first advance payment, covering 1 March to 31 October 2026, is due in November 2026.</p>
<p>The tax revenue will help offset losses in VAT and excise tax receipts arising from government measures to contain fuel price increases.</p>
<p>The new regulations will enter into force on 1 November 2026.</p>
<p>The proposal marks the second attempt by the government to pass this legislation. President Karol Nawrocki rejected the bill in July and referred it to Poland&#8217;s Constitutional Tribunal for review. The tribunal has not yet issued a ruling on the constitutionality of the measure.</p>
<p>Despite the earlier rejection, the government cabinet approved the resubmitted bill on 15 September and prepared to send it to parliament once more. Tusk stated that the president should sign the law, arguing that oil companies and not Polish citizens should bear responsibility for rising fuel costs.</p>
<p>Poland introduced a fuel price cap programme from March to July that cost the state budget approximately PLN 4.7 billion. The government also reduced the VAT tax on fuel during the last two weeks of August as an additional measure.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/poland-to-tax-fuel-companies-windfall-profits-recover-government-spending/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, Poland’s government introduced emergency legislation imposing a temporary windfall tax on fuel companies that have earned unusually high profits amid Middle East-driven energy turmoil. Effective 1 August 2026, the measure aims to recover part of the state subsidies used to keep fuel prices affordable for consumers and businesses.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) issued new guidance on tax relief for farmers and ranchers across the country who sold or exchanged livestock due to severe drought on 15 September 2026. The extension allows affected producers to defer taxes on gains from forced livestock sales and take additional time to replace their animals. Who...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) <a href="https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/irs-announces-extension-of-tax-relief-for-farmers-and-ranchers-affected-by-drought-in-49-states-other-regions" target="_blank" rel="noopener">issued</a> new guidance on tax relief for farmers and ranchers across the country who sold or exchanged livestock due to severe drought on 15 September 2026. The extension allows affected producers to defer taxes on gains from forced livestock sales and take additional time to replace their animals.</p>
<p><strong>Who qualifies for the relief </strong></p>
<p>Eligible farmers and ranchers must meet two conditions: the livestock must have been held for draft, dairy, or breeding purposes, and the sale or exchange must have occurred in an area with a federal drought designation. Livestock raised for slaughter or held for sporting purposes do not qualify for this relief. Sales of poultry also fall outside the program&#8217;s scope.</p>
<p><strong>Timeline for livestock replacement</strong></p>
<p>The standard tax rule requires farmers to replace sold livestock within two years. Notice 2026-54 extends this replacement period to four years for eligible producers in drought-affected areas. If drought conditions continue, the IRS can extend the deadline further.</p>
<p>The extended deadline also includes a provision that gives farmers until the end of their first tax year after the first drought-free year to complete the replacement. For producers whose original four-year window was set to close at the end of 2026, this means they now have until the end of their next tax year to replace the livestock.</p>
<p><strong>Geographic scope and determination</strong></p>
<p>The relief covers 49 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and other designated areas. Qualification depends on whether the region received a federal drought designation during the 12 months ending 31 August 2026. The National Drought Mitigation Centre identifies regions experiencing exceptional, extreme, or severe drought between 1 September 2025 and 31 August 2026.</p>
<p>IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano stated that the extension provides support to farmers and ranchers facing ongoing drought hardship. Full details and examples appear in <a href="https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-06-82.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Notice 2006-82</a>, available on IRS.gov.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=88004</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[France plans to lower the exceptional corporate tax surcharge paid by very large companies in 2027, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said in a letter to business executives today, 16 September 2026. The measure would stop short of abolishing the surcharge, which was introduced in 2025 as a temporary levy and subsequently extended into 2026 under...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>France plans to lower the exceptional corporate tax surcharge paid by very large companies in 2027, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said in a letter to business executives today, 16 September 2026.</p>
<p>The measure would stop short of abolishing the surcharge, which was introduced in 2025 as a temporary levy and subsequently extended into 2026 under a Budget compromise. Lecornu said the 2027 Budget would not introduce new taxes, with the government seeking to support investment while addressing pressure on public finances.</p>
<p>The government is expected to present its Budget proposal in the coming weeks. It does not hold a majority in the lower house, and several opposition parties have already indicated that they would reject the proposal.</p>
<p><strong>Employee buyout incentives planned</strong></p>
<p>Lecornu also outlined plans for a new tax incentive aimed at encouraging business transfers, particularly acquisitions by employees.</p>
<p>Under the proposed &#8220;Papin Pact&#8221;, businesses taken over by their employees would receive accelerated depreciation for new equipment required for production. The planned support would provide enhanced treatment for small businesses.</p>
<p>The measure is intended to facilitate business succession, particularly where existing owners do not have family successors or an external buyer. The final design of the incentive will depend on the provisions included in the 2027 Budget.</p>
<p><strong>Review of business support</strong></p>
<p>The government also plans to examine existing state support for businesses. Lecornu said the review would assess whether such measures were delivering their intended objectives in areas including investment, innovation, decarbonisation and production in France.</p>
<p>Support considered ineffective would be subject to review, according to the letter.</p>
<p>The approach comes as the government seeks to reconcile measures aimed at encouraging economic activity with constraints arising from France&#8217;s public finances. Corporate taxation remains part of that balance, as changes to temporary levies can affect companies&#8217; longer-term investment and tax planning.</p>
<p><strong>Business groups welcome message</strong></p>
<p>Lecornu said France could not restore its public finances by weakening economic growth and therefore ruled out additional taxes in the 2027 Budget.</p>
<p>The commitment to reduce the exceptional surcharge, rather than remove it altogether, would leave part of the additional corporate tax burden in place while changing its level for 2027.</p>
<p>France&#8217;s largest employers&#8217; organisation, Medef, welcomed Lecornu&#8217;s message, saying that it was necessary to respond to concerns raised by business leaders.</p>
<p>The precise reduction in the surcharge and the final structure of the employee-buyout measures have yet to be determined. Their impact will therefore depend on the detailed Budget legislation presented by the government.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Colombia’s Congress approved the <a href="https://www.camara.gov.co/comisiones-economicas-aprobaron-el-monto-del-presupuesto-general-de-la-nacion-en-6349-billones/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">government’s 2027 spending budget</a> on 14 September 2026, setting expenditure at COP 634.9 trillion (USD 206.6 billion) as public finances faced a projected record fiscal deficit. The Senate and lower house backed the revised bill after an earlier proposal was returned for changes.</p>
<p>The revised budget incorporated additional funding requirements, including needs linked to the 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck Colombia in August. The final amount was also consistent with the revised draft previously assessed by Banco de la República, which put the budget at COP 634.9 trillion.</p>
<p>Finance Minister Miguel Gomez told Congress, “This is not the budget we would have liked to start our term with, but it is the budget we can afford given the current state of the national economy.”</p>
<p><strong>Fiscal deficit and debt</strong></p>
<p>The approved budget was based on a projected fiscal deficit of 9.4% of gross domestic product (GDP) for 2027. The gap was expected to require substantial additional public borrowing. Banco de la República had previously noted that the updated Financial Plan showed a 9.4% of GDP fiscal deficit and net debt of 66.2% of GDP, compared with the lower deficit projection contained in the 2026 Medium-Term Fiscal Framework.</p>
<p>The government planned to introduce a tax reform package known as the “Rescue Law”. Finance Minister Gomez said the package would seek to reduce public spending in 2027 and bring the fiscal deficit down to 7.2% of GDP, matching the level projected for 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Concerns over public finances</strong></p>
<p>Juan Carlos Ramirez, head of the Independent Committee for Fiscal Rule Management (CARF), told Reuters in late August that Colombia’s public finance position would become more critical if the government’s proposed 2027 budget was approved.</p>
<p>President Abelardo De La Espriella said on 13 September that the country’s fiscal situation was critical and attributed the deterioration to the previous administration led by Gustavo Petro. He alleged that corruption and misuse of resources had contributed to the situation, without providing evidence for those claims.</p>
<p>The exchange rate used in the source report was USD 1 = COP 3,072.27.</p>
<p>The approved budget followed a revised proposal that was COP 59.3 trillion higher than the initial draft submitted in July. Banco de la República said the revised amount represented a 14.2% increase from the COP 555.8 trillion appropriation for 2026, with COP 392.6 trillion allocated to operating expenditure, COP 87.0 trillion to investment and COP 155.4 trillion to debt service.</p>

The initiative, called the Productivity Mega Deduction, expands a previous tax incentive introduced in Budget 2025 and makes it permanent. Canada’s Budget 2025 introduces a Productivity Mega Deduction combining...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney <a href="https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/news-releases/2026/09/15/prime-minister-carney-introduces-new-productivity-mega-deduction" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> a new tax measure on 15 August 2026 aimed at strengthening Canada&#8217;s economy and drawing foreign investors to the country.</p>
<p>The initiative, called the <a href="https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/news-releases/2026/09/15/prime-minister-carney-introduces-new-productivity-mega-deduction" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Productivity Mega Deduction</a>, expands a previous tax incentive introduced in <a href="https://budget.canada.ca/2025/home-accueil-en.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Budget 2025</a> and makes it permanent.</p>
<p>Canada’s Budget 2025 introduces a Productivity Mega Deduction combining accelerated investment incentives and immediate expensing for productivity-enhancing assets, manufacturing equipment and buildings, clean-energy technologies, and eligible R&amp;D expenditures. The measures are intended to reduce investment costs, encourage private investment, and lower Canada’s marginal effective tax rate on new business investment to 13.2%.</p>
<p><strong>How the new tax break works</strong></p>
<p>The Mega Deduction allows businesses to immediately write off the cost of most new capital investments for tax purposes. The measure broadens eligible assets from roughly 15% to more than 65%,  including fibre-optic cable, mining property, oil and gas pipelines, software, research and development, computer equipment, aircraft, vehicles, patents, rail track, bridges, and roads.</p>
<p>The effect is immediate. Canada&#8217;s marginal effective tax rate on new business investment will drop from approximately 13% to 6.4%. This becomes the lowest rate among major economies worldwide and less than half the rate in the US, according to government statements.</p>
<p><strong>Investment targets and competition</strong></p>
<p>Carney has set a goal to attract CAD 1 trillion in new investment over five years through the tax incentive and other measures. The announcement came at the first Canada Investment Summit, which drew senior investors and executives from BlackRock, Blackstone, Apollo, JPMorgan, and sovereign wealth funds from Norway, Singapore, Qatar, and China.</p>
<p>The Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers said the measure closes a significant competitive gap with the US on capital expense deductions. CEO Lisa Baiton stated that the move positions Canada as one of the best places in the world to invest in energy.</p>
<p><strong>Other competitive changes</strong></p>
<p>The government is also streamlining regulatory processes for major projects. Carney emphasised that high standards do not require slow decision-making processes.</p>
<p>The government announced plans to seek private investment through long-term concessions to operate Canada&#8217;s four largest airports in Toronto, Montreal, Calgary, and Vancouver, while retaining ownership of underlying land and assets.</p>
<p>The policy marks a shift from the priorities of Carney&#8217;s predecessor, Justin Trudeau, who emphasised climate change, human rights, and Indigenous issues. Canadian labour groups have expressed opposition to airport privatisation, citing concerns about rising travel costs.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Australian Treasury has released draft legislation to overhaul the nation&#8217;s tax framework for emerging businesses and research ventures. The Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 5) Bill 2026: Better targeting the Research and Development Tax Incentive implements key elements of the tax reform package announced in the 2026–27 Budget, following recommendations from DISR&#8217;s Ambitious...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Australian Treasury has released <a href="https://consult.treasury.gov.au/c2026-792804" target="_blank" rel="noopener">draft legislation</a> to overhaul the nation&#8217;s tax framework for emerging businesses and research ventures. <a href="https://storage.googleapis.com/files-au-treasury/treasury/p/prj3e6ae3f30a89f03d68017/page/fil3f2427bb4d0f4658f9716_c2026_792804_explanatory_material.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">The Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 5) Bill 2026: Better targeting the Research and Development Tax Incentive</a> implements key elements of the tax reform package announced in the 2026–27 Budget, following recommendations from DISR&#8217;s Ambitious Australia Report (March 2026).</p>
<p>Applying to income years commencing on or after 1 July 2028, these amendments seek to balance broader access for growing firms with tighter focus and simplified administrative rules.</p>
<p>The reform also aims to focus government support on high-impact R&amp;D by increasing expenditure and turnover thresholds while narrowing the scope of eligible activities. Specifically, the new laws eliminate tax offsets for supporting activities, restricting benefits solely to primary research and development projects.</p>
<p>The Treasury opened consultation on the exposure draft materials on 11 September 2026, with feedback due by 28 September 2026.</p>
<p>The key aspects of the draft legislation are:</p>
<p><strong>Increased offset rates and adjusted incentive thresholds</strong></p>
<p>Australia’s proposed R&amp;D tax incentive changes would increase all offset rates by 4.5%, raising the highest rate to 23%, the lower non-refundable rate to 13%, and the higher non-refundable rate to 21%.</p>
<p>The R&amp;D intensity threshold for the higher premium rate would fall from 2% to 1.5%, while the aggregated turnover threshold for the refundable offset would rise from AUD 20 million to AUD 50 million.</p>
<p>The minimum eligible expenditure threshold would increase from AUD 20,000 to AUD 50,000, with Cooperative Research Centres and Research Service Providers exempt, and the maximum expenditure cap would rise from AUD 150 million to AUD 200 million.</p>
<p><strong>Restricting the refundable offset to early-stage entities (with medtech extension)</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>10-year age limit for general entities:</strong> Entities can access the refundable offset only if the income year falls on or before the 10th anniversary of the earlier of starting an enterprise or first registering for the R&amp;DTI.</li>
<li><strong>15-year extension for therapeutic goods:</strong> Biotech and medtech companies undertaking R&amp;D where the dominant purpose is generating new knowledge regarding therapeutic goods or therapeutic use can access the refundable offset for up to 15 years, provided they registered for R&amp;D activities within their first 10 income years.</li>
<li><strong>Role of Industry Innovation and Science Australia (the Board):</strong> The Board can issue binding findings on whether R&amp;D activities meet the dominant purpose test for therapeutic goods [10, 22, 24–28].</li>
<li><strong>Transition for mature entities:</strong> Companies older than 10 years (or 15 years for therapeutic goods) with aggregated turnover under AUD 50 million are transitioned to a non-refundable offset at the highest tax offset rate (23% above the corporate tax rate).</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Focus on core activities and removal of supporting R&amp;D</strong></p>
<p>Supporting R&amp;D expenditure that does not independently meet the substantive criteria for an R&amp;D activity would no longer qualify for the tax offset. The term “core R&amp;D activities” would also be replaced with “R&amp;D activities,” requiring previously supporting activities to satisfy the relevant criteria in their own right.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Ukraine&#8217;s Parliamentary (Verkhovna Rada) Committee on Finance, Tax and Customs Policy has recommended that parliament adopt revised draft laws introducing new VAT rules for small international postal and express shipments purchased through online marketplaces.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Government of Russia has extended the export customs duty on oilseed flax leaving the country for destinations outside the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), under a decree adopted in Moscow on 25 August 2026.</p>
<p><a href="http://publication.pravo.gov.ru/document/0001202608260026" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Decree No. 1073</a>, signed by Chairman of the Government Mikhail Mishustin, amends an earlier decree, No. 2068 of 27 November 2021, which sets export customs duty rates on goods leaving the Russian Federation beyond the EAEU customs territory. 										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UK’s HM Revenue &amp; Customs (HMRC) has updated the rules for <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/revenue-and-customs-brief-8-2026-uk-vat-refunds-for-non-uk-businesses-in-a-vat-group/uk-vat-refunds-for-non-uk-businesses-in-a-vat-group" target="_blank" rel="noopener">UK VAT refunds claimed by non-UK businesses</a> that are members of VAT groups, according to a policy paper issued on 8 September 2026.</p>
<p>Under the revised rules, non-UK VAT group members must submit their own claims for UK VAT they incurred. HMRC will no longer accept claims from a VAT group’s representative member unless that member incurred the VAT.</p>
<p>The overseas VAT refund scheme is available to non-UK businesses that meet certain conditions. Businesses must not be registered, liable or eligible to register for UK VAT, must not have a business establishment or other fixed establishment in the UK, and must not make supplies in the UK, subject to specified exceptions.</p>
<p>Before 1 January 2021, different rules applied to businesses belonging to VAT groups depending on whether they were established in the EU or outside the EU. From that date, all non-UK VAT group members were required to submit claims through the representative member. HMRC said this had resulted in some eligible businesses being unable to recover UK VAT and described the outcome as an unintended consequence of the UK’s exit from the EU.</p>
<p>For the 2025 to 2026 prescribed year, covering 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026, HMRC will accept claims from either the individual VAT group member that incurred the VAT or the representative member. Claims for this period must be submitted by 31 December 2026.</p>
<p>HMRC will also reconsider claims for VAT incurred from 1 January 2021 that were rejected because the representative member did not submit the claim, provided the VAT was not included in a later claim by the representative member.</p>
<p>Businesses seeking reconsideration must contact HMRC’s Overseas Repayments Unit by email using the subject line ‘Reconsideration of a previously refused VAT group claim’. Requests must include the business name, unique reference and claim number, claim period and value, decision letter date, the names of all VAT group members during the claim period, and confirmation that the VAT was not included in a later claim.</p>
<p>Requests for reconsideration must be submitted by 31 August 2027. HMRC said requests received after that date would not be considered.</p>

		<title>Australia: Federal Court upholds AUD 173.3m tax benefit adjustment against Hilton</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/australia-federal-court-upholds-aud-173-3m-tax-benefit-adjustment-against-hilton/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=australia-federal-court-upholds-aud-173-3m-tax-benefit-adjustment-against-hilton</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Mohammed Al Mamun]]></dc:creator>

				<category><![CDATA[Loans and guarantee fees]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[Australia]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=87938</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The Federal Court of Australia rejected Hilton International Australia Pty Ltd&#8217;s challenge to the Commissioner of Taxation on 9 September 2026 (Case: Hilton International Australia Pty Ltd v Commissioner of Taxation (No 2) [2026] FCA 1325). Justice Younan upheld the Commissioner&#8217;s decision to add AUD 173,300,032.00 to the company&#8217;s assessable income for the 2015 income...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Federal Court of Australia rejected Hilton International Australia Pty Ltd&#8217;s challenge to the Commissioner of Taxation on 9 September 2026 (Case: <a href="https://www.judgments.fedcourt.gov.au/judgments/Judgments/fca/single/2026/2026fca1325" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Hilton International Australia Pty Ltd v Commissioner of Taxation (No 2) [2026] FCA 1325</a>). Justice Younan upheld the Commissioner&#8217;s decision to add AUD 173,300,032.00 to the company&#8217;s assessable income for the 2015 income year under Part IVA of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (ITAA 1936).</p>
<p><strong>The restructuring sequence</strong></p>
<p>Hilton group entities purchased the Sydney Hilton hotel at 488 George Street in 2000 for approximately AUD 180 million. Three subsidiaries held ownership: Admiral I Pty Ltd (70%), Admiral II Pty Ltd (16.25%), and Admiral III Pty Ltd (13.75%), operating under Admiral Investments Pty Ltd.</p>
<p>On 29 June 2014, the group formed a Multiple Entry Consolidated (MEC) group under Part 3-90 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (ITAA 1997), with Hilton International Australia Pty Ltd (HIA) as head company. On 24 June 2014, the group incorporated Admiral Holdings Australia Pty Ltd (AHA) as an eligible tier-1 company.</p>
<p>On 1 March 2015, AHA acquired the hotel&#8217;s freehold and operational assets for AUD 425 million, satisfied by an intercompany loan note. On 29 April 2015, Hilton Worldwide International Luxembourg Holding S.à.r.l. (HWIH) agreed to sell AHA to Glory Property III Investment Pty Ltd, completing on 1 July 2015. Glory Property III paid AUD 29,021,785.50 for the AHA share and AUD 420 million to HIA to discharge the intercompany loan, totalling approximately AUD 442 million.</p>
<p><strong>Tax dispute and court decision</strong></p>
<p>Under Subdivision 719-K of the ITAA 1997, AHA&#8217;s tax cost base was reset upon leaving the MEC group. HWIH reported a net capital gain of only AUD 21,010,283, while HIA recorded zero taxable gain. The Commissioner applied section 177F, determining HIA obtained a tax benefit.</p>
<p>HIA argued that Part IVA requires identifying a single most reasonable alternative transaction. The Federal Court rejected this interpretation. Justice Younan held that section 177CB(3) permits multiple reasonable alternatives. The Court examined four possible structures. Three satisfied reasonableness and each generated the same AUD 173,300,032.00 taxable gain to HIA.</p>
<p>The first alternative involved direct asset sale to Glory Property III for approximately AUD 449 million, producing AUD 173,300,032.50 taxable gain to HIA. The Court accepted this as reasonable and reflective of standard Australian hotel market practice.</p>
<p>The second alternative examined a share sale of Admiral Investments Pty Ltd for approximately AUD 449 million, generating the same AUD 173,300,032.50 gain to HIA. The Court found it reasonable, though noted AIPL&#8217;s 14-year history made it less preferred.</p>
<p>The third postulate involved a new entity acquiring assets and selling shares for approximately AUD 449 million, also producing AUD 173,300,032.50 to HIA. The Court accepted this alternative as simpler and debt-free.</p>
<p>HIA&#8217;s proposed alternative involved converting debt to AUD 420 million share capital before sale, resulting in zero gain to HIA but AUD 113 million to HWIH. The Court rejected this entirely, holding that an alternative postulate cannot itself constitute a Part IVA tax-avoidance scheme. Using such a scheme as comparison would create circular reasoning and defeat section 177C&#8217;s purpose.</p>
<p><strong>Legal precedent and dominant purpose</strong></p>
<p>The Federal Court applied Commissioner of Taxation v PepsiCo Inc [2025] HCA 30. The High Court established that alternative postulates must represent reliable predictions grounded in commercial and economic reality. This decision clarifies that while PepsiCo sets the reasonableness threshold, it does not mandate a single most reasonable option when multiple alternatives satisfy that threshold.</p>
<p>The Court determined the scheme&#8217;s dominant purpose was obtaining the tax benefit. Although the transaction delivered genuine commercial benefits including favourable sale terms and 50-year management rights, these outcomes did not explain the specific structure chosen. Investment Committee records referenced minimising &#8220;tax leakage&#8221; and maximising proceeds to reduce corporate debt. Hilton Group&#8217;s strong bargaining position secured the high price and favourable terms, not the tax-driven structure.</p>
<p><strong>Final ruling</strong></p>
<p>The Federal Court dismissed Hilton International Australia Pty Ltd&#8217;s appeal with costs. The Commissioner&#8217;s application of section 177F to include AUD 173,300,032.00 in HIA&#8217;s assessable income for the 2015 income year stands upheld.</p>
<p>The judgment establishes that Part IVA analysis permits multiple reasonable alternative postulates without requiring identification of a single preferred counterfactual. However, alternative postulates themselves must not constitute tax-avoidance schemes, and the dominant purpose test remains central to Part IVA application.</p>
<p>Hilton International Australia Pty Ltd retains the option to pursue an appeal to the Full Federal Court.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR), through the Trade Policy Staff Committee (TPSC), <a href="https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/september/ustr-seeks-public-comment-foreign-trade-barriers-2027-national-trade-estimate-report" target="_blank" rel="noopener">invited</a> public comment on 14 September 2026 on foreign barriers to US exports of goods and services and US foreign direct investment for inclusion in the 2027 National Trade Estimate Report.</p>
<p>The deadline to submit comments is 29 October 2026.</p>
<p>The submissions will help identify issues for inclusion in the annual National Trade Estimate Report on Foreign Trade Barriers. USTR will also use the comments in its annual assessment of the operation and effectiveness of US trade agreements covering telecommunications products and services.</p>
<p>The report inventories major obstacles to US exports of goods, services, agricultural products, and intellectual property. It also covers barriers to foreign investment and digital commerce. USTR uses this information to negotiate with trading partners and enforce US trade laws.</p>
<p><strong>What counts as a trade barrier</strong></p>
<p>USTR identifies 15 categories of barriers it wants to hear about. These include import tariffs, import restrictions, and customs problems. They also cover technical standards that unfairly block US goods, food safety rules that lack scientific support, and government procurement that excludes American companies.</p>
<p>Intellectual property protection matters too. Countries that fail to protect patents, copyrights, trademarks, or trade secrets create problems for US businesses. Service sector barriers include foreign ownership limits, discriminatory licensing, and restrictions on data movement.</p>
<p>Investment barriers come next. These include caps on foreign ownership, local content requirements, joint venture mandates, and technology transfer demands. USTR also tracks subsidies that help foreign competitors, state-owned enterprises that operate outside market forces, and labour practices that suppress wages or violate workers&#8217; rights.</p>
<p>Environmental concerns round out the list. USTR seeks information on weak enforcement of environmental laws, illegal logging and wildlife trade, and practices that allow countries to undercut environmental standards.</p>
<p><strong>60 trading partners in focus</strong></p>
<p>The report covers trade barriers in more than 60 countries and regional bodies. The list includes major economies like China, India, Japan, and the European Union, alongside emerging markets in Southeast Asia, Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East.</p>
<p>The 2026 National Trade Estimate Report is available on the USTR website. USTR plans to use public comments to decide which barriers merit inclusion in the report.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[Belgium&#8217;s Advance Tax Rulings Service (SDA) has issued Newsflash SDA 2026/05, confirming that the country&#8217;s favourable copyright tax regime has been extended to computer programs with effect from 1 January 2026. The extension follows the Law of 15 July 2026 on Personal Income Tax Reforms, which reversed the earlier exclusion of software royalties introduced under...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Belgium&#8217;s Advance Tax Rulings Service (SDA) has issued <a href="https://www.ruling.be/fr/telechargements/regime-fiscal-des-droits-dauteur-et-programmes-informatiques" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Newsflash SDA 2026/05</a>, confirming that the country&#8217;s favourable copyright tax regime has been extended to computer programs with effect from 1 January 2026.</p>
<p>The extension follows the Law of 15 July 2026 on Personal Income Tax Reforms, which reversed the earlier exclusion of software royalties introduced under the Programme Law of 26 December 2022.</p>
<p><strong>Tax benefit and threshold</strong></p>
<p>Under the regime, copyright royalties are taxed at a flat withholding rate of 15% rather than at standard progressive income tax rates, provided the annual amount does not exceed a set threshold, fixed at EUR 77,220 for income year 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Surge in ruling requests</strong></p>
<p>The SDA said it had seen a sharp rise in ruling requests from the IT sector since the extension was announced. Although the requests relate to a specific sector, the authority said it must continue to handle each one individually and assess it in accordance with the law, despite its limited resources.</p>
<p><strong>Conditions for the regime to apply</strong></p>
<p>The SDA stressed that each application is assessed against the conditions set out in Article 17, § 1, 5° of the 1992 Income Tax Code (CIR 92). This assessment covers the legal characterisation of the rights involved, the originality of the underlying work, the terms of assignment or licensing, how the rights are actually exploited, and the economic valuation attached to the copyright remuneration claimed.</p>
<p>The authority made clear that the regime&#8217;s extension to software does not mean all software-related income automatically qualifies for the reduced rate, nor that valuation approaches used in other sectors can simply be carried over without independent review. Each case, it said, will continue to be judged on its own facts and on whether the proposed valuation reflects the genuine economic reality of the rights being exploited.</p>
<p><strong>Retroactive application of rulings</strong></p>
<p>To give taxpayers certainty while these new requests are examined, the SDA confirmed that advance rulings issued up to 30 June 2027 may apply retroactively to copyright remuneration granted from 1 January 2026, so long as all statutory conditions are satisfied.</p>
<p><strong>Next steps</strong></p>
<p>The SDA said it would continue reviewing the matter in light of ongoing legislative developments and the practical issues raised by cases submitted to it, with a view to ensuring consistent application of the copyright regime to computer programs.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Canada’s Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne <a href="https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/news/2026/09/greater-tax-certainty-for-major-investments-in-canada.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> on 14 September 2026 that the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) will fast-track advance income tax ruling requests for investments worth CAD 1 billion or more. The priority system began immediately and affects all applications submitted through the Advance Income Tax Rulings (AITR) programme.</p>
<p><strong>What the new priority system does</strong></p>
<p>Investors can now receive binding tax decisions from the CRA before committing capital to major projects. By getting confirmation on how Canadian income tax law applies to a proposed deal, investors gain the clarity needed to move forward with confidence. This reduces financial risk and helps companies make better financing decisions.</p>
<p>Large investors seeking these fast-tracked rulings must demonstrate investments of CAD 1 billion or higher. All other requests continue to follow the standard 90-business-day timeline.</p>
<p><strong>Programme details and performance</strong></p>
<p>The Advance Income Tax Rulings programme has provided binding tax guidance to Canadian businesses for more than 50 years. The CRA maintains a 90-business-day service standard for all ruling requests, whether prioritised or standard</p>
<p>Recent performance data shows the programme delivers results on time. Between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2025, the CRA issued 91% of rulings within the 90-business-day window or agreed-upon completion dates.</p>
<p><strong>Why this matters</strong></p>
<p>The announcement comes ahead of Canada&#8217;s Investment Summit and builds on measures outlined in the <a href="https://regfollower.com/canada-spring-economic-update-2026-receives-royal-assent/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">2026 Spring Economic Update</a>. 					<description><![CDATA[Kazakhstan&#8217;s Ministry of National Economy has opened a public consultation on a draft law proposing amendments and additions to the country&#8217;s Tax Code. The draft was published on the Open NPAs portal on 3 September 2026 and reflected feedback from government bodies, working groups and the business community. The proposals cover investment incentives, digital assets,...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Kazakhstan&#8217;s Ministry of National Economy has opened a <a href="https://legalacts.egov.kz/npa/view?id=15902818" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation</a> on a draft law proposing amendments and additions to the country&#8217;s Tax Code. The draft was published on the Open NPAs portal on 3 September 2026 and reflected feedback from government bodies, working groups and the business community.</p>
<p>The proposals cover investment incentives, digital assets, VAT, tax administration, special tax regimes and sector-specific taxation. The draft law is generally scheduled to come into force on 1 January 2027, with certain provisions taking effect later.</p>
<p>The proposed amendments are open for public comments until 25 September 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Investment and tax incentives</strong></p>
<p>The draft would restore tax incentives for priority investment projects and entities that have concluded Investment Agreements. It would also introduce a specific tax regime for &#8220;Altyn Visa&#8221; holders and their family members and remove the 7,000 MRP fee previously charged to AIFC investors for documents confirming RK tax residency.</p>
<p>Businesses would also deduct 150% of actual expenses incurred for goods labelling and marking. Investment Agreements and Investment Contracts would receive a two-year VAT exemption on imported raw materials and inputs, starting from the commissioning of fixed assets.</p>
<p>For Investment Agreements, the proposed incentives would include a 100% CIT reduction for up to 10 years, a 0 coefficient for land tax for up to 10 years and a 0% property tax rate for up to eight years.</p>
<p><strong>Digital assets and digital taxation</strong></p>
<p>Individuals would be exempt from PIT on income from digital asset transactions conducted through licensed Kazakhstani digital asset service providers from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2028.</p>
<p>The draft would also provide an amnesty for taxpayers transferring digital assets from unlicensed platforms to licensed providers before 31 December 2028, with related tax arrears, penalties and administrative fines written off.</p>
<p>A mechanism would allow excess VAT to be returned without a tax audit within 10 working days where transactions and refunds were processed using the digital tenge.</p>
<p><strong>VAT and excise measures</strong></p>
<p>The draft would gradually reduce the additional VAT offset coefficient for agricultural producers, starting at 80% in 2026–2027 and reaching 10% in 2033–2034, with the mechanism due to be eliminated by 2035.</p>
<p>It would also introduce hookah mixtures as a new excise product category and set progressive excise rates for spirits, wines, tobacco products and hookah mixtures for 2026–2030.</p>
<p><strong>Tax administration and online platforms</strong></p>
<p>The proposals would tighten the special tax regime for self-employed individuals by preventing founders of LLPs and shareholders of JSCs from using the regime.</p>
<p>Internet platform operators and banks would act as tax agents for self-employed individuals, withholding and transferring individual income tax and social payments. They would also be required to integrate with a special mobile application for issuing digital receipts.</p>
<p>Tax authorities would gain powers to suspend sales through internet resources or online platforms where businesses failed to address tax violation notifications or camera control discrepancies within three working days.</p>
<p>The draft would also clarify Electronic Invoice (ESF) requirements, non-resident income from financial loans and VAT offsets relating to payments made on behalf of non-residents.</p>
<p><strong>Sector-specific measures</strong></p>
<p>For the oil sector, the draft would revise the world market oil price calculation using North Sea Dated (Brent Dtd) quotations and price spreads or premiums relative to KEBCO.</p>
<p>Reduced MET rates would remain available for certain low-rent, high-viscosity, water-flooded, low-yield and depleted oil fields, subject to annual recalculation where profitability exceeded specified thresholds.</p>
<p>The proposals would also establish special amortisation rules for geology, exploration and preparatory costs related to complex onshore and offshore hydrocarbon projects, using conditional multipliers of 1.5 and 2.0 respectively.</p>
<p><strong>Relief for micro and small businesses</strong></p>
<p>The draft would provide several measures for micro and small businesses, including protection from camera control and tax audits for certain historical filings and relief from administrative penalties relating to earlier tax registration and filing failures.</p>
<p>It would also provide for the write-off of penalties and administrative fines where qualifying businesses had settled specified principal tax debts during the relevant period, while penalty accruals on unpaid tax obligations would be halted during 2026.</p>

<p><strong>What changed</strong></p>
<p>The original GloBE Information Return, released in January 2025, would have required American companies to report financial details for operations in every country where they do business. This served the OECD Pillar Two framework, a global minimum tax deal from 145 countries in the OECD and G20 group.</p>
<p>In January 2026, the Treasury negotiated a separate agreement with these countries. Under this &#8220;side-by-side&#8221; arrangement, US companies can skip the foreign reporting required by Pillar Two rules. They remain subject only to American tax law instead.</p>
<p><strong>How it works</strong></p>
<p>The revised return lets American companies elect the side-by-side safe harbour. This exemption removes two specific Pillar Two obligations: the Income Inclusion Rule and the Undertaxed Profits Rule.</p>
<p>The new framework also protects valuable American tax benefits. Companies can apply the Research and Development tax credit without facing Pillar Two adjustments. Foreign companies operating in the US receive the same R&amp;D credit protection.</p>
<p>The revised return serves as a standardised reporting tool for local minimum taxes in other countries. Information companies provide for one country&#8217;s tax rules stays within that country and is not shared internationally.</p>
<p><strong>Next steps</strong></p>
<p>The Treasury indicated that countries are adopting the side-by-side safe harbour through their own legislative processes. The department plans to continue coordinating with international partners as the framework is implemented.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Italian Revenue Agency has issued a <a href="https://www.fiscooggi.it/portale/-/dichiarazione-integrativa-ammessa-ma-i-nuovi-dati-devono-essere-provati" target="_blank" rel="noopener">release</a> on 14 September 2026 regarding a recent decision by the Italian Supreme Court of Cassation (Ordinance No. 24863/2026) concerning the correction of VAT reporting errors. The ruling confirms that taxpayers may file an amended VAT return to correct mistakes, even after receiving a formal deficiency notice from the tax authority.</p>
<p>A company filing a supplementary VAT return that eliminates a tax debt cannot rely solely on the amended declaration itself. The taxpayer must demonstrate that the corrected figures are accurate and explain why the original return contained different data. This is the holding of Italy&#8217;s Supreme Court Order No. 24863/2026, which upheld a EUR 70,000 assessment after an automated VAT check.</p>
<p>The case involved a 2017 VAT return that the company originally submitted on 28 April 2018. Following an automated review under Article 54 bis of Presidential Decree no. 633/1972, tax authorities identified an unpaid tax of approximately 70,000 euros.</p>
<p>The company challenged the assessment. It submitted a supplementary tax return on 25 November 2021, three weeks after receiving the irregularity notice on 8 November 2021. The supplementary return eliminated the tax liability, claiming taxable transactions had fallen from over EUR 600,000 to roughly half that amount.</p>
<p><strong>Evidence fell short of the court&#8217;s standard</strong></p>
<p>The appeal court recognised that the supplementary return was timely and legally valid, even though it arrived after the irregularity notice. However, the court found the company&#8217;s evidence insufficient.</p>
<p>The company produced VAT records and periodic settlement statements but never explained why the original return contained such different figures. The Spesometro data from 2017, which logs purchase and sales transactions, matched the original figures rather than the supplementary ones. This mismatch raised questions about the reliability of the correction.</p>
<p><strong>Supreme Court rejects appeal</strong></p>
<p>The Supreme Court sided with the appeal court. It clarified that the lower court had not rejected the supplementary return as invalid. Rather, the court had examined whether the tax debt had truly been eliminated based on the evidence presented and concluded it had not.</p>
<p>Tax proceedings, the Supreme Court stated, operate on a &#8220;merits appeal&#8221; basis. Judges can verify both the formal legitimacy of tax decisions and the factual accuracy of the underlying figures. The company&#8217;s failure to account for the radical swing in declared transactions constituted insufficient proof of accuracy. The court therefore confirmed the assessment and ordered the taxpayer to cover legal costs.</p>
