										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Italy’s Revenue Agency <a href="https://www.fiscooggi.it/portale/-/fusione-tra-ets-e-societ%C3%A0-semplice-s%C3%AC-alle-indirette-fisse-e-niente-iva" target="_blank" rel="noopener">confirmed</a> on 11 September 2026 that a foundation can merge with a simple agricultural partnership while avoiding capital gains tax, VAT, and most other direct taxes. The ruling, contained in <a href="https://www.agenziaentrate.gov.it/portale/documents/20143/10289089/Risposta+n.+171_2026.pdf/f3dc699d-cdcc-49fe-781c-72b20843c4ab?t=1789127058519" target="_blank" rel="noopener">response no. 171</a>, applies to transactions where the transferred assets remain outside the foundation&#8217;s commercial activities.</p>
<p><strong>How the merger worked</strong></p>
<p>A foundation registered with Runts (the national registry for Third Sector organisations) acquired full ownership of an agricultural partnership. The partnership had originally received a controlling interest from a German company.</p>
<p>Over time, the partnership leased its entire farm to another agricultural company and stopped conducting independent business. In 2025, the foundation completed the merger by incorporation, transferring all farm properties directly to the foundation&#8217;s assets.</p>
<p>The foundation intended to use these holdings to pursue its stated mission of protecting and enhancing cultural and landscape heritage.</p>
<p><strong>No tax on the transferred assets</strong></p>
<p>The Revenue Agency determined that no capital gains tax applies to the transfer. Under Article 172 and Article 174 of the TUIR (the national income tax code), mergers between companies normally generate no taxable gains.</p>
<p>This protection extends to non-commercial entities when the transferred assets stay outside their commercial activities. Since the foundation declared that all acquired property would be used exclusively for its institutional, non-commercial work, the tax authorities concluded that any gains remain non-taxable. The agricultural holding continues to operate under its existing lease agreement.</p>
<p><strong>VAT is not triggered</strong></p>
<p>The simple partnership no longer qualified for VAT purposes. It had already leased the entire farm and ceased all direct agricultural activity. The partnership had also excluded rental income from the VAT scope and abandoned its right to deduct input tax. Because the partnership lacked the status required for VAT application at the time of merger, the transaction falls completely outside VAT rules. This outcome occurred under Article 2, paragraph 3, letter f) of Presidential Decree No. 633/1972.</p>
<p><strong>Fixed rates apply to indirect taxes</strong></p>
<p>The most favourable element came from Article 82, paragraph 3 of the Third Sector Code (Legislative Decree No. 117/2017). This provision grants fixed rates for registration tax, mortgage tax, and land registry tax on mergers conducted by Third Sector entities.</p>
<p>Although one merging party was a simple partnership rather than a Third Sector organisation, the foundation retained its registered status throughout. Consequently, the merger deed qualifies for the fixed-rate treatment designed to ensure tax neutrality for Third Sector reorganisations.</p>
<p>The ruling demonstrates that when transferred assets continue serving purposes aligned with a foundation&#8217;s mission and do not enter commercial operations, the transaction achieves substantial tax neutrality: no capital gains taxation, no VAT, and application of fixed indirect tax rates.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Netherlands government has issued Letter No. 2026-0000288216 of 11 September 2026, detailing the strategic implementation framework for electronic invoicing (e-invoicing) and digital reporting in the Netherlands. This policy transposes Council Directive (EU) 2025/516 under the EU&#8217;s VAT in the Digital Age (ViDA) package into national tax legislation. To combat tax fraud and modernise the...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Netherlands government has issued <a href="https://open.overheid.nl/overheid/openbaarmakingen/api/v0/attachment/71c66f1c-c2a4-4efb-a4c3-80956ddb04f0" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Letter No. 2026-0000288216 </a>of 11 September 2026, detailing the strategic implementation framework for electronic invoicing (e-invoicing) and digital reporting in the Netherlands. This policy transposes <a href="https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202500516" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Council Directive (EU) 2025/516 under the EU&#8217;s VAT in the Digital Age (ViDA) package</a> into national tax legislation.</p>
<p>To combat tax fraud and modernise the economy, the government mandates electronic invoicing for domestic business transactions starting in July 2030, followed by a digital reporting requirement in July 2031. While these measures aim to reduce administrative burdens and lower costs for businesses, the cabinet acknowledges significant concerns regarding data privacy and sensitive information storage.</p>
<p><strong>Phased timelines and implementation scope</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Mandatory domestic B2B e-invoicing (1 July 2030):</strong> Extending beyond ViDA&#8217;s baseline mandate for cross-border trade, all domestic business-to-business (B2B) transactions will require structured electronic invoicing starting 1 July 2030.</li>
<li><strong>Intra-EU digital reporting (1 July 2030):</strong> Mandatory digital reporting for intra-Community supplies and acquisitions will take effect on 1 July 2030.</li>
<li><strong>Domestic B2B digital reporting (1 July 2031):</strong> Transaction-level digital reporting to the Dutch Tax Administration for domestic B2B transactions will apply from 1 July 2031.</li>
<li><strong>Near real-time issuance window:</strong> E-invoices must be issued within 10 days following the supply of goods or services, replacing periodic aggregated reporting (such as monthly/quarterly ICP declarations) with near real-time, invoice-by-invoice transaction transmission.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Standardisation and policy choices</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Single EU standard (EN 16931):</strong> To avoid national fragmentation, the Netherlands will exclusively adopt the European invoicing standard (EN 16931 / Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2017/1870) without creating additional domestic standards or extensions.</li>
<li><strong>EU data minimisation model:</strong> The domestic digital reporting dataset will be restricted to a limited subset of invoice data fields, aligning directly with the EU-level data minimisation standard to lower administrative compliance costs and preserve cross-border interoperability.</li>
<li><strong>Micro-enterprises &amp; small business exemption:</strong> No separate revenue threshold or special regime will be created for micro-enterprises. Businesses under the existing Small Businesses Scheme (Kleineondernemersregeling &#8211; KOR) remain exempt from domestic e-invoicing requirements.</li>
<li><strong>Invoicing exceptions:</strong> The government will maintain existing invoicing exemptions where possible and avoid creating new domestic exceptions.</li>
<li><strong>Exchange infrastructure:</strong> Following an EY evaluation recommending the Peppol network (already used for Dutch B2G e-invoicing), the government is evaluating Peppol alongside emerging European standards like the European Business Wallet.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Tax administration goals and business impact</strong></p>
<p>Digitisation is expected to strengthen VAT fraud detection, automate taxpayer services such as error checks and pre-filled returns, and significantly reduce invoice processing costs. Businesses could save 55–70% per invoice, averaging around EUR 5–EUR 6 per sent invoice and EUR 8 per received invoice.</p>
<p><strong>Privacy safeguards and data security</strong></p>
<p>The proposed legislation includes safeguards to protect taxpayer data, including review by the Dutch Data Protection Authority and a Data Protection Impact Assessment. It will also require role-based access, comprehensive data-query logging, active monitoring, and testing of risk models for algorithmic bias. National data will be retained for a maximum of 10 years, while the Tax Administration aims to strengthen digital sovereignty and reduce reliance on non-EU technology providers.</p>
<p><strong>Parliamentary and legislative roadmap</strong></p>
<p>The legislative process is expected to begin with a public consultation in late 2026, followed by submission of the draft bill before the parliamentary summer recess in mid-2027.</p>
<p>Parliamentary approval is targeted before 1 July 2028, providing businesses and software vendors with a two-year preparation and testing period before the legislation takes effect on 1 July 2030.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/netherlands-considers-extending-e-invoicing-to-domestic-b2b-transactions-under-eu-vida-reforms/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier,</a> the Dutch government revealed that it is considering extending mandatory e-invoicing to domestic B2B transactions alongside EU cross-border transactions under the new European VAT rules and released a cover letter on 10 March 2026 accompanying its ViDA e-invoicing and digital reporting report.</p>

New tax rate and scope The authorities set the individual income tax rate at 20% on...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>China’s Ministry of Finance, the State Taxation Administration, and the China Securities Regulatory Commission released<a href="https://fgk.chinatax.gov.cn/zcfgk/c102416/c5252027/content.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Announcement No. 26 </a>on 28 August 2026 to establish uniform rules for taxing the sale of restricted shares by individual shareholders of listed companies.</p>
<p><strong>New tax rate and scope</strong></p>
<p>The authorities set the individual income tax rate at 20% on gains from transferring restricted shares. This rate applies to the original restricted shares covered under prior guidance (Cai Shui [2009] No. 167), along with bonus shares and shares sold after restrictions lift and registered following the announcement&#8217;s effective date.</p>
<p>When companies issue bonus shares, split shares, or consolidate shares, the securities registration and settlement company must adjust the cost basis of restricted shares proportionally.</p>
<p><strong>Requirements for listed companies</strong></p>
<p>Listed companies trading on the Shanghai Stock Exchange or Shenzhen Stock Exchange must provide the original cost information for restricted shares when applying for initial registration. They must also submit verification reports from accounting firms or tax firms. This requirement stems from earlier guidance (Cai Shui [2011] No. 108).</p>
<p>Companies that fail to submit cost documentation face consequences when shareholders sell shares. Securities institutions will withhold tax at the full 20% rate on the entire transfer income. Shareholders can then file a final tax settlement by 30 June following the year of sale to claim refunds or pay any shortfall.</p>
<p>For companies that registered shares before the announcement but never declared original costs, securities institutions may withhold 15% as a prepayment based on transfer proceeds. Shareholders remain required to file their final settlement.</p>
<p><strong>Settlement process</strong></p>
<p>Shareholders bear responsibility for filing liquidation declarations with tax authorities if their calculated tax differs from the withheld amount. The 30 June deadline applies to the year after the share sale occurs. Supporting documentation of original costs and expenses must accompany all settlement filings.</p>
<p><strong>Coverage of other markets</strong></p>
<p>The rules extend to original shares sold on the National Equities Exchange and Quotations and the Beijing Stock Exchange. For shares that complete initial registration before the announcement, then list publicly on the Beijing Stock Exchange afterwards, securities institutions may withhold 15% in advance. These shareholders must also complete liquidation declarations under the same process.</p>
<p>The announcement takes effect from its publication date, superseding any conflicting prior regulations.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Belgian Minister of Finance has submitted draft legislative bill DOC 56 1718/001 to the Parliament on 10 September 2026. 										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Belgian Minister of Finance has submitted draft legislative bill <a href="https://www.dekamer.be/flwb/pdf/56/1718/56K1718001.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">DOC 56 1718/001</a> to the Parliament on 10 September 2026. This bill partially transposes <a href="https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202500516" target="_blank" rel="noopener">EU Directive 2025/516</a> (adopted on 11 March 2025), which forms a core element of the European Union’s VAT in the Digital Age (ViDA) framework.</p>
<p>While the overall ViDA framework rests on three pillars—e-invoicing and digital reporting, single VAT registration/One-Stop-Shop (OSS) expansions, and platform economy rules—this specific proposal implements Article 2 (effective 1 January 2027) and Article 4 (effective 1 July 2029) of the Directive to modernise cross-border B2C e-commerce and logistics rules</p>
<p>The key provisions of the proposal are summarised below:</p>
<p><strong>End of the consignment stock regime</strong></p>
<p>The current consignment stock system allows businesses to move goods to other EU Member States without immediate VAT registration in the destination country. Ownership must transfer within 12 months under existing rules.</p>
<p>Suppliers can initiate new transfers only until 30 June 2028. After that date, the One-Stop-Shop (OSS) framework under Articles 369quinvicies bis to 369quinvicies duodecies of Directive 2006/112/EC takes over. Goods already transferred by 30 June 2028 remain subject to old rules for 12 months, creating a run-off period ending 30 June 2029.</p>
<p>Once the run-off expires on 1 July 2029, Article 12ter of the VAT Code is formally repealed. Articles 53sexies and 54bis, which govern consignment stock registers and reporting, are also removed effective the same date.</p>
<p><strong>New platform liability and distance sales rules</strong></p>
<p>The bill expands when online marketplaces are treated as actual suppliers. Article 13bis § 2 of the VAT Code now covers a broader range of buyers:</p>
<p>Platforms facilitating intra-EU sales by non-EU suppliers to taxable persons whose acquisitions are exempt under Article 3(1) of Directive 2006/112/EC are now deemed suppliers. This applies equally to non-taxable legal entities and consumers meeting the exemption criteria.</p>
<p>Distance sales to Belgium follow destination taxation. The EUR 10,000 annual threshold allows small suppliers to tax sales in their home country if they operate in only one EU Member State outside Belgium and dispatch goods from that single location.</p>
<p>The bill clarifies that only shipments from the supplier&#8217;s home state count toward this threshold. Suppliers already registered under the Union OSS scheme are automatically presumed to have chosen destination taxation.</p>
<p><strong>Expanded one-stop-shop access and small business restrictions</strong></p>
<p>From 1 January 2027 through 30 June 2028, cross-border supplies of natural gas, electricity, and heating/cooling energy to non-taxable persons qualify for OSS treatment. The law treats these utility transfers as distance sales to simplify reporting across grid infrastructure. This temporary extension expires when utilities integrate permanently into the broader ViDA OSS framework on 1 July 2028.</p>
<p>Small businesses using the SME VAT exemption cannot simultaneously access the Import One-Stop-Shop (IOSS). Those wishing to use IOSS must formally withdraw from the SME exemption scheme first.</p>
<p>Non-EU service providers using the Non-Union OSS no longer need to prove clients reside in the EU. It is sufficient that the service qualifies as EU-located for VAT purposes. Registration for Non-Union OSS and IOSS now requires an email address and company website if available.</p>
<p><strong>Timeline for implementation</strong></p>
<p>The amendments take effect on 1 January 2027. The consignment stock provisions have a later date: they activate on 1 July 2029.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Czech Republic’s Ministry of Finance and the Chamber of Deputies have <a href="https://mf.gov.cz/cs/ministerstvo/media/tiskove-zpravy/2026/snemovna-prehlasovala-senat-a-stvrdila-zavedeni-ee-65151" target="_blank" rel="noopener">approved</a> the Sales Registration Act on 9 September 2026 after overriding the Senate’s proposed amendments.</p>

<p>The key aspect of this legislative proposal is the reintroduction of electronic sales records (Elektronická Evidence Tržeb &#8211; EET 2.0) in the Czech Republic, scheduled to take effect in 2027.</p>
<p>The bill aims to create a fairer business environment and improve tax compliance through real-time transaction reporting. It focuses on personal contact transactions rather than payment methods, removes mandatory physical receipts, and introduces tax relief measures, including credits for compliant businesses, hospitality tip exemptions, and restored student and childcare deductions.</p>
<p><strong>What EET 2.0 covers</strong></p>
<p>EET 2.0 applies only to contact payments made in person at physical business locations or vehicles. Online and distance transactions are excluded.</p>
<p>Paper receipts are no longer required, ending the customer receipt lottery program. All reporting occurs through a single real-time online XML stream; offline and paper alternatives have been eliminated.</p>
<p>The Financial Administration provides free software for small merchants with lower volumes. Enforcement has been softened. Authorities can no longer immediately close premises or suspend operations for non-compliance.</p>
<p><strong>VAT changes for beverages and tips</strong></p>
<p>Non-alcoholic beverages in catering now carry 12% VAT, aligning with food taxation. Alcoholic drinks over 0.5% ethanol remain at 21%. Employee tips in gastronomy establishments are exempt from income tax and social security contributions, capped at 7% of monthly catering revenue. This applies only to venues equipped for on-site consumption.</p>
<p><strong>Tax credits and deductions for businesses</strong></p>
<p>Self-employed individuals can claim a one-time income tax deduction of CZK 5,000 in their first EET 2.0 year. Taxpayers in the flat-rate regime with revenues up to CZK 1,000,000 may opt out by paying CZK 1,400 monthly. The student tax credit of CZK 4,020 and preschool placement credit have been restored.</p>
<p><strong>VAT relief and employee benefits</strong></p>
<p>Annual caps on non-cash employee leisure and wellness benefits have been removed. Vacation benefits carry a CZK 20,000 annual cap. VAT relief on unpaid invoices now allows claims after three months instead of six, with debt thresholds raised from CZK 10,000 to CZK 20,000 and an annual cap of CZK 100,000.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>After a quiet start, regulatory activity in the European Union surged, defined by a multi-faceted focus on the iron and steel sector. A massive preparatory update loaded over 8,000 future-dated technical requirements for steel products, immediately followed by the implementation of new trade defence duties targeting imports from China and Türkiye. This combination of administrative overhaul and targeted protectionism signals intense scrutiny of the sector, even as routine but commercially significant updates in agriculture, including new rice quotas and seasonal produce prices, continued.</p>
<p><strong>The week in brief</strong></p>
<p>After three days of inactivity, the EU’s customs tariff system saw a burst of regulatory movement concentrated in the second half of the week. The dominant theme was an intense, multi-pronged focus on the iron and steel sector, which saw both a massive forward-looking administrative update and the immediate implementation of new trade defence measures. This dual track of technical preparation and active protectionism defined the week’s posture. Alongside this, agricultural trade saw significant but more routine activity with the introduction and subsequent adjustment of rice quotas and a wave of seasonal price changes for fresh produce. A third stream of new, complex controls on basic commodities like cement and fertilisers also emerged, signalling a broadening of compliance requirements beyond traditional duties.</p>
<p><strong>What mattered most</strong></p>
<p>Four key developments shaped the week:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Massive future-dated steel update: </strong>The week&#8217;s most significant event by volume was the loading of over 8,000 future-dated records for iron and steel products in Chapters 72 and 73. Classified as “new requirements/conditions,” these changes point to a large-scale technical or administrative project on the horizon, rather than an immediate change in duties or quotas. This follows substantial administrative activity in the steel quota system in the prior week.</li>
<li><strong>New steel trade defence measures:</strong> The administrative focus on steel was matched by policy action. New trade defence measures took effect, targeting specific products from China and Turkey. The changes included new measures and requirements for steel grill, netting, and fencing (Chapter 73) from both countries, as well as for steel shelving units (Chapter 94) from China.</li>
<li><strong>New controls on basic commodities: </strong>A broad set of 79 duty changes took effect, imposing new controls on foundational goods from all non-EU countries. The updates, linked to regulation R0956/23, affect products like cement (Chapter 25), iron ores (Chapter 26), fertilisers (Chapter 31), and certain chemicals. They introduce a complex mix of certificate requirements and conditional duties, including specific duties of 50.00 EUR per tonne in some cases.</li>
<li><strong>Agricultural quotas and pricing: </strong>The agricultural sector saw a series of commercially significant changes. Fourteen new tariff quotas for various types of husked rice (HS code 1006) from Bangladesh became effective, with in-quota rates of 16.910 EUR per tonne for most varieties. This was followed by a large administrative adjustment to these new quotas. Separately, dozens of new seasonal entry prices came into force for fresh produce, affecting the landed cost of imports like tomatoes, lemons, grapes, and oranges.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Threads to watch</strong></p>
<p>The week’s activity points to several escalating storylines. The primary focus is the impending compliance event for the iron and steel sector heralded by the 8,000+ future-dated changes; importers will need to understand the substance and effective date of these new requirements. The implementation of new trade defence measures on top of this administrative activity confirms that steel remains under intense regulatory pressure from all angles. Furthermore, the emergence of complex certificate-based controls on basic materials like cement and fertilisers suggests a trend towards more intricate non-tariff compliance regimes that traders in those sectors must now navigate. Finally, a steady stream of future-dated technical updates for the machinery sector (Chapter 84) indicates that ongoing rule changes are not confined to steel alone.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Australian Senate passed the <a href="https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr7514%22" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Treasury Laws Amendment (Strengthening Accountability for Tax Adviser Misconduct and Other Measures) Bill 2026</a> on 10 September 2026, a legislative proposal from the Australian Parliament designed to increase oversight within the financial and tax sectors.</p>
<p>The bill proposes enhancements to the foreign resident capital gains tax regime and implements critical updates to the merger primary law framework under competition policy.</p>
<p>The reform to Australia&#8217;s foreign resident capital gains tax (CGT) framework is enacted through Schedules 2 and 3 of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Strengthening Accountability for Tax Adviser Misconduct and Other Measures) Bill 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Broadened definition of real property and connected infrastructure (Schedule 2)</strong></p>
<p>The legislation amends section 995-1(1) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 to introduce a comprehensive statutory definition of real property. The definition covers interests and rights over Australian land, contractual and personal rights relating to land, and fixed or installed infrastructure regardless of its classification under State or Territory law.</p>
<p>It also includes leases, licences, and contractual rights over such assets. Section 855-20 further treats water entitlements, options, and rights to acquire covered real property as taxable Australian real property. Mining, quarrying, or prospecting information relating to an area in Australia is also included for the principal asset test.</p>
<p><strong>Strengthened indirect interest rules: 365-day lookback test (Schedule 2)</strong></p>
<p>The legislation strengthens the indirect interest rules by introducing a 365-day lookback period for the principal asset test. A foreign resident’s disposal of an entity interest may be taxable if the entity met the test either at the time of disposal or at any point during the preceding 365 days, preventing temporary restructuring or dilution of assets before a sale from avoiding tax.</p>
<p><strong>Renewable energy concession &amp; 50% CGT discount (Schedule 3)</strong></p>
<p>Schedule 3 introduces a 50% CGT discount for foreign resident entities and foreign trusts on gains from eligible Australian renewable energy assets or qualifying membership interests. An interest qualifies where the entity’s Australian renewable energy assets are worth at least three times its other taxable Australian real property assets. The concession applies to CGT events from commencement until 30 June 2040.</p>
<p><strong>Commencement and application rules</strong></p>
<p>The Treasury Laws Amendment (Strengthening Accountability for Tax Adviser Misconduct and Other Measures) Bill 2026 will become law upon receiving Royal Assent.</p>
<p>Schedules 1, 2, and 3 will commence on the first 1 January, 1 April, 1 July, or 1 October following Royal Assent. The foreign resident CGT amendments apply prospectively to CGT events occurring on or after commencement, including disposals of existing holdings. Earlier tax assessments generally cannot be amended retrospectively, except in limited circumstances such as fraud, evasion, or prior objections.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Italian Revenue Agency <a href="https://www.fiscooggi.it/portale/-/redditi-da-strumenti-finanziari-digitali-inapplicabile-il-regime-fiscale-speciale" target="_blank" rel="noopener">clarified</a>, on 10 September 2026, that companies managing digital registers for blockchain-based financial instruments cannot operate as traditional banks under tax law. In response to question <a href="https://www.agenziaentrate.gov.it/portale/documents/20143/10289089/Risposta+n.+170_2026.pdf/cf260cc9-ef23-5f54-c489-7f7b1cf9069c?t=1789042548768" target="_blank" rel="noopener">no. 170/2026</a>, the Agency ruled that these managers lack authority to collect investor certifications, communicate with tax authorities, or file required tax forms.</p>
<p><strong>The regulatory disconnect</strong></p>
<p>A company operating a distributed ledger technology (DLT) platform sought to clarify its tax treatment under Italian law. The platform issues and transfers bonds and debt securities in digital form through blockchain technology, implementing the Fintech Decree (Legislative Decree no. 25/2023). The company argued that its registry manager function resembled that of a first-tier bank as defined by Ministry of Finance Decree no. 632/1996.</p>
<p>The taxpayer&#8217;s organisational model separated functions between the registry manager (handling issuance and ownership records) and an internal trust company (handling tax withholding calculations and investor communications).</p>
<p>The company wanted confirmation that this setup qualified it to collect self-certifications from non-resident investors, report to the Data Exchange System (SID), and submit Form 118/IMP for tax purposes.</p>
<p><strong>The Agency&#8217;s position</strong></p>
<p>The Revenue Agency rejected this interpretation. No regulatory provision extends first-tier bank status to digital register managers, the Agency stated. Legislative Decree no. 239/1996, which governs tax withholding on bond income, identifies only specific entities authorised to exempt non-resident investors from this tax, and register managers are not among them.</p>
<p>The Fintech Decree itself maintains tax neutrality. Article 8 of the explanatory memorandum explicitly states that tax rules for digital financial instruments remain identical to those for traditional securities. This means the substitute tax continues to apply under Article 5, paragraph 2 of Legislative Decree no. 239/1996. When securities are not deposited with authorised intermediaries, the tax falls to the entity making the payment or the issuer itself.</p>
<p>Complete disintermediation of digital instruments does not exempt them from standard tax treatment. The principle of technological neutrality cannot stretch statutory definitions to cover entities the legislature did not authorise.</p>

The measure was set for announcement on 23 September 2026 but was dropped following pressure from India, which imports roughly one third of the EU&#8217;s scrap shipments.</p>
<p>India raised objections to the plan during trade negotiations. The Commission under President Ursula von der Leyen plans to sign a free trade deal with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in December 2026. Indian government officials had requested relief from the planned restrictions in late June.</p>
<p><strong>Export volumes and price pressure</strong></p>
<p>EU aluminium scrap exports surged 51% since 2019, reaching 1.26 million metric tons in 2025. Third countries currently pay up to 26% above the prices charged within the EU, partly due to subsidies and trade distortions. The original proposal included exemptions for 91 countries and territories, with India listed among them. The industry had requested a 30% duty, but the Commission had settled on 15%.</p>
<p><strong>Environmental rules replace trade measure</strong></p>
<p>The Commission will now rely on its Waste Shipment Regulation to control scrap exports. The regulation is expected to be finalised in November 2026. Starting in May 2027, the EU will ban exports of non-hazardous waste to non-OECD countries.</p>
<p>Thirty-two non-OECD countries have applied for exemptions from this ban. India, Thailand, and Malaysia do not meet the environmental standards required for exemptions on metal waste, so they cannot import metal scrap directly from the EU under the revised rules.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>European Union member states plan to request safeguard investigations into chemicals and plastics, according to officials familiar with ongoing discussions. France, Germany, and Italy are preparing to submit formal requests within weeks to activate one of the EU&#8217;s least-used trade defence tools, targeting what leaders view as damaging import waves from China and other suppliers.</p>
<p>The proposed safeguards would cover three product categories: polyethene terephthalate (PET), a polymer widely used in packaging; epoxy resin; and glass fibres. These products have flooded European markets at prices that undercut domestic producers.</p>
<p>A spokesperson for France&#8217;s trade ministry stated that the government considers a safeguard investigation into certain chemicals and plastics necessary. The French position reflects concerns that Europe&#8217;s chemical sector is currently facing significant difficulties. Italy echoed this view, noting particular interest in protecting chemicals used across defence, automotive, energy, shipbuilding, and infrastructure industries.</p>
<p><strong>A shift in EU trade strategy</strong></p>
<p>The move marks a notable reversal in Brussels&#8217; traditional approach. The EU currently maintains over 150 trade measures, mostly narrowly focused tariffs on specific products. Only one safeguard system exists across the bloc, targeting ferro-alloys. A separate framework covers steel.</p>
<p>Safeguards operate differently from targeted tariffs. They apply blanket protections to all trading partners, including nations with free trade agreements with the EU such as Japan and Canada. This broad reach has made EU members reluctant to deploy them historically, viewing safeguards as overtly protectionist.</p>
<p>Recent shifts in global trade dynamics have altered calculations. The Trump administration&#8217;s tariffs on European goods and China&#8217;s expanding share of global chemical exports have prompted governments to reconsider their protective stance.</p>
<p>EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič acknowledged this change, noting that the Commission was reviewing its historical reluctance to use safeguards.</p>
<p><strong>Industry crisis deepens</strong></p>
<p>Europe&#8217;s chemical sector faces its worst crisis in three decades. High energy costs, weak demand, and competition from Asian suppliers have forced major manufacturers to slash operations. BASF, Lanxess, and Wacker are among companies cutting thousands of jobs across the region.</p>
<p>German chemical industry representatives confirmed that member companies are preparing to support safeguard requests currently being developed by EU governments.</p>
<p>Requests submitted by EU member states require approval through a qualified majority vote, meaning at least 15 member states representing 65% of the EU&#8217;s total population must support the measure. This threshold was previously considered unreachable but now appears within reach given shifting political sentiment across the bloc.</p>

<p>The arrangement sets procedures for arbitration requests, minimum information, terms of reference, and the appointment of independent arbitrators, alongside strict confidentiality and impartiality requirements.</p>
<p>Final-offer arbitration is the default process, while the competent authorities may adopt an independent-opinion arbitration process. <p>The competent authorities must implement decisions within 180 days. The CAA also establishes rules on costs, invalidation of decisions, and termination, while preserving ongoing arbitrations after termination. Australia excludes certain cases involving general anti-avoidance rules, while France reserves the right to exclude cases involving tax fraud penalties, taxable income below EUR 150,000, and certain EU arbitration procedures.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Netherlands Ministry of Finance has initiated a public consultation on changes to how the Netherlands will handle taxation of service income in future tax treaties. The consultation runs from 9 September 2026 to 23 October 2026 and invites responses from companies, tax advisors, employers&#8217; organisations, NGOs, and other interested parties. Current policy and why...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Netherlands Ministry of Finance has initiated a <a href="https://www.internetconsultatie.nl/verdragsbeleid/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation</a> on changes to how the Netherlands will handle taxation of service income in future tax treaties. The consultation runs from 9 September 2026 to 23 October 2026 and invites responses from companies, tax advisors, employers&#8217; organisations, NGOs, and other interested parties.</p>
<p><strong>Current policy and why it&#8217;s changing</strong></p>
<p>The Netherlands&#8217; existing tax treaty policy, established in 2020, generally refuses to give source countries the right to tax payments for services. The reasoning behind this stance centres on how source-state withholding taxes work. These taxes apply to total payment amounts without subtracting actual business costs or accounting for losses. This system can produce excessive taxation and result in double taxation, both of which obstruct cross-border commerce.</p>
<p>However, concluding new treaties or amending existing ones with developing countries has proven difficult under these restrictions. The Ministry now recognises the need for greater room to negotiate.</p>
<p><strong>What the proposed changes allow</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>The Netherlands would be prepared to agree to a source state levy on service payments in tax treaty negotiations with all developing countries, rather than only the poorest and most vulnerable countries.</li>
<li>The measure would apply to all types of services, not just technical services.</li>
<li>The Netherlands would accept the levy only as part of an acceptable overall compromise and would seek to limit its impact by considering expected profit margins for low-risk services when setting the tax rate.</li>
<li>Taxpayers would preferably have the option to be taxed on a net basis.</li>
<li>The existing requirement that services must be performed in the developing country would be abolished.</li>
</ul>
<p>The consultation welcomes input from internationally operating businesses, domestic service providers, tax specialists, academic researchers, and civil society organisations.</p>
<p>Responses must arrive by 23 October 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Internal Revenue Service has <a href="https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/irs-reminder-direct-pay-offers-free-easy-way-to-pay-taxes" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a>, on 10 September 2026, that <a href="https://www.irs.gov/payments/direct-pay-with-bank-account" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Direct Pay</a> provides a free alternative for settling federal tax obligations directly through bank accounts. The platform operates on IRS.gov without requiring user registration or charging processing fees.</p>
<p><strong>How Direct Pay works</strong></p>
<p>The system verifies taxpayer identity through basic information from previous tax returns or current business records. Individual filers provide prior-year return details, while business accounts require confirmation of the company name and employer identification number against IRS records.</p>
<p>The payment process allows for same-day transactions or advance scheduling up to 365 days ahead. A confirmation number and optional email receipt follow each submission. Filers can modify or cancel scheduled payments up to two business days before the transaction processes. The system accepts bank routing and account numbers from any US financial institution.</p>
<p><strong>Payment types and limits</strong></p>
<p>Direct Pay handles individual payments including balances due, estimated tax payments, amended return payments, and extension payments. Business users can balance due amounts, make federal tax deposits, and pay other federal tax obligations through the same platform.</p>
<p>Each transaction carries a maximum of USD 10 million. Filers needing to submit larger amounts can arrange same-day wire transfers or enrol in the <a href="https://www.irs.gov/payments/eftps-the-electronic-federal-tax-payment-system" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Electronic Federal Tax Payment System (EFTPS)</a> instead.</p>
<p>Direct Pay does not process refund deposits. Individuals who have never filed a return or who have not filed within the past six years should explore alternative payment methods before using this tool.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan&#8217;s Southern District National Taxation Bureau of the Ministry of Finance has said that small passenger car rental companies and passenger transport operators providing transportation services for long-term care beneficiaries are exempt from business tax, provided certain requirements are met.</p>
<p>Amid growing demand for long-term care services in an ageing society, many small passenger car rental companies and taxi operators have taken up providing transportation services for long-term care. The Bureau said operators qualifying as contracted long-term care units under Article 32-1 of the Long-Term Care Services Act — by signing administrative contracts with municipal or county (city) authorities — are exempt from business tax on transportation services provided under Article 11, Subparagraph 8 of the same Act.</p>

<p>The Bureau reminded that if small passenger car rental companies or passenger transport operators also provide general passenger transport, rental, or other services not related to long-term care transportation, the income from those services remains subject to business tax. Operators, the Bureau said, must accurately declare their business tax returns based on the actual services provided and whether they qualify for the exemption when filing.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and Treasury Department have issued a notice of proposed rulemaking titled <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/11/2026-18645/allocation-and-apportionment-of-deductions-to-foreign-source-section-951a-category-income-and" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Allocation and Apportionment of Deductions to Foreign Source Section 951A Category Income and Deduction Eligible Income</a>, published in the Federal Register on 11 September 2026.</p>
<p>This document contains proposed regulations related to the allocation and apportionment of deductions to foreign source section 951A category income for foreign tax credit limitation purposes and for purposes of calculating deduction eligible income. The proposed regulations would affect taxpayers that operate in foreign countries through foreign corporations and domestic corporations that claim the deduction for foreign-derived deduction eligible income.</p>
<p>These tax rules, influenced by the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act, detail how expenses like research expenditures and interest are handled for tax credit purposes. Finally, the Forest Service provides a brief notice extending the public comment period for a proposed rule regarding roadless area conservation.</p>
<p><strong>Affected taxpayers and scope</strong></p>
<p>The proposed regulations apply to domestic corporations claiming Foreign Derived Deduction Eligible Income deductions under Section 250 and taxpayers with Controlled Foreign Corporations that earn Section 951A category income. They provide rules for allocating expenses and deductions when taxpayers calculate taxable income and Foreign Tax Credit limitations.</p>
<p><strong>Updates to Section 250 (DEI and FDDEI calculations)</strong></p>
<p>The OBBBA changed how taxpayers calculate Deduction Eligible Income and Foreign Derived Deduction Eligible Income. Taxpayers must exclude interest expenses and Research and Experimental expenditures when allocating deductions to gross DEI and FDDEI. They must reduce these amounts only by other properly allocable deductions. The IRS said it will issue separate guidance on other Section 250 changes, including the removal of the deemed tangible income return.</p>
<p><strong>FTC limitations for Section 951A income (Section 904(b)(5))</strong></p>
<p>The OBBBA added Section 904(b)(5), which sets special rules for allocating deductions to foreign source Section 951A category income.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Permissible allocable deductions: </strong>Only three types of deductions can reduce Section 951A category income. These include Section 250 deductions, certain state and local income taxes directly linked to Section 951A income, and deductions with a direct factual connection to that income.</li>
<li><strong>Directly allocable vs. excluded expenses:</strong> The proposed rules narrowly define directly allocable deductions. Expenses allocated using general measures, such as assets or gross income, cannot reduce Section 951A income. These excluded expenses include stewardship costs, legal and accounting fees, damages, settlements, and general administrative expenses. Some expenses can qualify when they directly relate to Section 951A income. Examples include certain foreign currency losses and NOL deductions. Interest expenses and R&amp;E expenditures cannot reduce Section 951A category income.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Reallocation mechanism and impact on domestic loss (ODL)</strong></p>
<p>The proposed rules require taxpayers to reallocate certain excluded deductions to US source income. This can reduce US source income and create or increase an Overall Domestic Loss. An ODL may allow taxpayers to treat some future US source income as foreign source income, which can increase their Foreign Tax Credit capacity. The rules also address NOLs. They prevent excluded deductions from creating separate limitation losses that could improperly reduce Section 951A income in later years.</p>
<p><strong>Applicability, reliance, and comments timeline</strong></p>
<p>The proposed regulations apply to taxable years beginning after 31 December 2025. Taxpayers may rely on the proposed rules before finalisation for these taxable years, provided they follow the regulations in their entirety. The IRS will accept electronic or written comments and requests for a public hearing through 10 November 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan&#8217;s National Taxation Bureau of the Central Area, Ministry of Finance, has said profit-seeking enterprises organised as companies with a permanent establishment in Taiwan are required to pay provisional income tax and file their provisional income tax return between 1 and 30 September 2026.</p>
<p>The Changhua Branch of the Bureau said the obligation covers all such enterprises, which must complete both payment and filing within the one-month window.</p>
<p>According to the Branch, Article 67 of the Income Tax Act sets the provisional tax payment at &#8220;one-half of the amount of tax payable as declared in its profit-seeking enterprise income tax return filed in the preceding year&#8221;. Enterprises that maintain a complete set of account books and evidential documents, use the Blue Return under Article 77 of the Income Tax Act, or have their accounts audited and attested by a certified public accountant, may instead calculate their provisional payment based on operating income generated during the first six months of the current year, applying the relevant tax rates under the Income Tax Act, provided they file within the specified period.</p>
<p>Enterprises that do not use investment tax credits, refundable tax from administrative remedy, or withholding tax to offset the provisional payment are exempt from filing a provisional income tax return altogether.</p>
<p>The Branch outlined several payment channels available to enterprises. Tax can be settled in cash or by cheque at designated collecting financial institutions, or via ATM transfer. Convenience store payment using the barcode on the tax bill is limited to amounts under TWD 30,000. Enterprises may also pay through the electronic provisional income tax filing and payment system using a credit card registered to the business owner or the enterprise, or by transferring funds from the enterprise&#8217;s demand deposit account. A further option allows payment via chip debit card, either through the filing system or the online tax payment service.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[Belgium’s Minister of Finance submitted a draft bill (Doc 56 1719/001) to the parliament on 10 September 2026 that establishes the operational and statutory framework for implementing Council Directive (EU) 2025/872 (DAC9) into Belgian domestic tax law. This directive amends Directive 2011/16/EU on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation. The draft bill&#8217;s primary purpose...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Belgium’s Minister of Finance submitted a <a href="https://www.dekamer.be/flwb/pdf/56/1719/56K1719001.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">draft bill (Doc 56 1719/001)</a> to the parliament on 10 September 2026 that establishes the operational and statutory framework for implementing Council Directive (EU) 2025/872 (DAC9) into Belgian domestic tax law. This directive amends Directive 2011/16/EU on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation.</p>
<p>The draft bill&#8217;s primary purpose is to establish the automatic exchange of information on the Pillar Two Information Report. This operationalises the reporting obligations introduced by EU Minimum Taxation Directive 2022/2523 and the Belgian Pillar Two Law of 19 December 2023, ensuring global minimum tax compliance across international group entities.</p>
<p><strong>Integration with domestic rules &amp; third-country frameworks</strong></p>
<p>Belgium’s Pillar Two law uses the existing automatic exchange framework under Article 338 of the Belgian Income Tax Code 1992 instead of creating separate procedures. For exchanges with non-EU countries, Belgium will use the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework’s Multilateral Competent Authority Agreement on the Exchange of GloBE Information. Belgium is currently ratifying the agreement.</p>
<p><strong>Filing requirements &amp; correction deadlines</strong></p>
<p>The DAC9 Information Report can be submitted centrally by the Ultimate Parent Entity (UPE) or a Designated Filing Entity established in Belgium or another EU Member State with an active qualifying agreement. When filed centrally, local Belgian constituent entities are exempt from filing duplicate reports under Article 53 (though notification rules apply).</p>
<p>If the Belgian tax authority issues a formal correction request (following internal audit or notification from another Member State), the reporting entity established in Belgium must submit a corrected information report within one month from receiving the request.</p>
<p>A correction request is legally presumed to be received on the 3rd business day following its mailing under a closed envelope or its electronic upload to the SPF Finances platform</p>
<p><strong>Penalties and sanctions regime (Article 61 of the Pillar Two Law)</strong></p>
<p>The draft bill proposes new penalties for Pillar Two violations.</p>
<p>Failing to file, filing late, or failing to pay top-up tax could result in fines of EUR 2,500 to EUR 125,000, rising to EUR 250,000 in cases involving fraud or intent to cause harm. Incorrect or incomplete filings could attract fines of EUR 1,250 to EUR 62,500, or up to EUR 125,000 where fraud or intent to cause harm is involved.</p>
<p>The tax administration may waive penalties where there is no bad faith. Judges may also reduce fines for mitigating circumstances, but not below 40% of the applicable minimum.</p>
<p>The King would be authorised to set graduated penalty scales based on the seriousness and repetition of violations.</p>
<p><strong>Implementation timeline, technical adjustments &amp; entry into force</strong></p>
<p>Belgium will make its first automatic DAC9 information exchange no earlier than 1 December 2026. The bill also makes technical changes to the Pillar Two Law to correct references, align filing deadlines, and clearly separate local tax declarations from the global DAC9 report.</p>
<p>The bill will take effect when it is published in the Belgian Official Gazette, but will apply retroactively from 1 January 2026.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/belgium-council-of-ministers-approves-draft-law-for-transposition-of-dac9/&amp;apos;" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, Belgium’s government announced on 22 May 2026 that the Council of Ministers approved a preliminary draft law to transpose the DAC9 Directive into Belgian law and amend the legislation implementing the minimum tax for multinational and large domestic groups.</p>

The package includes a framework for the full legislative review process, updates to the GloBE Information Return (GIR), and...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The OECD has <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/about/news/announcements/2026/09/global-minimum-tax-inclusive-framework-releases-a-package-to-strengthen-consistency-and-certainty-for-mnes-and-jurisdictions.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> on 11 September 2026 that the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS has released a package on the Pillar Two Global Minimum Tax aimed at strengthening consistency and certainty for MNEs and jurisdictions.</p>
<p>The package includes a framework for the full legislative review process, updates to the GloBE Information Return (GIR), and new administrative guidance on the application of the GloBE Model Rules.</p>
<p>The<a href="https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-sub-issues/global-minimum-tax/terms-of-reference-and-assessment-methodology-for-the-full-legislative-review.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Terms of Reference and Methodology for the Full Legislative Review</a> set out the framework that Inclusive Framework members will use to assess the consistency of domestic rules implementing the Global Minimum Tax (GMT).</p>
<p>This framework will allow Inclusive Framework members to undertake detailed peer reviews of implementing jurisdiction’s legislation to ensure alignment with the<a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/global-minimum-tax/global-anti-base-erosion-model-rules-pillar-two.html#rules" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> GloBE Model Rules</a> and<a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/global-minimum-tax/global-anti-base-erosion-model-rules-pillar-two.html#commentary" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Commentary</a>. Where inconsistencies are identified, the Inclusive Framework will issue recommendations to help jurisdictions address them.</p>
<p>The peer review process is designed to ensure the GMT is consistently applied across jurisdictions, helping to maintain a level playing field among implementing jurisdictions while providing greater tax certainty and reducing compliance costs for businesses through consistent and co-ordinated outcomes.</p>
<p>The Inclusive Framework has also released an update to the<a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/09/tax-challenges-arising-from-the-digitalisation-of-the-economy-globe-information-return-september-2026_16d0f09e.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> GIR</a>. The GIR is a standard information return used by implementing jurisdictions to collect the information needed to evaluate the accuracy of an MNE’s liability under the GMT.</p>
<p>The updated GIR incorporates the simplifications included in the<a href="https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-sub-issues/global-minimum-tax/side-by-side-package.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Side-by-Side package</a> agreed by the Inclusive Framework in January 2026.  These revisions to the GIR will apply only to GIRs filed in respect of Fiscal Years commencing on or after 31 December 2025. A revised XML Schema is now being developed to incorporate these agreed changes.  Inclusive Framework members are working to ensure this schema will be released shortly, allowing tax administrations and MNEs ample time to update their information collection, reporting, GIR filing and exchange systems.</p>
<p>In addition, further<a href="https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-sub-issues/global-minimum-tax/administrative-guidance-on-the-global-anti-base-erosion-model-rules-pillar-two-september-2026.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Administrative Guidance</a> has been released to address the treatment of Explicitly Conditional Taxes and the use of Local Financial Accounting Standards under a QDMTT.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Explicitly conditional taxes:</strong> The Side-by-Side package confirmed that conditional or discriminatory taxes will not be creditable as Covered Taxes and stated that further work would be undertaken to ensure this principle is consistently applied. This guidance confirms that taxes that explicitly apply to taxpayers only if they are subject to the IIR or UTPR in other jurisdictions, are not creditable as Covered Taxes. The Inclusive Framework will issue further guidance on other features of a tax that would result in such tax being considered discriminatory and therefore not being treated as a Covered Tax, with a view to releasing such guidance by the end of the year.</li>
<li><strong>Use of Local Financial Accounting Standards under a QDMTT in case of mismatching fiscal periods:</strong> Under certain conditions, a QDMTT may need to be calculated using financial accounts prepared based on the local financial accounting standard. This guidance clarifies that the QDMTT Safe Harbour continues to apply when the QDMTT is calculated based on the local financial accounting standard and the required QDMTT fiscal period does not align with the UPE’s Fiscal Year.</li>
</ul>

<p>Under the framework, unutilised tax losses may be carried forward to the transferee, and policy liabilities are adjusted between the transferor and transferee accordingly. 		<title>New Zealand: 2026/27 Budget implementation bill proposes R&#038;D tax reforms</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/new-zealand-2026-27-budget-implementation-bill-proposes-rd-tax-reforms/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=new-zealand-2026-27-budget-implementation-bill-proposes-rd-tax-reforms</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Abdur Rouf]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 14 Sep 2026 11:35:02 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Draft legislation]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Computation of taxable income]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Asia-Pacific]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[New Zealand]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=87769</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[New Zealand’s Minister of Revenue has introduced the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2026–27, FBT Simplification, Foreign Investment Funds, and Remedial Measures) Bill into Parliament, proposing changes to tax legislation to implement measures announced in Budget 2026/2027. Introduced on 10 September 2026, the Bill proposes changes to the Foreign Investment Fund (FIF) rules, Fringe Benefit Tax...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>New Zealand’s Minister of Revenue has introduced the <a href="https://www.taxpolicy.ird.govt.nz/bills/2026-fbt-simplification-tax-bill" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Taxation (Annual Rates for 2026–27, FBT Simplification, Foreign Investment Funds, and Remedial Measures) Bill into Parliament</a>, proposing changes to tax legislation to implement measures announced in Budget 2026/2027.</p>
<p>Introduced on 10 September 2026, the Bill proposes changes to the Foreign Investment Fund (FIF) rules, Fringe Benefit Tax (FBT), Goods and Services Tax (GST), the Research and Development Tax Incentive (RDTI), tax administration, and other areas of the tax system.</p>
<p><strong>Research and development tax incentive</strong></p>
<p>The Bill proposes an in-year advance payment scheme under the RDTI, allowing approved taxpayers to receive quarterly payments equal to 15% of estimated eligible expenditure, subject to a cap of 80% of the estimated total credit and a labour-related cap. Payments would be reconciled at year-end.</p>
<p>The Commissioner would receive discretion to extend filing deadlines or accept late amendments where failures resulted from genuine mistakes or events outside the taxpayer&#8217;s control.</p>
<p>The internal software development expenditure cap would be reduced from NZD 25 million to NZD 3 million per income year. Mineral, petroleum, gas and geothermal prospecting, exploration and drilling would also be excluded from qualifying R&amp;D activities.</p>
<p><strong>Foreign investment fund rules</strong></p>
<p>The Bill proposes several changes to the FIF regime aimed at reducing compliance costs and removing tax barriers for New Zealand residents with offshore investments.</p>
<p>The FIF de minimis threshold would increase from NZD 50,000 to NZD 100,000 of cost price, with the change applying from 1 April 2026. Investors whose offshore investments remain below the threshold would not be required to apply the FIF rules.</p>
<p>Eligibility for the Revenue Account Method (RAM) would also be expanded. The method, which taxes 70% of realised gains together with actual dividends received, would become available to all New Zealand residents holding unlisted foreign shares, rather than only recent migrants. Residents who are also subject to tax in another jurisdiction because of citizenship or work rights would be able to use RAM for both listed and unlisted foreign shares.</p>
<p>The Bill would extend the RAM exit tax to cases where an individual becomes non-resident under a double tax agreement (DTA), with the change applying from 1 April 2027. Taxpayers switching out of RAM would also have to remain outside the method for five years before being able to return.</p>
<p>Other FIF proposals would allow active investors, founders and key employees to continue using the Attributable FIF Income (AFI) method when their interest falls below 10% during business expansion. The Bill would also clarify eligibility for the 10-year FIF exemption when an acquired business subsequently lists offshore.</p>
<p>For unlisted FIF shares without a readily available market value, taxpayers would be able to choose the cost method, while the Fair Dividend Rate (FDR) and Comparative Value (CV) methods would remain available for listed shares.</p>
<p><strong>Cryptoassets, banking and tax administration</strong></p>
<p>The Bill proposes a share-lending-style cost-base preservation rule for certain decentralised finance (DeFi) cryptoasset-lending transfers. The measure would apply to arm&#8217;s-length transfers of one year or less and is intended to prevent temporary transfers from creating an interim tax point.</p>
<p>Qualifying fiat-pegged stablecoins, where the peg remains within a 2% variance, would be excluded from the revenue account rule for personal property acquired for disposal.</p>
<p>For banking groups, the thin capitalisation equity thresholds would increase to 12% for foreign-owned domestic systemically important banking groups and 11% for other banking groups. The thresholds would be linked dynamically to changes in the Reserve Bank&#8217;s countercyclical capital buffer.</p>
<p>The Bill would also provide legislative authority for Inland Revenue to use automated systems for high-volume, rules-based decisions. Their use would be subject to a mandatory operational standard, which would be reviewed every three years.</p>
<p>Other proposed measures include new statutory categories and integrity rules for Digital Services Providers and Bookkeepers, as well as rules setting the tax cost base of non-monetary redress assets transferred under Treaty settlement legislation at market value at the time of transfer.</p>
<p><strong>FBT and motor vehicle rules</strong></p>
<p>The Bill proposes to simplify the FBT rules applying to motor vehicles by removing several existing tests and calculations.</p>
<p>These include the &#8220;made available&#8221; test, 24-hour periods, test periods and the statutory &#8220;work-related vehicle&#8221; definition. The existing formulas would be replaced by a schedule setting out private-use categories from 100% to 0%, alongside revised valuation rates for petrol/diesel, hybrid and electric vehicles.</p>
<p>Certain business-use categories would also be subject to permanent exterior branding requirements. Exceptions would apply to certain existing vehicle leases and purchases, non-widely-held farming businesses and cases where the Commissioner grants a waiver for sensitive operations.</p>
<p>The Bill would formally exempt emergency vehicles operated by police, fire, ambulance, defence force, civil defence and accredited volunteer organisations from FBT.</p>
<p><strong>GST reforms</strong></p>
<p>A new Subpart 3A would be inserted into the GST Act to establish a unified framework for correcting return errors, supply errors and supply inaccuracies.</p>
<p>Minor errors falling within the proposed small-value threshold could be corrected in a subsequent return. The threshold would be the lower of NZD 10,000 or 5% of total supplies / NZD 1,000, as applicable.</p>
<p>The Bill would also introduce Section 20BA, allowing input tax deductions for goods and services acquired before GST registration once they begin being used in a taxable activity.</p>
<p>Other GST changes would clarify that non-resident suppliers working at clients&#8217; premises in New Zealand would not establish a fixed or permanent establishment solely because of those premises. Supplies of electricity generated at or connected through residential installation control points and supplied to retailers would also be zero-rated.</p>
<p><strong>Non-resident contractors&#8217; tax and financial arrangements</strong></p>
<p>The monetary withholding exemption threshold for Non-Resident Contractors&#8217; Tax (NRCT) would increase from NZD 15,000 to NZD 75,000 per contract over a 12-month period. The proposed rules would apply a single-payer approach to both monetary and 92-day thresholds.</p>
<p>Low-risk contractors that had been registered in New Zealand for at least 24 months would also be excluded from NRCT.</p>
<p>For financial arrangements, the portfolio threshold for using the straight-line calculation method would rise from NZD 1,850,000 to NZD 3 million.</p>
<p>The Bill would introduce an elective regime allowing natural persons and complying trusts to calculate financial arrangements in foreign currency. It would also provide relief for &#8220;quarantined foreign financial arrangements&#8221; where individuals are taxed overseas under a DTA.</p>
<p><strong>Not-for-profits, charities and KiwiSaver</strong></p>
<p>The proposed measures would retain the non-taxable treatment of membership subscriptions and levies for not-for-profits. The tax deduction available to small not-for-profits would increase from NZD 1,000 to NZD 10,000, while organisations with net income of NZD 10,000 or less would not be required to file income tax returns.</p>
<p>Volunteer honoraria could also be treated as salary or wages.</p>
<p>The Bill would repeal the income tax exemption for foreign charities receiving New Zealand investment income without registration under the Charities Act 2005, with the change applying from 1 April 2028.</p>
<p>Donors would be able to claim and receive refunds for charitable tax credits during the tax year rather than waiting until year-end. The proposals would also allow 16- and 17-year-olds with estranged guardians to enrol in KiwiSaver alongside an Unsupported Child&#8217;s Benefit caregiver.</p>
<p>The measures will now progress through the parliamentary legislative process.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>South Africa’s South African Revenue Service (SARS) has clarified how the increased VAT registration thresholds will apply from 1 April 2026, confirming that the higher compulsory registration threshold is being used for new registration and deregistration requests, but VAT registrations will not be automatically cancelled.</p>
<p>The clarification was included in <a href="https://www.sars.gov.za/businesses-and-employers/my-business-and-tax/vat-connect-issue-21-september-2026/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">VAT Connect Issue 21</a>, published on 8 September 2026, following changes announced in the 2026 Budget Speech and subsequently enacted.</p>
<p><strong>Increased registration thresholds</strong></p>
<p>The compulsory VAT registration threshold increased from ZAR  1 million to ZAR 2.3 million per annum, while the voluntary registration threshold increased from ZAR 50 000 to ZAR 120 000 per annum, with effect from 1 April 2026.</p>
<p>The changes were introduced to give smaller businesses more scope to grow without immediately facing the administrative and compliance costs associated with VAT registration.</p>
<p>Although the amendments were proposed to apply retrospectively from 1 April 2026, SARS said it was applying the new compulsory registration threshold to new registration and deregistration requests.</p>
<p>However, SARS is not automatically cancelling existing VAT registrations where vendors fall below the new threshold.</p>
<p>Once the legislation was promulgated, SARS could initiate cancellations for vendors below the new voluntary threshold, provided the affected vendors were notified.</p>
<p><strong>VAT amendments</strong></p>
<p>SARS also highlighted several other VAT amendments that took effect on 1 April 2026. These include provisions covering refunds to foreign electronic services suppliers on deregistration, interest on delayed VAT refunds, VAT modernisation and the treatment of electronic services supplied through intermediaries.</p>
<p>Other changes address short-term insurance, debit- and credit notes in going concern and reorganisation transactions, zero-rated silver exports, testing services supplied to non-residents, temporary letting of residential property by property developers and airtime vouchers used outside South Africa.</p>
<p>The amendments also removed VAT relief for certain low value imports and clarified the VAT treatment of national housing programme payments and supplies made by educational institutions and public schools.</p>
<p>The revised thresholds and related VAT amendments form part of South Africa’s broader efforts to simplify VAT administration, reduce compliance burdens and modernise the VAT system. SARS has said the changes will also support more consistent VAT treatment across affected transactions and improve the administration of the tax.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Federal Ministry of Finance has adopted new rules governing the issuance of tax certificates by the Federal Tax Administration (FTA), covering taxpayers’ tax liabilities, registration status and residency.</p>
<p>The Rulebook on issuing Certificates from Official Records of the Tax Administration of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) was published in<a href="https://feb.ba/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Pravilnik-o-izdavanju-uvjerenja-o-cinjenicama-iz-sl-evidencija-PU.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Official Gazette No. 68/26 on 2 September 2026</a> and entered into force on 10 September 2026.</p>

<p><strong>Taxpayer registration</strong></p>
<p>The Certificate of Status in the Register of Taxpayers will confirm whether a taxpayer is registered, not registered, has had its tax ID revoked or has been deleted from the Register of Taxpayers.</p>
<p><strong>Tax paid</strong></p>
<p>The Certificate of Calculated and Paid Tax will confirm relevant tax information recorded by the FTA. Applications will be checked against the nPIS system before the certificate is issued.</p>
<p><strong>Residency status</strong></p>
<p>The FTA will also issue Certificate of Residency and Certificate of Non-Residency in accordance with the forms and requirements under the Rulebook on Tax Residency.</p>
<p><strong>Applications and deadlines</strong></p>
<p>Applications may be submitted in person, by post or electronically. Complete applications will generally be processed within five days. Applicants will have five days to correct an incomplete application, after which it will be treated as not submitted.</p>
<p>An administrative fee of 15.00 KM applies under the Law on Federal Administrative Fees. The certificates issued under the new rules have the status of official public documents.</p>
<p>Applications submitted before the rulebook entered into force will continue to be processed under the previous rules.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Turkey’s Revenue Administration published a <a href="https://www.gib.gov.tr/duyuru-arsivi/guncel/18801_yurt_disindan_elde_edilen_kazanc_ve_iratlarda_vergi_istisnasi_rehberi_ile_infografik_yayimlandi_" target="_blank" rel="noopener">guidance</a> on 7 September 2026 outlining a 20-year income tax exemption for qualifying individuals who establish residency in the country and earn income and earnings derived abroad.</p>
<p>The guidance set out the eligibility conditions, application deadlines and tax office review procedures under the exemption regime introduced by Law No. 7582.</p>
<p><strong>Tax exemption under Law No. 7582</strong></p>
<p>The exemption was introduced under Article 4 of Law No. 7582, which added repeated Article 20/D to the Income Tax Law. The implementation procedures and principles were set out in Income Tax General Communiqué No. 333.</p>
<p>Under the regime, eligible individuals may benefit from an income tax exemption on income and earnings derived abroad for 20 years, subject to specified conditions.</p>
<p><strong>Eligibility conditions</strong></p>
<p>Individuals must establish residency in Turkey on or after 1 January 2026 to qualify. They must also not have had a residence in Turkey during the three calendar years immediately preceding the year in which they establish residency.</p>
<p>Applicants must meet additional past tax liability requirements. Commercial or wage-earning tax liabilities in Turkey during the previous three calendar years generally disqualify an applicant.</p>
<p>An exception applies to passive income, including real estate capital income, securities capital income and capital gains.</p>
<p>Application deadline</p>
<p>Eligible individuals must generally apply to their authorised tax office for an exemption certificate by the end of the calendar year in which they establish residency.</p>
<p>Those who establish residency during the final two months of a calendar year must apply by the end of the second month of the following year.</p>
<p><strong>Tax office review</strong></p>
<p>The Guide sets out the checks to be carried out by tax offices before an exemption certificate is issued. It also explains the procedures and penalties that apply if it is subsequently determined that the conditions for the exemption were not met.</p>
<p>Scope of the exemption</p>
<p>The exemption applies only to income and earnings derived abroad. Income sourced within Turkey remains subject to the applicable domestic tax rules.</p>
<p>The published “Guide on Tax Exemption for Income and Earnings Derived Abroad” provides further explanations and examples on who may benefit, the conditions for eligibility, where applications must be submitted, the documents required and the procedures applicable after approval.</p>

</ul>
<p>The deadline for submitting claims for the 2025 to 2026 prescribed year is 31 December 2026.</p>
<p>HMRC will also review claims for VAT incurred from 1 January 2021 that it rejected because the representative member did not submit the claim, provided the VAT was not included in a later claim submitted by the representative member.</p>

<p>Use the subject line: ‘Reconsideration of a previously refused VAT group claim’.</p>
<p>Include the following information in your email:</p>
<ul>
<li>the business name</li>
<li>the unique reference number issued by the Overseas Repayments Unit and the claim number</li>
<li>the claim period, claim value and the date of the decision letter</li>
<li>the full names of all VAT group members during the claim period</li>
<li>a statement confirming that the VAT was not included in a later claim</li>
</ul>
<p>In addition, HMRC will accept requests to review eligible previously rejected claims where the VAT was not included in a subsequent claim. Requests for reconsideration must be submitted by 31 August 2027, after which HMRC will not consider them.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Bosnia and Herzegovina has introduced rules governing the refund of overpaid public revenues and the calculation of default interest by the Tax Administration of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH).</p>
<p>The Federal Ministry of Finance adopted the Regulation on the Procedure for Refund of Overpaid Public Revenues and Default Interest Calculation in Refund Procedures. The regulation was published in <a href="https://feb.ba/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Pravilnik-o-postupku-povrata-preplacenih-javnih-prihoda-i-obracuna-zatezne-kamate.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Official Gazette No. 68/26 on 2 September 2026</a>.</p>
<p><strong>Refund procedure</strong></p>
<p>A refund procedure may be initiated by a taxpayer through a refund request or ex officio by the Tax Administration. Overpayments may be established from official tax records, taxpayer requests, enforceable decisions or amended tax returns.</p>
<p>Before issuing a refund decision, the Tax Administration must verify and offset the overpayment against any due and unpaid tax liabilities relating to the same public revenue beneficiary.</p>
<p>The head of the relevant tax branch office must issue a decision within 20 days of receiving a complete application or the required evidence.</p>
<p><strong>Default interest</strong></p>
<p>Refunds must be executed within 30 days of receiving a proper refund request. If the deadline is exceeded, the taxpayer is entitled to default interest, which the Tax Administration must calculate ex officio without a separate request.</p>
<p>Default interest is calculated at 0.04% per day on the refund principal, from the expiry of the 30-day deadline until the payment date. For refunds made in instalments, interest is calculated separately for each partial payment.</p>
<p><strong>Appeals and oversight</strong></p>
<p>Appeals against refund or default interest decisions may be filed within eight days of receipt and do not suspend execution.</p>
<p>Cases remanded following appeals or administrative litigation must be handled as a priority to limit further default interest. Officials may face corrective measures and disciplinary or material liability where unlawful or negligent action results in default interest or financial losses.</p>
<p>The Central Office of the FBiH Tax Administration will maintain records of default interest payments to monitor the efficiency of the refund process.</p>
<p>The regulation entered into force on 3 September 2026.</p>
