										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>China’s Ministry of Finance and State Taxation Administration released <a href="https://fgk.chinatax.gov.cn/zcfgk/c102416/c5252024/content.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Announcement No. 25 of 2026</a> on 27 August 2026, effective 1 September 2026, establishing definitive guidance on input tax deduction eligibility under the Value-Added Tax Law of the People&#8217;s Republic of China and its Implementing Regulations.</p>
<p><strong>Transactions eligible for input tax deduction</strong></p>
<p>Six categories of non-taxable transactions permit taxpayers to deduct corresponding input tax from output tax under Article 22 of the Value-Added Tax Law Implementing Regulations. These include insurance compensation received, donations of monetary or non-monetary assets, liquidated damages from broken contracts, free services (excluding financial products), transfers of accounts receivable linked to taxable transactions, and fiscal subsidies unrelated to sales volume or income.</p>
<p><strong>Transactions ineligible for input tax deduction</strong></p>
<p>Four categories remain non-deductible under the same provisions: sales of goods, services, intangible assets, and real estate outside Article 4&#8217;s territorial scope; equity transfers (excluding securities); dividends from equity holdings (including common stock); and commodity futures transactions without physical delivery.</p>
<p><strong>Pricing and discount treatment</strong></p>
<p>The announcement establishes specific rules for invoice documentation. When a single invoice separately itemises price and discount amount in the Amount column, the taxable sales amount equals the price after discount, excluding tax. If the invoice does not separately identify the discount amount, the full listed price applies as the taxable sales amount, and no deduction occurs. Telecommunications service providers offering complimentary goods must separately account for prices and apply appropriate tax rates to each item.</p>
<p><strong>Administrative clarifications and policy scope</strong></p>
<p>Agricultural product invoices under exemption policies refer only to ordinary invoices issued by agricultural producers selling their own products. Technical schools, senior technical schools, and technical colleges eligible for exemption include those established with approval from provincial or higher-level human resources and social security departments, or provincial governments.</p>
<p>Venue admission ticket revenue eligible for exemption covers only first-gate entry fees, excluding revenue from special exhibitions, performances, or temporary events held within specific areas.</p>
<p>Asset restructuring transactions retain the transferring party&#8217;s original purchase price for financial products involved. Real estate and land use rights acquired through purchase, donation, investment shares, self-construction, debt settlement, or asset restructuring all qualify within the scope.</p>
<p><strong>Waiver procedures and retroactive application</strong></p>
<p>General taxpayers choosing to waive VAT preferential policies must submit written waiver declarations indicating the effective date to the competent tax authority.</p>
<p>The announcement repealed Article 1 of Notice Cai Shui [2007] No. 127 and related documents. Unprocessed transactions occurring between 1 January 2026 and 31 August 2026 are handled under these new provisions, ensuring consistent treatment during the transition period.</p>

		<title>Angola introduces new beneficial ownership reporting regime</title>

					<description><![CDATA[Angola published Law No. 7/26 in the Official Gazette on 19 August 2026, introducing a new beneficial ownership information reporting regime. The legislation mandates the creation of a Central Register of Beneficial Ownership (CRBE) to enhance financial transparency and prevent financial crimes such as money laundering and terrorist financing. It applies to a broad range...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Angola published Law No. 7/26 in the Official Gazette on 19 August 2026, introducing a new beneficial ownership information reporting regime.</p>
<p>The legislation mandates the creation of a Central Register of Beneficial Ownership (CRBE) to enhance financial transparency and prevent financial crimes such as money laundering and terrorist financing. It applies to a broad range of entities, including commercial companies, non-profits, and trusts, requiring them to disclose the natural persons who ultimately control or profit from their activities. Its primary goals are to prevent the abuse of corporate vehicles—both for-profit and non-profit—for money laundering, terrorist financing, and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction.</p>
<p><strong>Who must comply</strong></p>
<p>The regime covers commercial companies, law firms, branches of foreign entities, NGOs, foundations, trusts, cooperatives, and political parties registered in Angola or conducting transactions requiring a Tax Identification Number (NIF). State agencies, diplomatic missions, and professional orders are exempt from the requirements.</p>
<p><strong>Defining beneficial ownership</strong></p>
<p>Only natural persons qualify as beneficial owners. The law identifies ownership through several mechanisms: direct or indirect holding of 25% or more of share capital or voting rights; receiving ultimate profits from company activity; occupying top management positions when ownership is unclear; or exercising control through powers of attorney, shareholders&#8217; agreements, or special voting privileges. For nonprofits and trusts, founders, board members, trustees, and protectors also qualify as beneficial owners.</p>
<p><strong>Registration and reporting requirements</strong></p>
<p>Existing entities have 180 days from 19 August 2026 to register their beneficial owners. New entities must declare ownership during incorporation. Any change in ownership structure requires notification within 15 days. Entities must submit annual confirmations by 31 March each year and maintain internal registries of all partners and indirect owners.</p>
<p>Partners who fail to inform their entity of changes face daily penalties of AOA 20,000 (natural persons) or AOA 200,000 (legal entities) after a 10-day notice period.</p>
<p><strong>The central registry and public access</strong></p>
<p>The Central Registry of Beneficial Owners (CRBE) operates as a public electronic database accessible by NIF, company name, or registration number. Public records include the owner&#8217;s name, birth date, nationality, residency, identification number, and NIF.</p>
<p>Financial institutions, lawyers, accountants, and real estate agents access the registry during customer due diligence. Personal data remains archived for 10 years after cancellation; historical records preserve information about former owners for the same period.</p>
<p><strong>Enforcement and penalties</strong></p>
<p>Non-compliance triggers financial and administrative consequences scaled by infraction severity and entity type.</p>
<p>Simple infractions—failing to update records or maintain internal documentation—carry fines ranging from AOA 25,000 to AOA 20,000,000 depending on entity classification.</p>
<p>Serious infractions involving defective or inaccurate reporting impose penalties from AOA 50,000 to AOA 30,000,000. Very serious infractions, including false declarations or missed annual deadlines, reach AOA 100,000 to AOA 50,000,000.</p>
<p>Beyond fines, authorities can impose disqualification from corporate positions for up to 3 years, suspension of business activity for up to 3 years or permanently, and mandatory publication of sanctions in national newspapers at the offender&#8217;s expense. Individuals providing false information face criminal liability under Article 350 of the Angolan Penal Code, plus civil liability for damages.</p>
<p>Entities guilty of criminal violations face mandatory registry cancellation and exclusion from the CRBE. Other entities conducting business with an excluded entity commit a very serious administrative infraction themselves.</p>
<p><strong>Transition period</strong></p>
<p>Administrative sanctions do not apply to existing entities until after the 180-day grace period expires, providing time for compliance without immediate penalty.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

The ruling, contained in Legal Advice No. 9 of 1 September 2026, resolves an interpretation question that had created uncertainty around transfer protections. The underlying...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Italian Revenue Agency <a href="https://www.fiscooggi.it/portale/-/crisi-e-cessione-di-impresa-esonero" target="_blank" rel="noopener">clarified </a>on 1 September 2026 that a business transferee retains full tax exemption even after a restructuring agreement fails due to the transferor&#8217;s breach of contract. The ruling, contained in <a href="https://www.agenziaentrate.gov.it/portale/documents/20143/10289093/Risposta+n.+9_2026/39fb6044-a7dc-8f35-011d-753ce9bd11ec" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Legal Advice No. 9</a> of 1 September 2026, resolves an interpretation question that had created uncertainty around transfer protections.</p>
<p><strong>The underlying legal framework</strong></p>
<p>Article 14 of Legislative Decree No. 472/1997 typically makes business transferees jointly liable for the transferor&#8217;s unpaid taxes and penalties from the transfer year and the two preceding years, capped at the acquired asset value.</p>
<p>Legislative Decree No. 158/2015 modified this rule by adding paragraph 5-bis to Article 14, which strips away joint liability when the transfer occurs within insolvency proceedings or as part of crisis management.</p>
<p>The provision aims to encourage acquisitions of distressed businesses by removing the threat of retroactive tax exposure for buyers.</p>
<p><strong>The central question</strong></p>
<p>The taxpayer sought clarification on whether the exemption from Article 14, paragraph 5-bis applies only if the restructuring agreement succeeds. If the transferor later defaults on tax obligations tied to the restructuring deal, does that termination strip away the buyer&#8217;s protection? The company contended that conditioning the exemption on the transferor&#8217;s compliance would impose unforeseeable risk on the transferee and violate principles of legal certainty.</p>
<p><strong>The Agency&#8217;s decision</strong></p>
<p>The Revenue Agency confirmed that the exemption operates unconditionally. The legislative intent was to remove barriers to successful restructuring by making acquisitions financially attractive. Allowing retroactive tax claims if deals later collapse would undermine this purpose and discourage investment in troubled businesses.</p>
<p>Accordingly, the transferee&#8217;s protection stands even after the restructuring transaction terminates due to the transferor&#8217;s default.</p>
<p>One boundary applies: Article 14, paragraph 4 of Legislative Decree No. 472/1997 still applies when the transfer itself involved tax fraud or asset concealment. Beyond that, the exemption remains permanent and irrevocable.</p>

<p>Draft Act UD459 establishes support mechanisms aligned with the European Commission&#8217;s Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (CISAF), published in Official Journal C/2025/3602 on 4 July 2025 and adopted in June 2025.</p>

<p>The rationale reflects two distinct circumstances: sustained competitive disadvantages in the industrial sector combined with extraordinary financial results in certain economic segments, particularly energy and fuel trading.</p>

<p>Brent crude oil prices rose from approximately USD 65 per barrel in January 2026 to USD 126 per barrel in March 2026, generating trading margins in European markets that exceeded historical averages by several multiples. These windfall gains provide a revenue source for targeted industrial support without expanding public spending.</p>
<p><strong>Energy sector financial dynamics</strong></p>
<p>Distribution companies within Poland&#8217;s energy sector have benefited from regulated tariff systems administered by the Energy Regulatory Office (URE). The tariff framework guarantees returns on capital through rising distribution charges, ensuring stable revenues independent of broader economic conditions.</p>
<p>This monopolistic model contrasts sharply with energy-intensive industry operations, where rising input costs directly threaten viability. The proposed legislation aims to redirect windfall gains from this stable segment toward support for industrial competitiveness and modernisation investments.</p>
<p><strong>Energy transition investment requirements</strong></p>
<p>Beyond immediate cost relief, the draft act emphasises stimulating targeted investment activity by enterprises in modernising energy-intensive production processes. The legislation creates mechanisms for broader cooperation between industrial entities and third parties with expertise in energy transition project implementation.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Brazil’s tax authority, the Federal Revenue Service (RFB) <a href="https://www.gov.br/receitafederal/pt-br/assuntos/noticias/2026/setembro/receita-federal-alerta-comeca-hoje-o-prazo-para-opcao-pelo-simples-nacional-e-para-a-escolha-do-modelo-de-recolhimento-do-ibs-e-da-cbs-em-2027" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> on 1 September 2026 that small and micro-enterprises face a critical decision window through 30 September 2026.</p>
<p>Companies must finalise their position on the Simplified National Tax System tax regime for 2027 and select how to handle two new consumption taxes: the Contribution on Goods and Services (CBS) and the Tax on Goods and Services (IBS).</p>
<p>This marks a significant scheduling shift, as enrollment deadlines have moved from January to September of the prior year due to adaptations to consumption tax reform.</p>
<p><strong>Two paths in September</strong></p>
<p>The action required depends on each company&#8217;s current tax status.</p>
<p>Companies not yet in the Simplified National Tax System (Simples Nacional) but wanting to join in 2027 must file their application between 1 and 30 September 2026. Approval means the change takes effect from 1 January 2027. The Federal Revenue Service advises verifying that no outstanding tax or registration problems exist before applying.</p>
<p>For firms already enrolled in the simplified national tax system, no action is needed to maintain enrollment unless they have a scheduled exclusion on file. However, these companies face a separate decision: whether to keep CBS and IBS taxes bundled into the simplified national tax system’s single payment slip or remove them and pay these two taxes under the standard regime.</p>
<p><strong>Withdrawal and special cases</strong></p>
<p>Companies regretting either choice have until 30 November 2026 to cancel their decisions. Individual microentrepreneurs (MEI) operate under different rules: their January enrollment deadline remains unchanged, and no CBS/IBS regime choice exists for them.</p>
<p>New registrations between 1 October and 31 December 2026 receive special treatment, with their selected tax regime covering both the remainder of 2026 and all of 2027.</p>
<p>The Federal Revenue Service emphasises that the CBS and IBS selection carries operational weight, affecting cash flow, vendor relationships, supply chain credits, and overall business strategy.</p>
<p><strong>The simplified national tax system variants explained</strong></p>
<p>The consumption tax reform introduces a new configuration choice.</p>
<p>Under the &#8220;pure&#8221; Simplified National Tax System, all taxes, including the new CBS and IBS, remain in the unified payment. This option becomes automatic if companies take no action by the September deadline.</p>
<p>The &#8220;hybrid&#8221; model allows firms to stay in the Simplified National Tax System for other taxes while calculating CBS and IBS separately under regular collection rules. This structure benefits companies conducting business-to-business transactions where clients need expanded tax credit access.</p>
<p>The decision applies to the first half of 2027, with another selection window opening in March 2027 for the second half.</p>

This version introduces crucial updates and clarifications regarding the implementation timeline, exemption thresholds, and group-level criteria that businesses must navigate. One key update is the increase in the annual turnover or revenue threshold for exemption from e-invoicing...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Inland Revenue Board of Malaysia (IRBM) has <a href="https://www.hasil.gov.my/en/e-invois/rujukan-pelaksanaan-e-invois/garis-panduan/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">published</a> the <a href="https://www.hasil.gov.my/wp-content/uploads/IRBM-e-Invoice-Guideline.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">e-Invoice Guideline Version 4.8</a> on 30 August 2026. This version introduces crucial updates and clarifications regarding the implementation timeline, exemption thresholds, and group-level criteria that businesses must navigate.</p>
<p>One key update is the increase in the annual turnover or revenue threshold for exemption from e-invoicing requirements, from MYR 1 million to MYR 3 million, along with further clarification on the scope of the exemption.</p>
<p><strong>Exemption threshold &amp; scope of eligibility</strong></p>
<p>According to the update, taxpayers with an annual turnover or revenue of less than MYR 3 million are exempted from issuing e-invoices (including self-billed e-invoices). This exemption applies across all categories of taxpayers, such as individuals, partnerships, companies, and co-operatives. For taxpayers falling below this threshold, existing receipts and standard commercial documents continue to serve as valid proof of expense for tax purposes.</p>
<p><strong>Corporate relationship restrictions (exclusion from exemption)</strong></p>
<p>The IRBM clarifies that eligibility for the MYR 3 million exemption is not evaluated solely on an individual entity&#8217;s turnover. The exemption is strictly disallowed if any of the following group-level conditions are met:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Non-individual shareholders: </strong>The taxpayer has one or more non-individual shareholders (or equivalent) with an annual turnover or revenue of at least MYR 3,000,000.</li>
<li><strong>Subsidiary status:</strong> The taxpayer is a subsidiary of a holding company with an annual turnover or revenue of at least MYR 3,000,000.</li>
<li><strong>Related companies &amp; joint ventures: </strong>The taxpayer has a related company or joint venture with an annual turnover or revenue of at least MYR 3,000,000. For this purpose, a &#8220;related company&#8221; is defined under Section 2 of the Promotion of Investments Act 1986.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Implementation timeline for newly established businesses</strong></p>
<p>For businesses commencing operations between 2023 and 2025 with an annual turnover of at least RM 3 million, the compliance deadline is 1 July 2026.</p>
<p>For those starting from 2026 onwards, implementation is set for 1 July 2026, or their operation commencement date, whichever is later.</p>
<p>If a new business expects its first-year revenue to be under MYR 3 million, implementation is deferred to 1 January of the second year after they actually reach the MYR 3 million threshold.</p>
<p>Timeline for public and international bodies</p>
<p>Statutory bodies, local authorities, and international organisations are required to implement e-invoicing for transactions involving goods sold or services performed starting from 1 July 2025. Any such transactions conducted before this date are exempt from the requirement.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Argentina: ARCA streamlines digital procedures for export declaration changes</title>

					<description><![CDATA[Argentina’s tax authority (ARCA) has published General Resolution 5891/2026 (signed on 27 August 2026) in the Official Gazette on 31 August 2026, establishing a unified procedure to request modifications and rehabilitations of export destinations in Argentina. The resolution also amends General Resolution No. 1.921 to adapt to current operational challenges in foreign trade, such as...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Argentina’s tax authority (ARCA) has published <a href="https://www.boletinoficial.gov.ar/detalleAviso/primera/346596/20260831" target="_blank" rel="noopener">General Resolution 5891/2026 </a>(signed on 27 August 2026) in the Official Gazette on 31 August 2026, establishing a unified procedure to request modifications and rehabilitations of export destinations in Argentina.</p>
<p>The resolution also amends General Resolution No. 1.921 to adapt to current operational challenges in foreign trade, such as shipping space shortages, low transport availability, and container scarcity.</p>
<p>Under the historical regulatory framework of Decree No. 1.001/1982, export requests remain valid for 31 days (or 45 days for terrestrial transit suspensive destinations). Because modern logistics bottlenecks frequently cause exporters to miss these tight shipping windows, ARCA has updated procedures to establish a unified, digital process for updating and renewing export declarations before they lapse.</p>
<p><strong>Key amendment and authorised modification fields</strong></p>
<p>The resolution modifies General Resolution No. 1.921, officially renaming the section previously known as &#8220;6. Perfection” to &#8220;6. Modification of the Export Destination. Under this updated framework, customs-designated dependencies are authorised to approve amendments to critical operational fields on the export declaration.</p>
<p>Exporters are allowed to update the shipment expiration date, customs office of exit, mode of transport, name and flag of the transport vessel, Customs Transport Agent (ATA), and the country of destination of the means of transport.</p>
<p><strong>SITA digital workflow for rectifications</strong></p>
<p>The amendment introduces a streamlined digital workflow handled entirely through the Sistema Informático de Trámites Aduaneros (SITA). For standard corrections, exporters must file a  “Rectification of the Export Declaration” on the SITA platform.</p>
<p>To prevent administrative bottlenecks and keep trade moving, the resolution enforces a strict three-hour deadline for the customs service to resolve these rectification requests, starting from the moment the digital submission shifts to the &#8220;INICIADO&#8221; status.</p>
<p><strong>The rehabilitation and extension process</strong></p>
<p>For extensions, exporters can request a “Rectification of the Export Declaration” through SITA by modifying the shipment expiration date. This renewal is granted only once and cannot exceed the original validity period of the declaration.</p>
<p>To qualify, the declaration must be in the &#8220;PRESENTADA&#8221; state or any subsequent operational state; if it is still in the &#8220;OFICIALIZADA&#8221; state, the rehabilitation is only valid if the goods have already physically entered a customs warehouse.</p>
<p><strong>Automatic integration, communications, and implementation</strong></p>
<p>Once customs approves the rehabilitation on SITA, the updated shipment expiration date automatically synchronises with the Sistema Informático MALVINA (SIM). Any communications, including requests for additional documentation, approvals, or official rejections, are delivered directly to the exporter&#8217;s electronic portal via the Sistema de Comunicación y Notificación Electrónica Aduanera (SICNEA).</p>
<p>The resolution entered into force upon its publication on 31 August 2026.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[Argentina’s tax authority (ARCA) has published General Resolution 5893/2026 on 31 August 2026 to modernise billing procedures. This regulation mandates the use of electronic invoices or fiscal controllers for specific taxpayer groups, including those in the Simplified Regime for Small Taxpayers and individuals not currently subject to Value Added Tax (VAT). The resolution phases out...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Argentina’s tax authority (ARCA) has published <a href="https://www.boletinoficial.gov.ar/detalleAviso/primera/346598/20260831" target="_blank" rel="noopener">General Resolution 5893/2026</a> on 31 August 2026 to modernise billing procedures. This regulation mandates the use of electronic invoices or fiscal controllers for specific taxpayer groups, including those in the Simplified Regime for Small Taxpayers and individuals not currently subject to Value Added Tax (VAT).</p>
<p>The resolution phases out manual paper-based invoicing under Resolution 100 for almost all remaining taxpayer categories, migrating them to mandatory electronic invoicing or Fiscal Controllers.</p>
<p>The primary goal is to achieve greater transaction transparency and traceability among taxpayers who were previously exempt from electronic invoicing.</p>
<p><strong>New obligated taxpayers</strong></p>
<p>The resolution expands mandatory electronic invoicing requirements to three additional taxpayer categories.</p>
<p>VAT-exempt and VAT-non-reached taxpayers now fall under the obligation, as do social monotributistas operating under the Social Inclusion and Promotion of Independent Work Regime.</p>
<p>Small taxpayers registered in the National Registry of Effectors of Local Development and Social Economy—previously managed by the Ministry of Social Development—face the same requirement.</p>
<p><strong>Execution and choice of invoicing modality</strong></p>
<p>Newly obligated taxpayers generally enjoy flexibility in how they comply. They can adopt original electronic invoicing under RG 4291, utilise a Fiscal Controller under RG 3561, or deploy both methods simultaneously without prior ARCA notification.</p>
<p>This discretion has limits. MiPyMEs invoicing large companies or other MiPyMEs registered under the &#8220;Factura de Crédito Electrónica MiPyMEs&#8221; system (Law 27.440) must use exclusive electronic invoicing.</p>
<p>The same requirement applies to VAT-non-reached subjects and specific taxpayers listed in Annex II of General Resolution 4291.</p>
<p><strong>Implementation and phased timeline</strong></p>
<p>The regulation staggers implementation across three dates. Insurance entities governed by Law 20.091 that conduct non-VAT-reached activities exclusively begin immediately upon publication on 31 August 2026.</p>
<p>General entry into force occurs on 1 November 2026, targeting social monotributistas and registered social effectors. VAT-non-reached taxpayers receive an extended deadline of 1 March 2027, during which they must continue issuing paper invoices under RG 100.</p>
<p><strong>Transition rules for printed invoice booklets</strong></p>
<p>After the applicable deadline passes—either 1 November 2026 or 1 March 2027—printed physical invoice booklets become permissible only as an exceptional contingency measure. Taxpayers experiencing technical system outages may use existing booklets for contingencies until their printed authorisation expires, after which no further use is allowed.</p>
<p><strong>Administrative simplification for monotributistas</strong></p>
<p>ARCA has introduced automatic sales point configuration to ease the migration. Monotributistas lacking an active point of sale will receive automatic system configuration linking to the &#8220;Comprobantes en línea&#8221; service and associated with the &#8220;Factura en línea &#8211; Monotributo&#8221; option and their declared fiscal domicile.  Adding further points of sale or modifying related data requires manual intervention through the &#8220;Administración de Puntos de Venta y Domicilios&#8221; service.</p>
<p><strong>Modified temporary authorisations for startups and status changes</strong></p>
<p>The resolution amends Article 20 of RG 100 to address new businesses or entities undergoing tax status changes such as becoming exempt, non-reached, or monotributistas.</p>
<p>Apart from Class &#8220;A&#8221; invoices governed by specific RG 5762 rules, other invoices receive temporary authorisation valid for 120 calendar days during the initial three months of operation. ARCA retains discretion to shorten or deny this temporary status if irregularities emerge.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

<p>IRS.gov offers secure, self-service options that can help taxpayers, businesses, and tax professionals get tax information and take action online. These tools can help users access tax records, check refund status, make payments, manage payment plans, view notices, request an Identity Protection PIN, and handle authorisation requests.</p>
<p><strong>IRS individual online account</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers can use <a href="https://www.irs.gov/payments/online-account-for-individuals" target="_blank" rel="noopener">IRS Individual Online Account</a> to securely access personal tax information and complete many tasks online. After signing in, taxpayers can:</p>
<ul>
<li>View balance information by tax year.</li>
<li>Make a same-day payment or schedule payments up to 365 days in advance from a bank account.</li>
<li>View payment history and pending or scheduled payments.</li>
<li>View key tax return information, including adjusted gross income.</li>
<li>Access transcripts and available information return documents, including Forms W-2 and certain Forms 1099.</li>
<li>Check the status of a refund or amended return.</li>
<li>View digital notices from the IRS.</li>
<li>Get an Identity Protection PIN.</li>
<li>View, approve, and electronically sign certain authorisation requests from tax professionals.</li>

<p><strong>Business tax account</strong></p>
<p>Eligible businesses can use <a href="https://www.irs.gov/businesses/business-tax-account" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Business Tax Account</a> to manage certain federal tax responsibilities online. Available features depend on the business structure and the user’s role.</p>

<ul>
<li>View business information on file with the IRS.</li>
<li>View account balances and payment history.</li>
<li>Make federal tax deposits, balance due payments, and other payments.</li>
<li>View tax transcripts, an employer identification number verification letter, and tax compliance reports.</li>
<li>View certain IRS notices and letters.</li>
<li>Manage account access for authorised users.</li>
</ul>
<p>Business Tax Account is available to several business and organisation types, including sole proprietors, partnerships, S corporations, C corporations, federal, state, and local governments, Indian tribal governments, and tax-exempt organisations. Some users may have limited access based on their role in the entity.</p>
<p><strong>Tax Pro Account</strong></p>
<p>Tax professionals can use <a href="https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/tax-pro-account" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Tax Pro Account</a> to manage certain authorisation requests and authorised taxpayer relationships online.</p>
<p>Tax Pro Account allows eligible tax professionals to request power of attorney and tax information authorisations, view taxpayer information, check authorisation request status, view active authorisations, and withdraw authorisations. When both the tax professional and individual taxpayer use IRS online accounts, certain authorisation requests can be handled electronically.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Irish Revenue has updated its guidance on the Irish Self-Assessment system to clarify which individuals are liable for Pay-Related Social Insurance (PRSI) contributions.</p>
<p>The changes were issued through <a href="https://www.revenue.ie/en/tax-professionals/ebrief/2026/no-1262026.aspx" target="_blank" rel="noopener">eBrief No. 126/26 on 28 August 2026</a>, which updates <a href="https://www.revenue.ie/en/tax-professionals/tdm/income-tax-capital-gains-tax-corporation-tax/part-41/41-00-28.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Tax and Duty Manual Part 41-00-28</a>: A Guide to Self-Assessment, including Section 6 on PRSI liability.</p>
<p><strong>Who is liable for PRSI</strong></p>
<p>Under the updated guidance, with very few exceptions, PRSI contributions apply to:</p>
<ul>
<li>Self-employed people with a minimum annual income who are aged 16 or over and under 66;</li>
<li>All employees, whether full-time or part-time, aged 16 or over and under 66; and</li>
<li>From 1 January 2024, employed or self-employed people aged between 66 and 70, born before 1 January 1958, who have not been awarded the State Pension (Contributory).</li>
</ul>
<p>The guidance also confirms that the Department of Social Protection (DSP) is responsible for determining the PRSI class that applies. Queries concerning PRSI should therefore be directed to the DSP.</p>
<p><strong>Scope of self-assessment</strong></p>
<p>The Irish Self-Assessment system covers Income Tax and Capital Gains Tax (CGT) for individuals who are chargeable to tax.</p>
<p>It applies to self-employed people carrying on a business, farming, profession or vocation. It also covers individuals with non-PAYE income where some or all of the tax cannot be collected through the PAYE system.</p>
<p>This can include rental profits, investment income, foreign income, foreign pensions, maintenance payments and other fees not subject to PAYE. Registration is generally required where net non-PAYE income exceeds EUR 5,000 or gross non-PAYE income exceeds EUR 30,000.</p>
<p>Individuals can register online through the eRegistration service or by submitting a paper Form TR1. Registration automatically registers the taxpayer for PRSI with the DSP. Taxpayers must use their PPS Number for registrations and communications with Revenue.</p>
<p><strong>Pay and File deadlines</strong></p>
<p>Self-assessment operates under the &#8220;Pay and File&#8221; system, with a standard deadline of 31 October.</p>
<p>Taxpayers must by that date pay Preliminary Tax for the current tax year, file their tax return and self-assessment for the previous tax year, and pay any remaining tax balance for that previous year.</p>
<p>For the 2025 income tax year, the electronic ROS Pay and File deadline has been extended to Wednesday, 18 November 2026.</p>
<p>Preliminary Tax is an estimate of the current year&#8217;s Income Tax, PRSI, and Universal Social Charge (USC). To avoid interest, the payment must generally meet the lowest applicable threshold of 90% of the current year&#8217;s final liability, 100% of the previous year&#8217;s final liability, or 105% of the final liability for the pre-preceding tax year where the direct debit conditions are met.</p>
<p>Late or insufficient Preliminary Tax can result in daily interest under Section 1080 of the Taxes Consolidation Act.</p>
<p><strong>Filing and record requirements</strong></p>
<p>Since January 2015, newly registering or re-registering self-assessed taxpayers have been required to file and pay electronically through ROS, subject to applicable rules.</p>
<p>Self-employed taxpayers must prepare full business accounts but do not generally submit them with their returns. Instead, relevant figures are entered in the &#8220;Extracts from Accounts&#8221; section of Form 11, or its ROS equivalent.</p>
<p>Late filing after 31 October can result in a surcharge of 5% of the tax, capped at EUR 12,695, where the return is filed within two months of the deadline. A 10% surcharge, capped at EUR 63,485, applies where the return is filed more than two months late.</p>
<p>Taxpayers are also required to retain full and accurate business records, including books of accounts, sales and purchase records, bank statements, receipts and invoices, for at least six years.</p>
<p><strong>CGT obligations</strong></p>
<p>The guidance also covers Capital Gains Tax (CGT), which applies to gains arising from the disposal of assets such as land, houses and shares through sales, gifts or donations.</p>
<p>Unlike Income Tax, CGT does not have a Preliminary Tax element and must be paid in full by the relevant deadlines. For disposals between 1 January and 30 November, payment is due by 15 December of the same tax year. For disposals between 1 December and 31 December, payment is due by 31 January of the following tax year.</p>
<p>The disposal must be reported through an Income Tax return, Form 11, or a dedicated Form CG1, by 31 October in the year following the disposal.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>France’s tax authority has updated its guidance on income tax reductions for investments in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), FCPI and FIP funds, and solidarity-based enterprises of social utility (ESUS).</p>
<p>The update <a href="https://bofip.impots.gouv.fr/bofip/15199-PGP.html/ACTU-2026-00156" target="_blank" rel="noopener">published</a> on 27 August 2026 incorporates changes introduced by legislation adopted since 2015, including the Finance Laws for 2025 and 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Changes to SME investment relief</strong></p>
<p>Under <a href="https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/codes/article_lc/LEGIARTI000053543691/2026-02-21" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Article 199 terdecies-0 A of the French General Tax Code (CGI)</a>, individuals who are tax residents in France may qualify for the “Madelin” tax reduction on cash subscriptions to the capital of eligible SMEs.</p>
<p>The relief applies to both direct subscriptions and investments made through a holding company. The updated guidance reflects changes to eligibility requirements, holding periods and financing limits.</p>
<p>The Finance Law for 2026 increased the financing ceiling for eligible enterprises from EUR 15 million to EUR 16.5 million.</p>
<p><strong>FCPI and FIP changes</strong></p>
<p>The guidance also reflects changes to the treatment of FCPI and FIP investments.</p>
<p>The Finance Law for 2025 removed the tax reduction for subscriptions for FIP units, except for FIPs invested in eligible enterprises located in Corsica or overseas territories. It also created a tax reduction for subscriptions for FCPI units invested in young innovative enterprises (JEI).</p>
<p>The Finance Law for 2026 subsequently removed the tax reduction for subscriptions for FCPI units under Article 199 terdecies-0 A of the CGI.</p>
<p>For FIPs in Corsica and overseas territories and FCPI-JEI, the investment period for meeting the required investment quota was extended from 30 months to 48 months.</p>
<p><strong>ESUS and JEI measures</strong></p>
<p>The updated guidance covers tax reductions for investments in solidarity-based enterprises of social utility (ESUS), as well as young innovative enterprises (JEI) and young innovative enterprises with impact (JEII).</p>
<p>The increased 25% rate of the “ESUS” tax reduction has been extended to payments made up to 31 December 2027.</p>
<p><strong>Holding period rules</strong></p>
<p>Investors generally must retain securities received in return for eligible subscriptions until 31 December of the fifth year following the year of subscription.</p>
<p>Legislation provides exceptions to this requirement, including circumstances where the transferor fully reinvests the relevant amount within a maximum period of 12 months.</p>
<p>The updated guidance brings the tax authorities’ comments into line with the latest legislative changes and clarifies the rules applying to the relevant income tax reductions.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Slovak Republic Ministry of Finance has proposed a <a href="https://rokovania.gov.sk/RVL/Material/32111/1" target="_blank" rel="noopener">draft amendment</a>, on 18 August 2026, to Act No. 507/2023 Coll. pertaining to top-up tax, ensuring a global minimum level of taxation for multinational enterprise (MNE) groups and large-scale domestic groups operating in the jurisdiction.</p>
<p>Along with amending Act No. 507/2023 Coll., the draft also introduces modifications to Act No. 563/2009 Coll. on Tax Administration (Tax Code) and several other related regulations.</p>
<p>The original Act No. 507/2023 Coll. transposed Council Directive (EU) 2022/2523 of 15 December 2022. This directive was designed to establish a consistent, global minimum taxation standard across the European Union, utilising the global model rules (Pillar Two) adopted by the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on 14 December 2021.</p>
<p>Key updates include the extension of transitional safe harbours and the introduction of new tax exemptions tied to economic substance. Furthermore, the document addresses administrative continuity by defining how tax obligations are handled when a taxpayer ceases to exist without a legal successor.</p>
<p><strong>Key technical amendments and safe harbours</strong></p>
<p>This draft amendment introduces crucial updates to harmonise Slovak national law with the latest international guidelines on corporate taxation.</p>
<p>The measure expands the transitional &#8220;Safe Harbour&#8221; exemption, which permits qualified Country-by-Country Reporting to replace or simplify top-up tax calculations.</p>
<p>A new substance-based safe harbour targets tax incentives contingent on genuine economic activity. The amendment designates OECD global model rules and their official commentary as authoritative interpretive guidance for implementation. It also establishes successor liability mechanisms to clarify which entity assumes tax obligations when a taxpayer dissolves without a legal heir.</p>
<p><strong>Societal, economic, and budgetary impacts</strong></p>
<p>The explanatory report identifies mixed fiscal consequences from the draft amendment. The public administration budget faces negative impacts, while the business environment and digitalisation of society stand to gain positive effects. The amendment produces no consequences for public expenditure limits, social welfare, environmental protection, citizen-facing public services, or matters related to marriage, parenting, and family structure.</p>
<p><strong>Interdepartmental comments and timeline to effectiveness</strong></p>
<p>The draft amendment underwent an interdepartmental review spanning 25 June to 15 July 2026.</p>
<p>Seventeen comments were submitted during this period, with the Republic Union of Employers (RÚZ SR) and Klub 500 each raising fundamental objections. All disputes arising from these comments were resolved by 28 July 2026.</p>
<p>The law takes effect on 30 December 2026 for point 8 specifically, with all other provisions becoming effective on 31 December 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Belgium&#8217;s Federal Public Service Finance has <a href="https://finances.belgium.be/fr/Actualites/nouveau-code-p%C3%A9nal-entr%C3%A9e-en-vigueur-le-1er-septembre-2026" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> a <a href="https://www.minfin.fgov.be/myminfin-web/pages/public/fisconet/document/2ce1b028-dd26-424c-a360-04bdd91eccba" target="_blank" rel="noopener">reformed Penal Code</a>, which is set to take effect on 1 September 2026. The update establishes parallel systems of eight penalty levels, one applicable to legal entities and another to natural persons, with each tier defined by specific thresholds and opportunities for reduction based on mitigating circumstances.</p>
<p><strong>Penalties for legal entities</strong></p>
<p>The framework organises corporate sanctions into eight tiers, progressing from least to most severe:</p>
<ul>
<li>Level 1: EUR 200–EUR 20,000 (or alternative sanctions such as community service, activity bans, confiscation, profit-based fines, establishment closure, or conviction)</li>
<li>Level 2: EUR 20,001–EUR 360,000 (or community service, probation exceeding 12 months up to two years, cumulative Level 1 sentences, or conviction)</li>
<li>Level 3: EUR 360,001–EUR 600,000</li>
<li>Level 4: EUR 600,001–EUR 800,000</li>
<li>Level 5: EUR 800,001–EUR 1,200,000</li>
<li>Level 6: EUR 1,200,001–EUR 1,600,000</li>
<li>Level 7: EUR 1,600,001–EUR 4,000,000</li>
<li>Level 8: EUR 4,000,001–EUR 5,760,000</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Penalties for natural persons</strong></p>
<p>Individual offenders face custodial and non-custodial measures across eight levels:</p>
<ul>
<li>Level 1: Fines EUR 200–EUR 20,000, community service 20–120 hours, probation six–twelve months, asset confiscation, profit-based penalties, or conviction</li>
<li>Level 2: Imprisonment six months to three years, deprivation of liberty six months to two years, electronic monitoring one month to one year, community service exceeding 120 hours up to 300 hours, probation exceeding 12 months up to two years, or conviction</li>
<li>Level 3: Imprisonment exceeding three years up to five years, or deprivation of liberty exceeding 2 years up to 4 years</li>
<li>Level 4: Imprisonment exceeding five years up to 10 years, or deprivation of liberty exceeding four years up to six years</li>
<li>Level 5: Imprisonment exceeding 10 years up to 15 years, or deprivation of liberty exceeding six years up to 11 years</li>
<li>Level 6: Imprisonment exceeding 15 years up to 20 years, or deprivation of liberty exceeding 11 years up to 16 years</li>
<li>Level 7: Imprisonment exceeding 20 years up to 30 years, or deprivation of liberty exceeding 16 years up to 18 years</li>
<li>Level 8: Life imprisonment or deprivation of liberty exceeding 18 years up to 20 years</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Mitigation and reduction</strong></p>
<p>Both systems permit downward reduction within the penalty hierarchy when mitigating circumstances exist.</p>
<p>For legal entities, a Level 8 offence can drop to Levels 7, 6, 5, 4, or 3; for natural persons, the same reduction pathways apply.</p>
<p>This cascading structure continues through lower levels, with reductions possible at each tier. When an accessory penalty accompanies a Level 1 principal offence and mitigation applies, courts may impose the accessory penalty in place of the principal one.</p>
<p>The penalty level may also be increased in cases of recidivism.</p>
<p>The judge may impose fines either as the primary penalty or as an additional sanction accompanying sentences for level 2 through level 8 infractions. The fine amount depends directly on the severity level assigned.</p>
<p><strong>Fine ranges by penalty level</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Level 2: EUR 200 to EUR 5,000</li>
<li>Level 3: EUR 200 to EUR 10,000</li>
<li>Level 4: EUR 200 to EUR 15,000</li>
<li>Level 5: EUR 200 to EUR 20,000</li>
<li>Level 6: EUR 200 to EUR 25,000</li>
<li>Level 7: EUR 200 to EUR 30,000</li>
<li>Level 8: EUR 200 to EUR 35,000</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Financial circumstances and discretionary reduction</strong></p>
<p>When determining the fine amount, the judge must consider evidence submitted regarding the defendant&#8217;s financial capacity and social circumstances. Should the defendant demonstrate a precarious financial position through documented proof, the judge retains authority to impose a fine below the statutory minimum.</p>
<p>Judges may also authorise instalment payments when case circumstances justify this accommodation, allowing defendants to satisfy fine obligations over time rather than in a single payment.</p>

		<title>Singapore updates EIS with AI activity</title>

					<description><![CDATA[Singapore’s Enterprise Innovation Scheme (EIS) has been expanded to cover the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), allowing businesses to claim a 400% tax deduction or allowance on up to SGD 50,000 of qualifying AI expenditure per Year of Assessment (YA) for YA 2027 and YA 2028. The change is set out in the Inland Revenue...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Singapore’s Enterprise Innovation Scheme (EIS) has been expanded to cover the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), allowing businesses to claim a 400% tax deduction or allowance on up to SGD 50,000 of qualifying AI expenditure per Year of Assessment (YA) for YA 2027 and YA 2028.</p>
<p>The change is set out in the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore’s (IRAS) <a href="https://www.iras.gov.sg/docs/default-source/e-tax/etaxguide_cit_enterprise-innovation-scheme.pdf?sfvrsn=3a36afd3_27" target="_blank" rel="noopener">e-Tax Guide on the Enterprise Innovation Scheme (Third Edition)</a>, which also expands the list of partner institutions under the scheme to include the Sectoral AI Centre of Excellence for Manufacturing. The new AI activity does not qualify for the EIS cash payout option.</p>
<p><strong>Six qualifying activities</strong></p>
<p>The EIS was introduced under Singapore’s Budget 2023 for YA 2024 to YA 2028 to encourage businesses to undertake R&amp;D, innovation and capability development activities.</p>
<p>Following the Budget 2026 enhancements, the scheme covers six qualifying activities:</p>
<ul>
<li>Qualifying R&amp;D activities undertaken in Singapore, with a cap of SGD 400,000 per YA.</li>
<li>Registration of Intellectual Property (IP), with a cap of SGD 400,000 per YA.</li>
<li>Acquisition and licensing of IP Rights (IPRs), subject to a combined cap of SGD 400,000 per YA.</li>
<li>Qualifying Training expenditure, capped at SGD 400,000 per YA.</li>
<li>Innovation projects carried out with partner institutions, capped at SGD 50,000 per YA.</li>
<li>Adoption of AI, capped at SGD 50,000 per YA for YA 2027 and YA 2028.</li>
</ul>
<p>A business incurring qualifying expenditure across all six activities can claim enhanced deductions on up to SGD 1.7 million of qualifying expenditure per YA.</p>
<p><strong>AI adoption expenditure</strong></p>
<p>The new AI activity applies to qualifying expenditure incurred for the adoption of AI during YA 2027 and YA 2028.</p>
<p>Eligible expenditure includes subscription or licensing costs for AI systems and qualifying AI business services. Physical infrastructure and hardware, including servers and computing equipment, are excluded.</p>
<p>Businesses can receive a 400% tax deduction or allowance on qualifying AI expenditure up to the SGD 50,000 annual cap.</p>
<p>However, AI adoption expenditure cannot be converted into an EIS cash payout.</p>
<p><strong>Enhanced deductions and allowances</strong></p>
<p>The EIS provides enhanced tax deductions and allowances in addition to prevailing base deductions. The total deductions or allowances are effectively 400% per dollar of qualifying expenditure, subject to the relevant expenditure cap for each activity.</p>
<p>Expenditure above the applicable caps continues to qualify for standard base deductions or allowances under prevailing income tax rules.</p>
<p>For the acquisition and licensing of qualifying IPRs, eligibility for the enhanced writing-down allowance (WDA) or tax deductions requires the business, or its group where applicable, to derive less than SGD 500 million in revenue in the basis period for the relevant YA.</p>
<p>Enhanced deductions that cannot be fully offset against business income are treated as unutilised trade losses or allowances. They may be carried forward, transferred under the Group Relief system or carried back to the preceding YA, subject to prevailing tax rules.</p>
<p><strong>Cash payout remains available for other activities</strong></p>
<p>Eligible businesses can choose a non-taxable cash payout instead of tax deductions or allowances for qualifying expenditure under activities other than AI adoption.</p>
<p>The cash conversion rate is 20% on up to SGD 100,000 of total qualifying expenditure across activities (a) to (e) per YA, giving a maximum cash payout of SGD 20,000 per YA.</p>
<p>The choice is irrevocable. Once expenditure has been converted into a cash payout, it cannot subsequently be claimed for tax deductions or allowances.</p>
<p>Each cash payout application must meet a minimum expenditure threshold of SGD 400, and only one application can be filed per YA.</p>
<p>For IP registration and IPR acquisition, cash conversion is determined separately for each registration or IPR. Any expenditure exceeding the applicable cash conversion cap is forfeited and cannot be claimed as tax deductions.</p>
<p><strong>Cash payout eligibility</strong></p>
<p>To qualify for the cash payout, a company, partnership or sole-proprietorship must carry on business operations in Singapore.</p>
<p>It must also employ at least three full-time local employees for six months or more during the basis period of the relevant YA. The employees must be Singapore Citizens or Permanent Residents with CPF contributions.</p>
<p>A full-time local employee must earn a gross monthly salary of at least SGD 1,400 and be contracted to work at least 35 hours a week.</p>
<p>The requirement excludes sole-proprietors, partners of a partnership except non-equity salaried partners under a contract of service, and shareholder-directors of a company.</p>
<p>The business must also be carrying on a trade or business and must not have ceased business when the cash payout is disbursed.</p>
<p><strong>Compliance and claw-back rules</strong></p>
<p>Where qualifying expenditure is subsidised by a government grant or subsidy, only the amount net of the grant or subsidy is eligible for enhanced deductions or cash payouts.</p>
<p>For IP registration and IPR acquisition, the business must own the related IPRs, or keep the application active, for at least one year.</p>
<p>If an IPR is disposed of, or an application is assigned or ceased, within one year, enhanced deductions are clawed back and treated as taxable income, while the entire cash payout is recovered.</p>
<p>For IPR acquisitions where a cash payout was received, disposal after the first year but within five years results in a proportionate claw-back of the cash payout.</p>
<p>Companies claim enhanced deductions through their income tax returns. Sole-proprietors and partners must submit claims through the IRAS digital service “Submit EIS Enhanced Deduction/Allowance Records” after filing their income tax returns and before the filing deadline.</p>
<p>Eligible businesses seeking a cash payout must submit an irrevocable application through “Apply for EIS Cash Payout” after filing their tax returns and before the filing due date.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

The changes were introduced by Article 16 of Law No. 2026-103 of...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>France has <a href="https://bofip.impots.gouv.fr/bofip/15132-PGP.html/ACTU-2026-00121" target="_blank" rel="noopener">clarified</a>, on 19 August 2026, the tax treatment of sole proprietorship restructuring where an individual entrepreneur elects for Corporate Income Tax (IS), introducing optional mechanisms to defer, suspend or spread taxation of capital gains and profits arising during the restructuring process.</p>
<p>The changes were introduced by Article 16 of Law No. 2026-103 of 19 February 2026 on finance for 2026. The measures allow an individual entrepreneur restructuring a sole proprietorship to benefit, on an elective basis, from tax neutrality for interim transactions.</p>
<p>The restructuring may be carried out in two stages. First, the individual entrepreneur can elect under paragraph 1 or 2 of Article 1655 sexies of the French General Tax Code (CGI) for the sole proprietorship to be assimilated to a single-member limited liability company (EURL) or a limited liability agricultural enterprise (EARL), resulting in an election for Corporate Income Tax (IS).</p>
<p>Second, the restructuring may continue through the contribution of the sole proprietorship, which is then subject to IS, to a company.</p>
<p><strong>Election for assimilation to an EURL or EARL</strong></p>
<p>Article 16 amended Article 1655 sexies of the CGI to clarify the consequences of electing to assimilate a sole proprietorship to an EURL or EARL. The election results in the cessation of the sole proprietorship and the transfer of its assets to the balance sheet of the sole proprietorship assimilated to an EURL or EARL and subject to IS.</p>
<p>To prevent the immediate taxation of capital gains and profits realised upon cessation of activity, Article 16 establishes an optional regime under Article 151 octies D of the CGI. The regime provides, in particular, for the deferral or spreading of taxation of capital gains.</p>
<p>The provisions apply to elections made from 1 January 2026 and to financial years closed from that date.</p>
<p><strong>Contribution of the business to a company</strong></p>
<p>The restructuring can subsequently continue through the contribution to a company of all the assets of the sole proprietorship assimilated to an EURL or EARL, or one of its complete branches of activity (BCA).</p>
<p>Article 16 establishes a second optional regime under Article 210 E bis of the CGI to prevent the immediate taxation of capital gains and profits realised through such a contribution. The regime provides, in particular, for the suspension or spreading of taxation of capital gains.</p>
<p>These provisions apply to contributions made from 1 January 2026 and to financial years closed from the same date.</p>
<p>Capital gains on the securities received in consideration for the contribution to the company also benefit from a suspension of taxation. They will therefore be taxed only when the securities are disposed of, in the name of the individual entrepreneur as a natural person, under the conditions set out in Article 150-0 D of the CGI.</p>
<p>The mechanism for suspending taxation of these capital gains will be addressed in a subsequent publication in the BOFiP-Impôts.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Malaysia’s government has published <a href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1SKGa0tZLN3vjfaWE27Al7LhVZAwbrBTz/view?usp=drive_link" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Order No. P.U. (A) 300/2026</a>, the Income Tax (Transfer Pricing) (Amendment) Rules 2026, in the Official Gazette on 27 August 2026, officially updating Malaysia&#8217;s regulatory framework regarding transactions between related entities, with retroactive effects beginning in assessment year 2023.</p>
<p>These rules refine the legal definition of services and clarify that a Multinational Enterprise Group must operate across at least two different jurisdictions.</p>
<p>The key amendments to the Income Tax (Transfer Pricing) (Amendment) Rules 2026 are:</p>
<p><strong>Revision of the definition of &#8220;service&#8221;</strong></p>
<p>The first measure amends Rule 3 of the principal Rules to refine the definition of a &#8220;service&#8221;. The amendment replaces the phrase &#8220;facilities provided, or are to be provided&#8221; with the grammatically corrected phrase &#8220;facilities that are or to be provided&#8221;. This linguistic update ensures grammatical and statutory precision within the transfer pricing framework.</p>
<p><strong>Standardised definition of a &#8220;multinational enterprise group&#8221; (MNE group)</strong></p>
<p>The second measure replaces subrule (4) of Rule 4 in the principal Rules to establish a clear definition of an MNE Group. Under the substituted subrule, a &#8220;Multinational Enterprise Group&#8221; is formally defined as a group of associated enterprises that maintain business establishments in two or more jurisdictions.</p>
<p><strong>Deletion of the transfer pricing provision under Rule 10</strong></p>
<p>The third measure alters Rule 10 of the principal Rules by deleting subrule (3) in its entirety. Although the amendment rules do not explicitly detail the contents of the original subrule (3), its formal deletion means that the specific transfer pricing requirement is no longer applicable under domestic law.</p>
<p><strong>Implementation of offsetting adjustments</strong></p>
<p>The fourth measure inserts a new subrule (1A) immediately after subrule (1) of Rule 13 in the principal Rules to govern offsetting adjustments. This amendment establishes that a transfer pricing adjustment made under subrule (1) against a person in a controlled transaction can be reflected by a corresponding offsetting adjustment on the assessment of the other person in that same transaction. To utilise this mechanism, the other person must formally submit a request, and the offsetting adjustment remains strictly subject to the approval of the Director General.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Cambodia’s General Department of Taxation (GDT) has clarified the scope of dental services that are non-taxable for VAT purposes, covering examinations, dental and gum treatments, surgery, restorative procedures, orthodontics and certain cosmetic services.</p>
<p>The<a href="https://www.tax.gov.kh/en/article?key=5XZ9ixY2234196x8173" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> clarification</a>, issued through an Instruction dated 17 August 2026, requires dental service providers to apply the VAT treatment when complying with their VAT self-declaration obligations. The guidance refers to the VAT exemption provided under Article 63 of the Law on Taxation.</p>
<p>The measure applies to dental clinics and enterprises registered under Cambodia’s self-declaration tax regime, with the covered services divided into four main categories.</p>

<p>The non-taxable treatment category covers basic or regular dental cleaning and scaling, including manual and mechanical procedures. It also includes surgical and non-surgical gum treatments, gum grafting and restorative dental fillings.</p>
<p><strong>Surgical and restorative services</strong></p>
<p>Services covered under this category include tooth extractions, oral and dental surgery, root canal treatments (endodontics), dental implant placement, dentures and tissue and bone grafting and regeneration.</p>
<p><strong>Maintenance, orthodontics and cosmetic services</strong></p>
<p>The exemption also extends to protective sealants and fluoride applications, dental crowns, veneers, bonding, polishing and bridges.</p>
<p>Orthodontic treatments, including braces and aligners, are also included. The guidance covers specialised orthodontic and protective appliances such as mouth muscle trainers, palate or jaw expanders, retainers, space maintainers and mouthguards or night guards/splints.</p>
<p>The placement of removable dentures and other dental prostheses is likewise included within the non-taxable scope.</p>
<p>The GDT expects all dental service providers to follow the Instruction when determining their VAT treatment and fulfilling their self-declaration obligations.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Belgium’s Ministry of Finance has published <a href="https://www.minfin.fgov.be/myminfin-web/pages/public/fisconet/document/086b50bf-71c6-42e8-994d-0a97e076ada6" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Circular No. 2026/C/79</a>, dated 26 August 2026, guiding the phase-out of the spousal income transfer regime introduced by the law of 15 July 2026.</p>
<p>Circular 2026/C/79 provides detailed guidance on the gradual phase-out and modification of the Belgian spousal income transfer regime (the marriage quotient). This regime historically allowed married or legally cohabiting partners to attribute up to 30% of their professional income (capped at a basic amount of EUR 6,700) to a partner with no or very low professional income to reduce their collective tax burden. These modifications aim to strengthen tax neutrality across cohabitation models and pivot away from single-earner tax incentives.</p>
<p>The circular details the following major changes:</p>
<p><strong>Freezing of indexation</strong></p>
<p>Starting in assessment year 2027, the indexation of the marriage quotient&#8217;s maximum amounts is permanently frozen. A fixed indexation coefficient is introduced into Article 178 of the Income Tax Code (WIB 92) to maintain static maximum values moving forward.</p>
<p><strong>Two phased reduction schemes</strong></p>
<p>From assessment year 2027, the application of the marriage quotient depends on the spouses&#8217; age as of January 1 of the assessment year:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Gradual phasing-out scheme (both spouses reached age 66/67): </strong>Where both spouses have reached age 66 (rising to 67 from 2031), the 30% rate will remain, but the maximum indexed amount will gradually decline from EUR 12,790 in 2027 to EUR 0 by 2046, when the regime will be fully abolished for this group.</li>
<li><strong>Gradual reduction scheme (one or both spouses under age 66/67):</strong> For other eligible couples, where at least one spouse is below the age threshold, the maximum indexed amount will decrease from EUR 11,780 in 2027 to EUR 6,730 from 2030 onwards. The 30% rate will remain unchanged throughout.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Joint tax return exclusions &amp; &#8220;maximum amount&#8221; replacement</strong></p>
<p>In certain scenarios, Belgian tax law excludes spouses from joint assessment—for instance, when one resident spouse has treaty-exempt professional income without a progression reservation, or when a non-resident spouse has exempt foreign or domestic professional income.</p>
<ul>
<li>Previously, joint assessment was avoided if this exempt income exceeded the &#8220;maximum amount of the marriage quotient&#8221;.</li>
<li>Because assessment year 2027 introduces two separate maximum amounts based on age, the law replaces this reference. The threshold is now linked to the basic amount of the tax-free allowance to prevent application conflicts.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Special provisions for scholarships</strong></p>
<p>From assessment year 2027, joint taxation will no longer apply where a spouse receives a fully tax-exempt study grant or scholarship that provides full or partial social security rights. The change primarily targets doctoral scholarship holders, whose exempt income could otherwise prevent their spouses from benefiting from the marriage quotient or transferred tax-free allowances.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Slovak Republic clarifies e-invoicing, Peppol and VAT coding rules ahead of 2027 mandate in updated FAQ </title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/slovak-republic-clarifies-e-invoicing-peppol-and-vat-coding-rules-ahead-of-2027-mandate-in-updated-faq/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=slovak-republic-clarifies-e-invoicing-peppol-and-vat-coding-rules-ahead-of-2027-mandate-in-updated-faq</link>

					<description><![CDATA[The Slovak Republic’s Financial Directorate updated its eFaktúra FAQ in August 2026, providing businesses and service providers with practical clarifications on the domestic e-invoicing requirements. The update also adds guidance on Peppol VAT Category Codes and VAT Exemption Reason Codes (VATEX) applicable in Slovakia ahead of the mandatory e-invoicing regime taking effect on 1 January...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Slovak Republic’s Financial Directorate updated its eFaktúra <a href="https://www.financnasprava.sk/_img/pfsedit/Dokumenty_PFS/Zverejnovanie_dok/Aktualne/DPH/2026/2026.08.26_009_DPH_2025_IM_FaQ_eFaktura.pdf.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">FAQ</a> in August 2026, providing businesses and service providers with practical clarifications on the domestic e-invoicing requirements. The update also adds guidance on Peppol VAT Category Codes and VAT Exemption Reason Codes (VATEX) applicable in Slovakia ahead of the mandatory e-invoicing regime taking effect on 1 January 2027.</p>
<p>Starting January 1, 2027, businesses and legal entities in Slovakia must transition to a structured XML format for domestic transactions to enhance automation and reduce administrative errors. This new system utilises the Peppol network and certified service providers, known as Digital Postal Workers, to securely transmit and receive data in real time.</p>
<p>While B2B and B2G transactions are the primary focus, the guide clarifies that consumers and certain classified government entities remain exempt. Taxpayers can enter a voluntary transition period throughout 2026 to test their systems before full enforcement begins.</p>
<p>Below is a detailed summary of the key updates:</p>
<p><strong>E-Invoice issuance and timing</strong></p>
<p>An e-invoice must be sent or made available to the customer within 15 days of the supply or payment receipt. Creating it in an accounting system alone does not meet the deadline. An invoice is considered issued when submitted to the Peppol delivery service. The issue date is when the invoice is sent or made available to the recipient.</p>
<p><strong>Peppol non-registration: Issuance, email delivery, and VAT deduction</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Fulfilment of the e-invoice obligation: </strong>Submitting a compliant XML e-invoice to an Accredited Service Provider within the statutory deadline discharges the supplier&#8217;s issuance and sending obligation, regardless of whether the recipient has registered with Peppol or secured a digital postman. The obligation is satisfied at submission to the ASP.</li>
<li><strong>Email as secondary delivery:</strong> When Peppol delivery fails, the supplier may resend the same standard-compliant XML invoice via email. This constitutes re-disclosure of an already-issued invoice, not a new issuance. The recipient&#8217;s consent is required for out-of-network transmission (email, for example), though consent carries no rigid formality requirement—written agreement, email confirmation, contractual language, or even implied acceptance (such as payment of the emailed invoice) all suffice.</li>
<li><strong>VAT deduction remains available: </strong>Recipients may claim input VAT deduction on the emailed invoice provided it complies with Section 85o of the VAT Act and meets the substantive and formal requirements under Sections 49 to 51. Email delivery following a failed Peppol attempt does not, by itself, disqualify the deduction.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Factoring (receivable assignment)</strong></p>
<p>The Slovak Republic’s VAT Act does not contain a specific mechanism for factoring or the assignment of receivables (regulated under Sections 524 to 530 of the Civil Code). Instead, businesses must follow the European EN 16931 standard and standard Civil Code requirements.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Scenario A (Assignment known at issuance): </strong>The supplier may include the factor’s details, payment information and assignment notes on the e-invoice. Invoice type 380 or 393 may be used.</li>
<li><strong>Scenario B (Assignment occurs after issuance):</strong> A new e-invoice or corrective document is not issued solely because a receivable is assigned after the fact. Instead, the supplier must notify the debtor under standard Civil Code rules, which is a separate communication process completely outside the Peppol network and does not change the original XML data.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>VAT group internal transactions</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Treatment of supplies:</strong> Supplies between members of the same registered VAT group are treated as internal supplies within a single taxable person. They are not subject to VAT and do not trigger any statutory invoice obligation under Section 72 or Section 85o of the VAT Act.</li>
<li><strong>No Peppol exchange obligation: </strong>There is no legal obligation to exchange these documents via Peppol, although doing so voluntarily is permitted. Members may also exchange these documents via email or internal systems, and doing so does not require DPH-compliant consent rules.</li>
<li><strong>Voluntary Peppol rules for group transactions:</strong> Group members exchanging documents voluntarily via Peppol must use each member’s unique DIČ as the EndpointID with prefix 0245 and apply VAT Category “O”. Under BR-O-02, the invoice must omit the Seller’s and Buyer’s VAT IDs (IČ DPH), including the group’s common VAT ID, to pass validation.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Self-billing reporting deadline and clarification</strong></p>
<p>Self-billed invoices remain permitted under the draft law when a written agreement establishes predefined conditions between supplier and customer.</p>
<p>Unlike standard e-invoices, which require real-time reporting to the tax authority upon issuance, self-billed invoices (issued by the customer on the supplier&#8217;s behalf) grant the supplier a five-day reporting window.</p>
<p>This deadline begins either from the date the self-billed invoice is issued or, where an invoice-issuance deadline applies, from its expiry—recognising that suppliers may not have immediate visibility into when customers generate the documents.</p>
<p><strong>New VAT category code and VATEX mapping section</strong></p>
<p>The updated guide introduces a Slovakia-specific mapping for Peppol VAT Category Codes (BT-118/BT-151) and European VATEX exemption codes (BT-121). The VAT category must be chosen based on the actual legal VAT regime, not simply on whether the VAT amount is zero (since DPH 0 EUR can represent various legal regimes).</p>
<p>The core mapped categories for Slovakia are:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Standard rate (S): </strong>Taxable domestic supplies under Section 27, covering basic and reduced rates (23%, 19%, or 5%). No VATEX code is used.</li>
<li><strong>Exempt from tax (E):</strong> Domestic VAT-exempt supplies under Sections 28 to 42 (such as postal, healthcare, social services, education, sports, cultural, financial, insurance, real estate, and other exempt supplies).</li>
<li><strong>Intra-community supply (K):</strong> VAT-exempt supply of goods from Slovakia to another EU member state (Section 43).</li>
<li><strong>Export outside the EU (G): </strong>VAT-exempt export of goods outside the EU (Section 47).</li>
<li><strong>Reverse charge (AE): </strong>Transactions under Section 69 where the customer accounts for the tax.</li>
<li><strong>Not subject to VAT (O): </strong>Transactions outside the scope of VAT, including certain internal transactions between members of the same Slovak VAT group.</li>
<li><strong>Zero-rated goods (Z): </strong>Applies only to goods with a legally established zero rate. No VATEX.</li>
</ul>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has updated its guidance on the permanent AUD 20,000 instant asset write-off for small businesses with annual turnover below AUD 10 million. The measure, previously due to end in June 2026, has been permanently extended under the <a href="https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2026A00071/asmade/text" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 2) Act 2026</a>.</p>
<p>The Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 2) Act 2026 is a legislative document from the Parliament of Australia designed to modify existing taxation frameworks. It introduces key changes to the simplified depreciation rules for small business entities, specifically focusing on the instant asset write-off threshold and the lockout rule.</p>
<p>A primary focus of this legislation is the introduction of a loss carry-back tax offset, which allows eligible corporate entities to apply current losses against prior tax liabilities to receive a refundable tax credit. Beyond this offset, the Act outlines specific financial provisions such as an instant asset write-off for small businesses and amendments regarding negative gearing and certain income tax exemptions.</p>
<p>The updated guidance includes:</p>
<p><strong><a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/depreciation-and-capital-expenses-and-allowances/simpler-depreciation-for-small-business/instant-asset-write-off" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Instant asset write-off for eligible businesses</a></strong></p>
<p>The instant asset write-off threshold is AUD 20,000 per asset from 1 July 2023. It applies to new and second-hand assets under the simplified depreciation rules. Businesses may also claim later additions costing less than the threshold to assets that were previously written off.</p>
<p>The threshold has changed several times, including AUD 20,000 (2016–January 2019), AUD 25,000 (January–April 2019), AUD 30,000 (April 2019–March 2020), AUD 150,000 (March 2020–June 2021), before returning to AUD 20,000 from July 2023.</p>
<p>For 2025–26, the car depreciation limit is AUD 69,674, meaning depreciation cannot be claimed on the portion of a passenger vehicle exceeding this amount. GST-registered businesses must exclude the GST credit when determining whether an asset falls below the threshold. Assets costing at or above the threshold are generally allocated to the small business pool.</p>
<p><strong><a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/depreciation-and-capital-expenses-and-allowances/simpler-depreciation-for-small-business" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Simpler depreciation rules for small businesses</a></strong></p>
<p>Businesses with aggregated annual turnover below AUD 10 million can generally use the simplified depreciation rules. These combine the instant asset write-off with a small business pool, which is depreciated at 15% in the first year and 30% in subsequent years. The pool can be fully deducted once its balance falls below the current write-off threshold.</p>
<p>The instant asset write-off was unavailable from 6 October 2020 to 30 June 2023, when temporary full expensing applied instead. Businesses opting into simplified depreciation must generally apply the rules to all eligible assets, while opting out prevents new assets from being added to the pool or immediately written off. Existing pool balances continue to depreciate at 30%.</p>
<p>The usual five-year re-entry restriction following an opt-out is suspended until 30 June 2027. Businesses must retain relevant depreciation records for five years, including pool balances, changes in business use and asset disposals.</p>
<p><strong><a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/income-and-deductions-for-business/deductions/deductions-for-depreciating-assets-and-capital-expenses" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Deductions for depreciating assets and capital expenses</a></strong></p>
<p>Depreciating assets are items with a limited effective life that decline in value over time, such as machinery, vehicles, computers and phones. Land, trading stock and most intangible assets generally do not qualify, although certain land improvements may be depreciable.</p>
<p>Outside the simplified rules, businesses can calculate depreciation using the Commissioner’s effective-life determinations or their own reasonable estimate. Only the business-use portion of an asset is deductible.</p>
<p>Certain capital expenses may also qualify for specific deductions. Eligible website development costs may be immediately deductible or depreciated over five years, while hosting and domain costs are generally deductible as incurred. Off-the-shelf software with an effective life of one year or less may qualify for an immediate deduction; otherwise, the cost is spread over its effective life.</p>
<p>Eligible business establishment and wind-down costs may generally be deducted over five years, although professional advice and certain government fees may qualify for immediate deductions for businesses with turnover below AUD 50 million.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/australia-senate-passes-tax-reform-bill-introducing-permanent-loss-carry-back-aud-20000-asset-write-off/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, the Australian Senate approved the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 2) Bill 2026 on 19 August 2026, following its passage by the House of Representatives on 18 August 2026.</p>
]]></content:encoded>
