										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Cyprus Ministry of Finance has opened a <a href="https://e-consultation.gov.cy/diavouleuseis/%CE%BF-%CF%80%CE%B5%CF%81%CE%AF-%CE%B5%CE%BE%CE%B1%CF%83%CF%86%CE%AC%CE%BB%CE%B9%CF%83%CE%B7%CF%82-%CF%80%CE%B1%CE%B3%CE%BA%CE%BF%CF%83%CE%BC%CE%AF%CE%BF%CF%85-%CE%B5%CE%BB%CE%AC%CF%87%CE%B9%CF%83" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation</a> on 30 July 2026, on the Global Minimum Level of Taxation for Multinational Enterprise Groups and Large-Scale Domestic Groups in the Union (Amendment) Law of 2026.</p>
<p>The amending bill was prepared following observations from the European Commission on the correct transposition of Council Directive (EU) 2022/2523, as amended by Council Directive (EU) 2023/2861 of 14 December 2023, concerning the Pillar Two global minimum tax rules.</p>
<p><strong>Amendments to QDMTT</strong></p>
<p>The bill proposes changes to the definitions and mechanics of the domestic top-up tax implemented by Cyprus. These amendments are intended to ensure that the measure meets the Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (QDMTT) standards established under the EU Directive and the OECD framework.</p>
<p>The bill also incorporates the option to apply a Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (QDMTT) with effect from 1 January 2026.</p>
<p>In addition, further amendments have been included to align Cyprus’ implementation of the Pillar Two rules with relevant OECD guidelines and recommendations.</p>
<p><strong>Scope of Pillar Two rules</strong></p>
<p>The Pillar Two framework applies a minimum effective tax rate of 15% to entities belonging to Multinational Enterprise Groups or large-scale domestic groups with annual revenues exceeding EUR 750 million.</p>
<p>The framework is intended to address arrangements that allow multinational enterprises to shift profits to jurisdictions where they face zero or very low taxation.</p>
<p>The proposed amendments will allow Cyprus to address the European Commission’s observations and make further changes based on OECD guidance ahead of the Republic of Cyprus’ assessment in autumn 2026. The assessment will consider whether Cyprus’ national legislative framework complies with the internationally agreed Pillar Two rules.</p>
<p>The consultation officer is Naya Syrimi, who can be contacted at nsyrimi@mof.gov.cy or 22601267. Stakeholders have until 5 September 2026 at 23:50 to submit comments.</p>

The proposed rules would generally apply to taxable years beginning on or after 1 January 2026 under the Personal Responsibility and Work...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The US Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) proposed regulations (<a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-16985/application-of-the-personal-responsibility-and-work-opportunity-reconciliation-act-of-1996-to-the" target="_blank" rel="noopener">REG-119882-25</a>)  on 20 August 2026 that would extend federal immigration-status restrictions to the refundable portions of four tax credits. The proposed rules would generally apply to taxable years beginning on or after 1 January 2026 under the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996.</p>
<p>The proposal seeks to classify the refunded portion of the Adoption Tax Credit, Child Tax Credit, American Opportunity Tax Credit, and Earned Income Credit as &#8220;Federal public benefits.&#8221; Under this designation, and under the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA), individuals who are not qualified aliens would be prohibited from receiving these payments.</p>
<p>The proposed regulations designate the refunded portion of four specific tax credits as &#8220;Federal public benefits&#8221;:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>The earned income tax credit (EITC): </strong>A fully refundable credit designed to encourage work. For tax year 2025, maximum benefits range from USD 649 (no children) to USD 8,046 (three or more qualifying children). The OLC categorised EITC refunds as welfare or similar benefits.</li>
<li><strong>The child tax credit (CTC) &amp; additional child tax credit (ACTC):</strong> For tax year 2025, the CTC is up to USD 2,200 per qualifying child. Taxpayers with insufficient tax liability claim the refundable portion as the ACTC, which is capped at USD 1,700 per child.</li>
<li><strong>The American opportunity tax credit (AOTC):</strong> A higher-education credit of up to USD 2,500 per student, of which 40% (up to USD 1,000) is refundable. The OLC classified this portion as a postsecondary education benefit.</li>
<li><strong>The adoption tax credit:</strong> Under section 23(a)(4), up to USD 5,000 of this credit is refundable starting in 2025. Although the OLC did not explicitly address this credit, the Treasury included it because the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has long classified federal adoption assistance programs as public benefits.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Exclusions from the proposed rules</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Premium tax credit (PTC): </strong>Although classified as a public benefit, the PTC is excluded because later laws, including the ACA and OBBBA, established more specific immigration rules that supersede PRWORA.</li>
<li><strong>Saver’s match:</strong> The Treasury and IRS will address this credit in separate proposed regulations before it takes effect in 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Trump accounts contribution pilot program:</strong> OBBBA already restricts the program to US citizens, overriding PRWORA restrictions.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Defining the &#8220;refunded portion&#8221;</strong></p>
<p>The proposed immigration-status restrictions apply only to the refunded portion of affected credits, not the entire credit. Non-qualified aliens may still use the credits to reduce their tax liability to zero but cannot receive any excess as a cash refund, carryover, or offset. Where multiple affected credits are claimed, their amounts are combined to determine the restricted overpayment.</p>
<p><strong>The &#8220;first claim&#8221; timing rule</strong></p>
<p>The regulations determine eligibility based on a taxpayer’s immigration status on the date they first claim the credit for a taxable year, whether through an original, late, or amended return. Thus, a taxpayer who was undocumented when first claiming the credit remains ineligible even if their status later changes, while a taxpayer who obtains qualified status before making their first claim may qualify.</p>
<p><strong>Public comments and hearing information</strong></p>
<p>The IRS is seeking public comments on the proposed eligibility rules, with written comments and requests to speak due by 5 October 2026. A public hearing is scheduled for 14 October 2026 at 10:00 AM ET, subject to cancellation if no speaking requests are received. Requests to attend the hearing must be submitted by 5:00 PM ET on 9 October 2026.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[Argentina’s tax administration (ARCA) announced on 27 August 2026 that it activated the Investment Management System (SGI), a web platform for registering investment projects, selecting tax benefits, and administering the Incentive Regime for Medium-Sized Investments (RIMI).  General Resolution 5889/2026, effective 25 August 2026, established the system to centralise and digitise tax incentive management tied to...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Argentina’s tax administration (ARCA) <a href="https://servicioscf.afip.gob.ar/publico/sitio/contenido/novedad/ver.aspx?id=5879" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> on 27 August 2026 that it activated the Investment Management System (SGI), a web platform for registering investment projects, selecting tax benefits, and administering the Incentive Regime for Medium-Sized Investments (RIMI).  General Resolution 5889/2026, effective 25 August 2026, established the system to centralise and digitise tax incentive management tied to productive investments.</p>
<p><strong>RIMI background</strong></p>
<p>Law 27,802 (Labour Modernisation), Title XXIII, created RIMI to support medium-sized investments—domestic and foreign—in Argentina&#8217;s productive sectors. The regime offers two tax benefits for investments in depreciable movable assets and works completed within a two-year investment window:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Accelerated depreciation applied to income tax calculations. </strong>This mechanism allows faster accounting of asset wear and economic consumption, advancing deductions from income tax.</li>
<li><strong>VAT tax credit recovery or refund. </strong>This benefit prevents tax credits generated by productive investments from remaining trapped in the system indefinitely.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>How the system operates</strong></p>
<p>ARCA made available through SGI is a centralised registry where project operators can report productive investments, document commencement dates, link supporting receipts, and select applicable tax benefits. The platform performs early validations using data already held in ARCA databases and presents electronic receipts to taxpayers for validation, with manual adjustment options through upload or data import.</p>
<p><strong>How are benefits managed?</strong></p>
<p>The tax incentive must be selected when the investment project is registered in the SGI, with the procedure varying according to the applicable incentive.</p>
<p>VAT credit recovery requires submission of a pre-application through SGI, followed by formal application under General Resolution 5.173.</p>
<p>Accelerated amortisation must be uploaded to SGI before the income tax return due date in which the deduction appears.</p>
<p>The regulation mandates alignment between SGI-reported assets and depreciation calculations and those declared in income tax filings.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Romania launches tech incentive and grants scheme for AI, biotech, green energy</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/romania-launches-tech-incentive-and-grants-scheme-for-ai-biotech-green-energy/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=romania-launches-tech-incentive-and-grants-scheme-for-ai-biotech-green-energy</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Mohammed Al Mamun]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Fri, 28 Aug 2026 10:45:31 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Industry/manufacturing]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Europe]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Romania]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=86892</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Romania published Government Decision (GD) No. 643/2026  in the Official Gazette (Monitorul Oficial, Nr. 699) on 24 August 2026, establishing the &#8220;TechUp Romania&#8221; state aid scheme. Approved by the Government on 20 August 2026,  the scheme operates as a block-exempted measure under European Commission Regulation (UE) No. 651/2014, meaning it does not require formal notification...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Romania published Government Decision (GD) No. 643/2026  in the <a href="https://monitoruloficial.ro/Monitorul-Oficial--PI--699--2026.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Official Gazette </a>(Monitorul Oficial, Nr. 699) on 24 August 2026, establishing the &#8220;TechUp Romania&#8221; state aid scheme.</p>
<p>Approved by the Government on 20 August 2026,  the scheme operates as a block-exempted measure under European Commission Regulation (UE) No. 651/2014, meaning it does not require formal notification to the European Commission.</p>
<p>The legislative framework for this scheme was set through Government Emergency Ordinance (GEO) No. 8/2026, and is designed to provide financial support for advanced technologies and high-impact innovation sectors, such as artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and green energy.</p>
<p>The scheme supports both research and development (R&amp;D) activities under Component I and subsequent regional investments in production, commercialisation, or technology services under Component II.</p>
<p>The key provisions are as follows:</p>
<p><strong>Targeted advanced technology domains (Annex 1)</strong></p>
<p>Eligible projects must focus on one of six advanced technology fields: AI, computing and microelectronics; biotechnology, agritech and precision health; green energy, storage and climate technology; mobility, space and autonomous systems; advanced materials and Industry 4.0; or cybersecurity and digital security.</p>
<p><strong>Two-component project structure and boundaries</strong></p>
<p>Eligible projects must be independent and separable, with total eligible costs (excluding VAT) between RON 5 million and RON 50 million. Each project must sequentially link two components:</p>
<p><strong>Component I (R&amp;D) </strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Must represent a minimum of RON 2 million in eligible costs.</li>
<li>The execution period is limited to 48 months (extendable to 60 months for sectors with longer development cycles specified in the Guidelines).</li>
<li>Stage 1 (Industrial research): Starts at Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 3, moving to TRL 4 (prototype development and validation).</li>
<li>Stage 2 (Experimental development): Focuses on scaling the prototype to reach TRL 8 (commercial system design). This stage is mandatory.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Component II (Regional investments in production/services)</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Must represent a minimum of RON 3 million in eligible costs.</li>
<li>Entails setting up production capacities or service provisions that directly deploy the deep tech developed in Component I.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Component I (R&amp;D): Combined funding and cost rules</strong></p>
<p>Beneficiaries may combine non-refundable grants with a 200% corporate income tax deduction for eligible R&amp;D expenditure, covering qualifying tangible and intangible assets, personnel and contracted research costs, and overheads of up to 20% of personnel costs. However, the same project costs cannot also benefit from general tax incentives under Articles 20 and 20¹ of the Romanian Fiscal Code.</p>
<p><strong>Component II (Regional investments): Cost routes and limits</strong></p>
<p>Under Component II, companies can choose between two cost routes: salary costs for two consecutive years for newly created project-related jobs, or investments in new tangible and intangible assets. The asset route caps construction costs at 40% of eligible tangible assets and intangible assets at 30% of total eligible costs, with assets required to remain operational and in the region for at least five years after project completion.</p>
<p><strong>Budget, timing, and target beneficiaries</strong></p>
<p>The scheme has a total budget of RON 5.313 billion (approximately EUR 1.05 billion), split almost equally between R&amp;D and regional investment support. State aid will be available from 2026 to 2032, with payments extending through 2041 and the 200% tax deduction available from 2027 to 2040.</p>
<p>The scheme is expected to support around 350 companies under each type of aid, with up to 70% of annual funding reserved for Category B companies.</p>
<p><strong>Maximum aid intensities and regional bonuses</strong></p>
<p>R&amp;D aid is capped at 50% for industrial research and 25% for experimental development, with additional bonuses of 15% or 5% for projects in qualifying assisted regions. Regional investment aid varies by county, with intensity rates ranging from 30% to 70% and maximum aid ceilings of up to EUR 57.75 million.</p>
<p><strong>Application, payment and verification safeguards</strong></p>
<p>Projects must not begin before the application is submitted, and applications are generally assessed within 45 business days. Grants may include advances of up to 30%, subject to reporting requirements, while R&amp;D payments require TRL validation.</p>
<p><strong>Project changes, revocation and recovery</strong></p>
<p>Projects must begin within six months of the financing agreement, while relocation is restricted to qualifying locations. Beneficiaries must meet turnover and five-year asset or employment maintenance requirements. Failure to meet key conditions, including TRL validation, reporting deadlines or project completion requirements, may result in revocation and recovery of aid with interest.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[Qatar published six General Tax Authority (GTA) decisions in Issue 14 of the Official Gazette on 27 August 2026, setting out rules for implementing the Pillar Two global minimum tax framework. A primary focus is the Ministry of Foreign Affairs&#8217; comprehensive guide for the description and classification of diplomatic and consular roles, outlining the formal...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Qatar published six General Tax Authority (GTA) decisions in <a href="https://www.almeezan.qa/PDF/2026/14.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Issue 14 of the Official Gazette</a> on 27 August 2026, setting out rules for implementing the Pillar Two global minimum tax framework.</p>
<p>A primary focus is the Ministry of Foreign Affairs&#8217; comprehensive guide for the description and classification of diplomatic and consular roles, outlining the formal hierarchy and career progression. These regulations establish specific appointment criteria, such as language proficiency and academic credentials, while also defining the minimum years of service required for professional promotion.</p>
<p><strong>Decision No. (17) on currency conversion rules</strong></p>
<p>This decision governs how multinational enterprise (MNE) groups translate their financial figures to satisfy the compliance requirements of Qatar&#8217;s minimum tax framework.</p>
<p>Qatar&#8217;s minimum tax framework decision establishes currency translation rules for multinational enterprise groups calculating their Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-Up Tax (QDMTT) and Income Inclusion Rule (IIR) obligations.</p>
<p>Groups must align both computations to their consolidated financial statement presentation currency and follow a prescribed exchange rate hierarchy: Qatar Central Bank rates first, then European Central Bank rates, then approved third-party sources. Threshold amounts translate to Euro using December average rates from the year before the fiscal year starts, and final tax liabilities convert to Qatari Riyal at fiscal year-end rates for settlement.</p>
<p>The rules apply to all fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025.</p>
<p><strong>Decision No. (18) on simplified reporting procedures</strong></p>
<p>This decision introduces simplified compliance measures for MNE groups during a transitional phase, balancing administrative relief with robust audit safeguards.</p>
<p>MNE groups can use a simplified compliance framework for fiscal years 2025–2030, reporting GloBE adjustments on a net basis rather than entity-by-entity. This relief applies only where no Top-Up Tax liability arises; jurisdictions with such liabilities require detailed constituent-level reporting. Groups must maintain capable accounting systems, reliable allocation processes, and contemporaneous documentation. Tax authorities retain full audit and information-gathering rights regardless of the simplified approach.</p>
<p>The framework takes effect 1 January 2025.</p>
<p><strong>Decision No. (19) on transitional CbC safe harbour</strong></p>
<p>This decision outlines the transitional safe harbour rules designed to reduce the compliance burden in low-risk jurisdictions.</p>
<p>The transitional safe harbour exempts tested jurisdictions from Pillar Two top-up tax calculations if they meet one of three conditions: annual revenue below EUR 10 million and profit below EUR 1 million; a simplified effective tax rate of 16–17% depending on fiscal year; or routine profits within substance-based limits.</p>
<p>The scheme runs through fiscal years ending by 30 June 2029. Critical safeguards include mandatory consistency in financial statement types across all entities in a jurisdiction (mixing sources disqualifies the jurisdiction), neutralisation of hybrid arbitrage arrangements entered into after 18 December 2023, and exclusion of net unrealised fair value losses exceeding EUR 50 million.</p>
<p>A &#8220;once out, always out&#8221; provision permanently bars any MNE group that failed to claim or qualify for the safe harbour in a prior year from future claims for that jurisdiction.</p>
<p>The rules take effect for fiscal years beginning 1 January 2025.</p>
<p><strong>Decision No. (20) on simplified NMCE calculations</strong></p>
<p>A new decision allows filing constituent entities to elect annually to use simplified calculations for their Non-Material Constituent Entities (NMCEs) under GloBE rules. Rather than apply default GloBE values, benefiting entities may substitute Country-by-Country revenue figures for Global Anti-Base Erosion Income and Revenue, and use accrued income tax expense from CbC reporting for Adjusted Covered Taxes.</p>
<p>The measure takes effect for all fiscal years commencing on or after 1 January 2025.</p>
<p><strong>Decision No. (21) on designated local entity (DLE)</strong></p>
<p>This decision defines how a designated local constituent entity represents the MNE group for Qatari tax administrative purposes.</p>
<p>Qatar&#8217;s tax authority designates one entity (DLE) per group to handle all compliance obligations—registrations, Pillar Two filings, and tax payments. When a DLE is replaced, the new entity assumes full responsibility for prior unpaid liabilities and shares joint liability with its predecessor.</p>
<p>If a DLE fails to act, other domestic group members must file returns or pay taxes within 60 days of GTA notice. A critical issue exists in the DLE replacement timeline: the English version requires a successor appointment within 60 days of disqualification, while the Arabic version (legally binding in Qatar) mandates 30 days.</p>
<p>The requirements apply to all fiscal years commencing on or after 1 January 2025.</p>
<p><strong>Decision No. (22) on registration requirements</strong></p>
<p>This decision establishes the administrative protocols for registration, updates, and deregistration under the minimum tax rules.</p>
<p>Multinational enterprise groups must register with the GTA through an electronic platform within three months of its launch for the 2025 fiscal year, then annually within six months of each subsequent year-end. The GTA may register groups unilaterally if they miss these deadlines. Groups that cease to qualify must apply for deregistration with supporting documentation. Non-compliance incurs penalties under the Income Tax Law, though transitional relief applies under Article 4 of Law No. 22/2024.</p>
<p>The framework takes effect for all fiscal years starting 1 January 2025 onwards.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) has amended the Rulebook on the Application of the Law on Personal Income Tax to allow employers to grant employees a monthly, tax-exempt financial assistance payment of up to BAM 300, available until 31 January 2027.</p>

<p>Under the revised rules, the tax-exempt allowance is optional for employers, who may decide whether to make the payment to their employees. The measure gives businesses in the Federation additional flexibility to support staff with untaxed monthly assistance for a defined period running through to the end of January 2027.</p>
<p>The amending Rulebook stipulates that it takes effect the day after its publication in the Official Gazette of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, confirming 13 August 2026 as its operative date.</p>

		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=86875</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The UAE Federal Tax Authority has issued Decision No. 13 of 2026 on 22 July 2026, establishing due diligence requirements for Taxable Persons seeking to deduct Input Tax. The Decision applies to the verification of the validity and integrity of supplies received before Input Tax is deducted, in accordance with Article 54(bis) of the VAT...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UAE Federal Tax Authority has issued <a href="https://tax.gov.ae//Datafolder/Files/Legislation/2026/FTA%20Decision%20No.%2013%20of%202026%20on%20Measures%2018%2008%202026.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Decision No. 13 of 2026 on 22 July 2026</a>, establishing due diligence requirements for Taxable Persons seeking to deduct Input Tax. The Decision applies to the verification of the validity and integrity of supplies received before Input Tax is deducted, in accordance with Article 54(bis) of the VAT Law.</p>
<p>The Decision requires Taxable Persons to verify both their suppliers and the circumstances surrounding supplies. It also sets requirements for documenting the checks and retaining evidence for review by the Authority.</p>
<p><b>Supplier identity and business checks</b></p>
<p>For natural persons, Taxable Persons must obtain a copy of valid proof of identity, including an Emirates ID or passport, and meet the supplier either in person or virtually before the supply is made.</p>
<p>Where the supplier is a legal person, the Taxable Person must verify its incorporation through official databases or obtain a certificate of incorporation. The incorporation details must be valid and consistent with the entity’s name, address, employees and other relevant information.</p>
<p>The identity of a director, agent or employee authorised to represent the supplier must also be verified using valid proof of identity, such as an Emirates ID or passport.</p>
<p>Taxable Persons must additionally establish that the supplier has an actual place of business, using appropriate electronic means or a field visit. The location must be compatible with the nature of the supplier’s activities.</p>
<p><b>Risk indicators and bank account checks</b></p>
<p>The Decision requires Taxable Persons to assess risks associated with suppliers. Relevant indicators include a supplier changing its address more than twice during the previous 12 months, changing key employees more than twice during that period, or undertaking commercial transactions that are disproportionate or unexpected in terms of volume, value or nature compared with the size and business history of the supplier.</p>
<p>Where such an indicator exists, the Taxable Person must retain a clear and justified explanation and provide it to the Authority upon request, provided the indicator does not conflict with available evidence or information.</p>
<p>Additional checks apply where supplies received from a supplier exceed AED 375,000 over the previous 12 months, or are expected to exceed that amount during the next 12 months.</p>
<p>In these circumstances, the Taxable Person must obtain written confirmation from an authorised bank in the State that the supplier has a bank account. The confirmation does not have to be issued to the recipient of the supply.</p>
<p>The Taxable Person must also review publicly available reviews and media coverage from reliable sources and assess whether these are consistent with the supplier’s business and whether they indicate suspected Tax Evasion.</p>
<p><b>Checks on transactions and payments</b></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">The Decision requires Taxable Persons to conduct a general assessment of each supply and establish that the supplier’s participation in the transaction has genuine commercial reasons.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">Payment arrangements must also be commercially justifiable. Where a third party is involved in making or receiving payment, or payment is made to a bank account outside the supplier’s country of incorporation, there must be a reasonable commercial explanation that is consistent with the information and evidence available to the Taxable Person.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">Consideration for a supply is to be paid by electronic means. Cash payments must have a documented commercial reason, comply with applicable thresholds under Tax legislation and be readily verifiable.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">Taxable Persons must also assess whether the prices or profit margin are commercially justifiable and whether they differ significantly from market conditions without a clear reason.</span></p>
<p><b>Authenticity and nature of supplies</b></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">The requirements extend to the nature and authenticity of the Goods or Services received.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">Taxable Persons must verify that the Goods or Services fall within the supplier’s ordinary activities or the activities it is licensed to conduct under its commercial licence.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">For Goods, they must verify their authenticity and origin, as well as the supplier’s ownership or right to dispose of them.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">Where a supplier acts as an intermediary, the Taxable Person must establish a clear and justifiable commercial explanation for the supplier’s role in the supply process.</span></p>
<p><b>Documentation requirements</b></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">The Decision requires supplier verification when a Taxable Person first deals with a supplier, or when dealing with a supplier again where that supplier has not been verified during the previous 12 months.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">Each Taxable Supply received or accepted must also be verified in accordance with the specified requirements.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">Taxable Persons must document the verification steps undertaken and retain supporting documents and records. These records must enable the Authority to assess whether the requirements have been correctly implemented.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">Businesses must also maintain a documented policy identifying the persons responsible for implementing, reviewing and supervising verification procedures. The policy must clearly set out their powers and responsibilities and be retained at the designated location for required documents. </span><span style="font-weight: 400">Exception for supplies below AED 10,000</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">Decision No. 13 of 2026 allows Taxable Persons to disregard the specified verification measures for Taxable Supplies where the Consideration, exclusive of Value Added Tax, is less than AED 10,000.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">The exception is not available where the total value of supplies received from the supplier exceeds AED 100,000 during the previous 12 months, or is expected to exceed AED 100,000 during the following 12 months.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400">Federal Tax Authority Decision No. 13 of 2026 is to be published in the Official Gazette. It will come into effect on 1 October 2026.</span></p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The State Secretariat for International Finance (SIF) has updated Switzerland&#8217;s list of jurisdictions for the automatic exchange of financial account information, reclassifying Trinidad and Tobago as a reciprocal jurisdiction, according to a <a href="https://www.sif.admin.ch/en/automatic-exchange-information-aeoi" target="_blank" rel="noopener">notice</a> published on 25 August 2026.</p>
<p>The change affects Switzerland&#8217;s implementation of the automatic exchange of information (AEOI) standard, which the country applies through the Common Reporting Standard Multilateral Competent Authority Agreement (CRS MCAA), as well as through its separate bilateral agreement with the European Union. Trinidad and Tobago had previously been listed as temporarily non-reciprocal.</p>
<p>Under the reciprocal status, Switzerland will now both send and receive CRS information to and from Trinidad and Tobago. Non-reciprocal jurisdictions, by contrast, only send information to Switzerland, with two-way exchange applying only once such jurisdictions meet certain requirements.</p>
<p>With this update, Switzerland has 116 partner states under the CRS framework, though the exchange of information with Russia remains suspended.</p>
<p>The AEOI standard is designed to increase tax transparency and prevent cross-border tax evasion by enabling the mutual exchange of financial account information between participating states and territories. More than 100 states and territories, including all major financial centres, have adopted the standard alongside Switzerland.</p>
<p>The legal basis for the AEOI in Switzerland entered into force on 1 January 2017. The Federal Tax Administration (FTA) is responsible for implementing the framework domestically. The full list of Switzerland&#8217;s activated bilateral exchange relationships is also available on the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) website, though the SIF has said its own list takes priority and is updated regularly.</p>

		<link>https://regfollower.com/lithuania-proposes-200-corporate-tax-deductions-for-investments-in-select-advanced-technologies/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=lithuania-proposes-200-corporate-tax-deductions-for-investments-in-select-advanced-technologies</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Abdur Rouf]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 27 Aug 2026 13:16:35 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Computation of taxable income]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[Lithuania is proposing a 200% tax deduction for companies investing in certain advanced technologies under draft amendments to the Law on Corporate Profit Tax published on 25 August 2026. The proposal would allow entities implementing investment projects to reduce taxable profit by twice the amount spent on qualifying long-term assets listed in a new Annex...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Lithuania is <a href="https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalActPrint/lt?jfwid=-1ch27kf8jf&amp;documentId=e424c1826af211f1aa9cfebedf36d56d&amp;category=TAP" target="_blank" rel="noopener">proposing</a> a 200% tax deduction for companies investing in certain advanced technologies under draft amendments to the Law on Corporate Profit Tax published on 25 August 2026.</p>
<p>The proposal would allow entities implementing investment projects to reduce taxable profit by twice the amount spent on qualifying long-term assets listed in a new Annex 2, “Technologies Accelerating Competitiveness”.</p>
<p><strong>Proposed 200% deduction</strong></p>
<p>The draft would amend Article 461 of the Law on Corporate Profit Tax No. IX-675 to expand the existing investment project tax relief.</p>
<p>Under the proposed rules, qualifying expenditure on long-term assets listed in Annex 2 could reduce taxable profit by double the amount incurred. For other eligible investment project assets, the existing 100% reduction would continue to apply.</p>
<p>Where eligible expenditure is higher than taxable profit for a tax period, the excess could be carried forward. The standard carry-forward period would remain four consecutive tax periods, while expenditure relating to Annex 2 assets could be carried forward for five consecutive tax periods.</p>
<p>The draft also provides that taxable profit may be reduced by up to 100% in each tax period.</p>
<p><strong>Technologies covered</strong></p>
<p>The proposed Annex 2 would cover tangible and intangible assets used in advanced manufacturing, automation and digital production.</p>
<p>The machinery and equipment category would include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Additive manufacturing machines and equipment for layer-based production processes using digital modelling;</li>
<li>Robotics, automation, and collaborative robotics machines and equipment;</li>
<li>Machine vision machines and equipment for real-time production monitoring;</li>
<li>Production machines and equipment based on computerised control systems, sensors, drives and data transmission systems;</li>
<li>Micro- and nano-processing machines and equipment; and</li>
<li>Autonomous internal logistics, warehousing, and transportation machines and equipment.</li>
</ul>
<p>For computer hardware and communication equipment, the proposed list includes Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) and equipment condition monitoring tools, human–machine interface (HMI) tools, and traceability and identification tools.</p>
<p>The latter would cover systems using RFID, QR codes, barcodes, sensors or digital registries to track raw materials, components or products in the value chain.</p>
<p><strong>Software and digital systems</strong></p>
<p>The proposed relief would also apply to specified software.</p>
<p>This includes artificial intelligence, data analytics, cloud computing and edge computing systems used to optimise, forecast and ensure quality in production processes.</p>
<p>Digitalised and integrated production management systems would also qualify, alongside digital twins used for the virtual representation and analysis of production processes, equipment or systems.</p>
<p>Resource and energy management software would be included where it is used to optimise energy, raw materials and waste, monitor energy consumption and manage loads.</p>
<p><strong>Conditions for qualifying assets</strong></p>
<p>The assets would need to be necessary for implementing an entity’s investment project and meet the conditions set out in Article 461.</p>
<p>They must fall within the relevant long-term asset groups under Annex 1 of the Law on Corporate Profit Tax, including “machinery and equipment”, “installations (structures, boreholes, etc.)”, “computer hardware and communication equipment (computers, networks, and devices)”, “software” and “acquired rights”.</p>
<p>The rules also cover “freight vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers, buses – not older than five years”, subject to the conditions in the law.</p>
<p>Qualifying assets must be unused and manufactured not earlier than two years before the start of their use as long-term assets.</p>
<p>For the technologies listed in Annex 2, the draft limits eligibility to the Annex 1 groups “machinery and equipment”, “computer hardware and communication equipment (computers, networks, and devices)” and “software”.</p>
<p>If adopted, the amendments would enter into force on 1 January 2027 and apply to corporate profit tax calculations and declarations for the 2027 and subsequent tax periods.</p>

		<title>Saudi Arabia: ZATCA sets out tax, customs rules for SEZs</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/saudi-arabia-zatca-sets-out-tax-customs-rules-for-sezs/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=saudi-arabia-zatca-sets-out-tax-customs-rules-for-sezs</link>

					<description><![CDATA[Saudi Arabia’s Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority (ZATCA) has issued a new guide outlining the tax and customs treatment for businesses operating in the country’s four Special Economic Zones (SEZs), along with the compliance requirements applicable to licensed entities. Four special economic zones Saudi Arabia currently has four SEZs: King Abdullah Economic City (KAEC) SEZ,...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Saudi Arabia’s Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority (ZATCA) has issued a <a href="https://zatca.gov.sa/ar/HelpCenter/guidelines/Documents/SEZ-Tax%26Customs-Procedures.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">new guide</a> outlining the tax and customs treatment for businesses operating in the country’s four Special Economic Zones (SEZs), along with the compliance requirements applicable to licensed entities.</p>
<p><strong>Four special economic zones</strong></p>
<p>Saudi Arabia currently has four SEZs: King Abdullah Economic City (KAEC) SEZ, Ras Al-Khair SEZ, Jazan SEZ and the Cloud Computing and Informatics SEZ.</p>
<p>KAEC SEZ covers manufacturing activities, including pharmaceuticals, medical devices, packaging, geochemicals and fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG), as well as logistics services and construction.</p>
<p>Ras Al-Khair SEZ focuses on maritime industries, shipbuilding, rig building and marine support services.</p>
<p>Jazan SEZ covers food processing, metal conversion and logistics services.</p>
<p>The Cloud Computing and Informatics SEZ covers cloud computing and information technology activities, including programming, fintech, Industry 4.0, digital health and smart mobility.</p>
<p>Entities must be licensed by the competent authority to conduct eligible activities within their respective zones to access the applicable incentives.</p>
<p><strong>Corporate income tax treatment</strong></p>
<p>Licensed entities conducting qualifying activities in KAEC, Ras Al-Khair and Jazan SEZs can benefit from a 5% corporate income tax rate on qualifying income for 20 years.</p>
<p>Income from non-qualifying activities is subject to the standard 20% corporate income tax rate. The guide requires qualifying and non-qualifying income to be calculated and reported separately.</p>
<p>Operating losses can be carried forward indefinitely, although the deduction in any single tax year is capped at 25% of the taxable profit reported in the annual tax return.</p>
<p>For the Cloud Computing and Informatics SEZ, entities remain subject to the standard 20% mainland corporate income tax rate. The zone instead operates under special tax treatment based on international agreements and the Income Tax Law.</p>
<p><strong>Withholding tax and VAT</strong></p>
<p>Licensed entities in KAEC, Ras Al-Khair and Jazan SEZs are exempt from withholding tax on payments to non-residents where the payments are directly related to their licensed eligible activities.</p>
<p>Standard withholding tax rules apply in the Cloud Computing and Informatics SEZ. Rates range from 5% on dividends, interest, rent and technical services to 15% on royalties and 20% on management fees.</p>
<p>For VAT, qualifying goods supplied between licensed entities within the same SEZ, or between different SEZs under customs suspension, are subject to 0% VAT.</p>
<p>Goods supplied from mainland Saudi Arabia to a licensed SEZ entity can also qualify for 0% VAT where they are under customs suspension and relate to eligible activities.</p>
<p>Goods imported directly into an SEZ from outside Saudi Arabia are treated as outside the scope of VAT while they remain under customs duty suspension.</p>
<p>Services supplied to, from or within SEZs generally follow standard mainland VAT rules, including the 15% rate unless they qualify for zero-rating or exemption under the regular VAT rules. Services exported from an SEZ entity to a non-resident are zero-rated.</p>
<p>SEZ entities whose supplies are entirely zero-rated are exempt from mandatory VAT registration, although they can register voluntarily to reclaim input VAT incurred on business expenses.</p>
<p>No special VAT treatment applies to the Cloud Computing and Informatics SEZ, where standard mainland VAT rules apply.</p>
<p><strong>Customs duty suspension</strong></p>
<p>Eligible goods entering SEZs from outside Saudi Arabia, or moving between zones under customs suspension, can benefit from suspension of customs duties.</p>
<p>When goods are released from an SEZ into mainland Saudi Arabia, they are treated as standard imports. Customs duties and VAT are calculated and become payable based on the customs tariff applicable when the goods enter free circulation.</p>
<p>Licensed SEZ entities must maintain an electronic inventory management system linked to ZATCA to track goods entering and leaving the zone and goods consumed or processed within it.</p>
<p>Production waste and scrap released into mainland Saudi Arabia are subject to customs duties and taxes where they have commercial value.</p>
<p><strong>Other tax and compliance requirements</strong></p>
<p>The guide also covers ZATCA’s supervisory and audit powers, registration requirements, documentation and filing obligations, customs procedures, movement of goods and anti-avoidance rules.</p>
<p>SEZ entities remain subject to the standard 5% Real Estate Transaction Tax (RETT) on property transfers, long-term leases and transfers of benefits exceeding 50 years.</p>
<p>They must also comply with ZATCA’s Transfer Pricing regulations and apply the arm’s length principle to transactions with related parties. Relevant documentation, including the Local File, Master File and Country-by-Country reports, must be disclosed with annual filings.</p>
<p>Standard mainland excise tax rules apply to excise goods handled within the SEZs.</p>
<p><strong>Pillar Two review</strong></p>
<p>ZATCA’s guide indicates that the 5% corporate income tax incentive is not isolated from Saudi Arabia’s wider implementation of international tax rules.</p>
<p>The authority states that the incentive rate will be subject to review and reconsideration once Pillar Two global minimum tax rules are implemented in Saudi Arabia for entities or groups falling within their scope.</p>
<p>The guide provides businesses operating in the SEZs with the procedures needed to apply the available tax and customs treatments while maintaining compliance with ZATCA requirements. It also distinguishes the incentive regime applicable to KAEC, Ras Al-Khair and Jazan from the separate treatment of the Cloud Computing and Informatics SEZ.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Northern Region National Taxation Bureau of the Ministry of Finance <a href="https://www.mof.gov.tw/singlehtml/384fb3077bb349ea973e7fc6f13b6974?cntId=38d30046b6db468ca8a693e4568e0097" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> on 25 August 2026 that profit-making enterprises using the calendar year as their accounting year must file provisional income tax returns for the 2026 fiscal year between 1 and 30 September 2026.</p>
<p>Similarly, the Taipei National Taxation Bureau of the Ministry of Finance <a href="https://www.mof.gov.tw/singlehtml/384fb3077bb349ea973e7fc6f13b6974?cntId=d410098a131545f281c9ad0a2ce9d148" target="_blank" rel="noopener">reminded</a> calendar-year profit-making enterprises on 26 August 2026 that provisional income tax for the 2026 fiscal year must be paid or the relevant provisional tax return filed between 1 and 30 September 2026.</p>
<p><strong>2026 provisional income tax filing deadline: 1–30 September </strong></p>
<p>The Northern Region National Taxation Bureau of the Ministry of Finance has set 1 September to 30 September 2026 as the filing window for 2026 provisional income tax returns. Qualifying enterprises can now verify identity and pay directly online through the electronic filing system using business registration credentials or credit cards.</p>
<p><strong>Two filing options</strong></p>
<p>Enterprises with tax obligations may file using the general method, which bases provisional tax on half the 2025 settlement declaration income tax (excluding Article 24-5, Paragraph 2 calculations). Payment alone completes the filing, unless the enterprise applies investment tax credits, administrative relief credits, or withholding tax credits—then a formal declaration with supporting documents is required.</p>
<p>Trial calculation declaration allows enterprises with complete accounting records or audited statements filed on time to calculate provisional tax based on first-half 2026 operating revenue (excluding Article 43-3 controlled foreign enterprise income), then apply the current tax rate.</p>
<p><strong>Exemptions from filing</strong></p>
<p>Enterprises exempt from provisional tax declarations include foreign entities without fixed Taiwan locations, sole proprietorships and partnerships, small-scale approved enterprises, entities exempt under tax law, newly established enterprises or those with zero 2025 liability, enterprises dissolved or merged before the deadline, and enterprises where provisional tax calculates to less than TWD 2,000. The Ministry may exempt additional enterprises as needed.</p>
<p><strong>2026 provisional tax filing window</strong></p>
<p>Meanwhile, the Taipei National Taxation Bureau of the Ministry of Finance requires profit-making enterprises to file provisional taxes between 1 September and 30 September 2026.</p>
<p><strong>How to calculate provisional tax</strong></p>
<p>Most enterprises pay half of their previous year&#8217;s income tax. Excluded from this calculation are real estate transaction income (Article 4-4) and certain taxes computed under Article 24-5, Paragraph 2. Alternatively, businesses with complete accounting records or accountant certification can calculate provisional tax using only their first six months of 2026 income, applying the current year&#8217;s tax rate. This method doesn&#8217;t include controlled foreign corporation investment income under Article 43-3.</p>
<p><strong>Payment options</strong></p>
<p>Enterprises can pay via the Ministry of Finance tax portal (https://www.etax.nat.gov.tw), financial institutions, ATMs, convenience stores (for amounts under TWD 30,000), or credit cards.</p>
<p><strong>Who is exempt</strong></p>
<p>Sole proprietorships, small businesses exempt from uniform invoices, newly established businesses, entities with zero previous-year tax liability, and those owing less than TWD 2,000 don&#8217;t need to file. Educational, cultural, and charitable organisations are also exempt, as are businesses undergoing dissolution or merger.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The US Internal Revenue Service (IRS), in a <a href="https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/irs-reminder-information-return-e-file-system-transitioning-to-a-new-platform" target="_blank" rel="noopener">release</a> on 24 August 2026, has reminded information return filers who currently use the Filing Information Returns Electronically (FIRE) system to prepare now for the system’s retirement and transition to the Information Returns Intake System (IRIS) before the 2027 filing season.</p>
<p>After the November maintenance window, filers will no longer be able to submit information returns through FIRE. Current FIRE users must transition to IRIS to file tax year 2026 information returns during the 2027 filing season.</p>
<p><strong>Key dates to remember</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>1 November 2026: Last day to file test information returns through the FIRE Trading Partner Test System.</li>
<li>9 November 2026: Last day to make changes to the Information Returns (IR) Applications for Transmitter Control Codes (TCC).</li>
<li>19 November 2026, at 3 PM ET: Last day to file information returns through the FIRE system.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Transitioning to IRIS</strong></p>
<p>IRIS is a modernised system that receives information returns through two channels: the IRIS Taxpayer Portal and IRIS Application to Application. IRIS became available in 2023 as part of a phased transition of forms from FIRE. Beginning in 2027, all forms previously supported by FIRE will be available through IRIS.</p>
<p>The IRIS Taxpayer Portal is a free, web-based filing system that allows filers to e-file up to 100 returns at a time. Filers can enter information manually or upload it using a CSV file. They can also download payee copies and maintain records of completed and filed forms.</p>
<p>Filers who use third-party software or develop their own software can use IRIS Application to Application to e-file larger volumes of information returns.</p>
<p><strong>To prepare for the transition, filers should:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Complete an IRIS Application for TCC.</li>
<li>Review available guidance on <a href="https://www.irs.gov/filing/e-file-information-returns-with-iris" target="_blank" rel="noopener">E-file Information Returns</a> with IRIS.</li>
<li><a href="https://www.irs.gov/e-file-providers/subscribe-to-quickalerts" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Subscribe to IRIS QuickAlerts</a> for updates about system changes, maintenance, and working group meetings.</li>
<li>Register for IRIS Working Group meetings and review meeting materials.</li>
</ul>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Croatian Ministry of Finance has issued <a href="https://esavjetovanja.gov.hr/Econ/10183" target="_blank" rel="noopener">draft legislation</a> proposing amendments to the VAT Act to partially implement Council Directive (EU) 2025/516, known as VAT in the Digital Age (ViDA), and align Croatia’s VAT framework with EU requirements. The proposal seeks to modernise VAT rules to reflect the needs of the digital economy.</p>
<p>The draft legislation is open for public consultation until 30 August 2026.</p>
<p>The key proposed changes are:</p>
<p><strong>Implementation of the ViDA Directive (EU) 2025/516</strong></p>
<p>The draft legislation directly proposes to align Croatian VAT law with Council Directive (EU) 2025/516 (issued 11 March 2025), which introduces the VAT in the Digital Age (ViDA) rules. The main focus of these amendments is to modernise and expand the existing One-Stop Shop (OSS) and Import One-Stop Shop (IOSS) systems. The proposed changes are slated to enter into force on 1 January 2027.</p>
<p><strong>Transition to OSS for transfers of own goods (Replacing call-off stock)</strong></p>
<p>The draft bill proposes phasing out the current call-off stock regime and replacing it with a simplified OSS mechanism for transfers of businesses’ own goods across EU Member States. No new call-off stock arrangements could begin after 30 June 2028, while existing arrangements would remain under the current rules until 30 June 2029. From 1 July 2028, new cross-border transfers of own goods would instead be reported through an adapted OSS registration, replacing the current Collective Declaration system.</p>
<p><strong>OSS expansion for non-EU providers and small business IOSS restrictions</strong></p>
<p>The draft bill expands the scope of the OSS to all B2C services supplied within the EU by non-EU service providers. Small businesses operating under the special VAT-exempt scheme will be explicitly prohibited from using the IOSS (Import One-Stop Shop).</p>
<p><strong>Electricity, heating, and cooling supplies</strong></p>
<p>As per the draft bill, the supply of gas through natural gas systems, as well as the supply of electricity, heating, or cooling via distribution networks to non-taxable persons (or entities whose acquisitions are not subject to VAT) by a non-established supplier, is treated as an intra-EU distance sale of goods for OSS purposes. This treatment is temporary and will remain in effect until 30 June 2028.</p>
<p><strong>VAT refund adjustments and the EUR 10,000 threshold</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>VAT refunds:</strong> The proposal clarifies VAT refund procedures for OSS and IOSS users. Non-EU taxable persons using the OSS scheme must claim input VAT refunds under the 13th Council Directive rather than through Croatia’s standard domestic procedure. It also sets out refund rules for OSS-registered businesses using Croatia as their Member State of identification.</li>
<li><strong>EUR 10,000 threshold:</strong> The draft clarifies that the EUR 10,000 threshold for cross-border B2C distance sales and certain electronic and telecommunications services applies only to supplies originating from the business’s Member State of establishment.</li>
<li><strong>Deemed opt-out:</strong> Businesses can choose whether to apply the EUR 10,000 threshold. However, registering for the OSS scheme automatically constitutes an opt-out, requiring VAT to be charged in the Member State of consumption from the outset.</li>
</ul>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Social Security Commission (SSC) of Namibia released a <a href="https://www.facebook.com/sscnamibia/posts/public-notice/1368116205463557/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public notice</a> on 7 August 2026 that outlines a progressive plan to increase the contribution ceiling for the Maternity Leave, Sick Leave, and Death Benefit Fund (MSD).</p>
<p>While the contribution ceiling increase was originally scheduled to take effect on 1 March 2026, its implementation was deferred to 1 September 2026. This delay was due to a postponement in publishing the required amendments in the Government Gazette.</p>
<p>The key amendments are:</p>
<p>The four-year progressive implementation schedule (2026–2029)</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Phase 1 (Financial Year 2025/2026):</strong> Effective 1 September 2026, the maximum basic salary ceiling will reach NAD 12,500 per month. The maximum monthly contribution at 0.9% will be NAD 112.50 for both employee and employer, an increase from the previous NAD 99 cap.</li>
<li><strong>Phase 2 (Financial Year 2026/2027):</strong> Starting 1 March 2027, the ceiling rises to NAD 14,000 per month, with maximum monthly contributions of NAD 126 each for employee and employer.</li>
<li><strong>Phase 3 (Financial Year 2027/2028):</strong> From 1 March 2028, the ceiling increases to NAD 15,000 per month, with maximum monthly contributions of NAD 135 each.</li>
<li><strong>Phase 4 (Financial Year 2028/2029):</strong> Effective 1 March 2029, the ceiling reaches NAD 16,000 per month, with maximum monthly contributions of NAD 144 each.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Monthly impact breakdown by salary bracket (September 2026)</strong></p>
<p>The MSD contribution rate is split equally, with the employee paying 0.9% and the employer matching with 0.9%. Starting 1 September 2026, the monthly contributions are structured as follows:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Basic salary of NAD 500 per month:</strong> No changes apply. Both employee and employer continue contributing NAD 4.50 per month.</li>
<li><strong>Basic salary between NAD 501 and NAD 12,499 per month:</strong> Contributions are calculated at 0.9% of the basic salary. A salary of NAD 10,000, for example, results in NAD 90 contributed by each party.</li>
<li><strong>Basic salary of NAD 12,500 or more per month:</strong> Contributions are capped at NAD 112.50 per employee and employer, up from the previous maximum of NAD 99. This represents an increase of NAD 13.50 per party.</li>
</ul>
<p>While the notice is highly detailed regarding the contribution structure, it does not outline the historical contribution ceilings before NAD 11,000, nor does it detail the specific benefit payout amounts or maximum durations for maternity, sick, or death claims.</p>

		<title>US:  Treasury, IRS propose regulations to reshape CFC income inclusion rules among US shareholders</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/us-treasury-irs-propose-regulations-to-reshape-cfc-income-inclusion-rules-among-us-shareholders/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=us-treasury-irs-propose-regulations-to-reshape-cfc-income-inclusion-rules-among-us-shareholders</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Mohammed Al Mamun]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 27 Aug 2026 11:27:50 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[CFC]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Americas]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[US]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=86827</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The US Treasury and the IRS have proposed regulations (REG-115646-25) establishing rules for allocating a controlled foreign corporation’s (CFC) subpart F income, tested income, and tested loss among US shareholders based on their respective periods of stock ownership during the CFC’s taxable year. The proposed IRS regulations follow the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA),...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The US Treasury and the IRS have proposed regulations (<a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-17365" target="_blank" rel="noopener">REG-115646-25</a>) establishing rules for allocating a controlled foreign corporation’s (CFC) subpart F income, tested income, and tested loss among US shareholders based on their respective periods of stock ownership during the CFC’s taxable year.</p>
<p>The proposed IRS regulations follow the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), specifically regarding how US shareholders must calculate and report their pro rata share of income from controlled foreign corporations (CFCs). The new rules shift from a &#8220;last day of the year&#8221; ownership test to a daily proration approach, ensuring tax liability is attributed to shareholders based on the specific duration of their ownership during the taxable year.</p>
<p>The key proposed regulations are:</p>
<p><strong>The Core shift: Section 951(a)(1)(A) and the OBBBA amendments</strong></p>
<p>The OBBBA amended <a href="https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title26-section951&amp;num=0&amp;edition=prelim" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Section 951(a)(1)(A)</a> so that a US shareholder may have a Subpart F income inclusion based on stock owned on any day during the CFC’s taxable year, rather than only on the last relevant day. Under revised Section 951(a)(3), the inclusion is generally recognised in the shareholder’s taxable year containing the last day they own the CFC stock.</p>
<p><strong>The daily proration allocation methodology</strong></p>
<p>Proposed Section 1.951-1 generally uses daily proration to allocate Subpart F income, tested income, and tested loss. Separate calculations apply to different CFC year blocks. Weighted-average shares are used when outstanding shares change, while multiple classes of stock require allocation among classes before daily proration. The acquisition day is excluded and the disposition day is included in the ownership period.</p>
<p><strong>Taxable year determinations: Mandatory closings (status change events)</strong></p>
<p>Under proposed Section 1.245A-5 and related Section 1.951-1 rules, a foreign corporation must close its taxable year when it becomes or ceases to be a CFC. The closing occurs at the end of the status-change day. Special rules under <a href="https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title26-section958&amp;num=0&amp;edition=prelim" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Section 958 </a>apply to determine the relevant US shareholders, including look-through treatment for domestic partnerships. The rules prevent income from non-CFC periods from affecting US tax inclusions.</p>
<p><strong>Taxable year determinations: Elective closings (significant ownership variances)</strong></p>
<p>Proposed Section 1.951-1 permits an elective taxable-year closing when a significant ownership variance results in an aggregate decrease of more than 50 percentage points in Section 958(a) US shareholder ownership. Specified transfers include sales, exchanges, redemptions, issuances, and certain partnership-interest changes. The election requires a binding written agreement, filing of an elective year-closing statement, notice to other US persons, and consistency across related CFCs. Anti-abuse rules address related-party transactions and F reorganisations.</p>
<p><strong>Section 951A tested income &amp; tested loss coordination</strong></p>
<p>Proposed <a href="https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/part-1/section-1.951A-1" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Section 1.951A-1</a> coordinates the new Subpart F rules with Section 951A. US shareholders generally determine their net CFC tested income inclusion amount, while previous rules for allocating QBAI, tested interest expense, and tested interest income are removed. Under the proposed rules, tested loss is generally allocated to common stock, with limited exceptions for preferred stock and equity with liquidation preferences. Subsequent tested income can first restore previously allocated tested losses.</p>
<p><strong>The OBBBA transition rule for Pre-2026 dividends and substantiation</strong></p>
<p>Proposed Section 1.951-4 implements the OBBBA transition rule for certain dividends paid during the transition period. A dividend generally cannot reduce a shareholder’s pro rata Subpart F or tested-income inclusion under former <a href="https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title26-section951&amp;num=0&amp;edition=prelim" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Section 951(a)(2)(B)</a> if it does not increase the taxable income of a US person subject to federal income tax. Special rules cover upper-tier CFCs, publicly held partnerships, RICs, REITs, and exempt organisations. Shareholders claiming the reduction must attach a Pro Rata Share Transition Rule Statement to Form 5471.</p>
<p><strong>Other key provisions</strong></p>
<p>The proposed Section 1.951-1 rules provide for allocation of foreign income taxes when a CFC’s US tax year closes mid-year, using principles similar to Section 1.1502-76(b). A partnership’s taxable year generally does not close solely because its foreign corporate partner’s year closes, with comments requested on potential Section 706 treatment.</p>
<p>Section 951B extends the rules to foreign controlled US shareholders (FCUSSs), although the elective closing is unavailable to them. Form 5471 Schedules A and B are expanded to capture detailed stock ownership changes. Certain outdated rules under Sections 1.245A-5(e) and (f) and 1.1502-80(j) are eliminated for post-2025 CFC years.</p>
<p><strong>Key dates and reliance</strong></p>
<p>The proposed regulations were published on 26 August 2026, with comments due 26 October 2026. They generally apply to foreign corporation taxable years beginning after 31 December 2025. Treasury and the IRS expect final regulations by 4 January 2027.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[The OECD published responses to its 1 June 2026 invitation for comments on a public consultation document proposing potential revisions to Chapter VII of the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administrations concerning the transfer pricing of intragroup services on 24 August 2026. The consultation received over 100 public comments from businesses,...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The OECD published responses to its 1 June 2026 <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/events/public-consultations/2026/06/public-consultation-on-taxation-revisions-to-chapter-vii-of-the-oecd-transfer-pricing-guidelines.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">invitation</a> for comments on a <a href="https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/events/public-consultations/2026/6/public-consultation-on-taxation--revisions-to-chapter-vii-of-the-oecd-transfer-pricing-guidelines/public-consultation-document-special-considerations-intra-group-services.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation document</a> proposing potential revisions to Chapter VII of the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administrations concerning the transfer pricing of intragroup services on 24 August 2026.</p>
<p>The consultation received over 100 public comments from businesses, industry associations, and professional services organisations.</p>
<p>It sought feedback on updating and modernising the existing guidance on applying the arm’s length principle to intragroup services, including more than 20 new examples. The proposed revisions are not intended to alter the general principles underlying the transfer pricing analysis of such services.</p>
<p>Recurring themes included calls for ex-ante application of the benefit test, proportionate documentation requirements, and clearer distinctions between intra-group services and intangible transfers, particularly for AI-enabled and digital service models. Commentators generally supported continued reliance on one-sided transfer pricing methods for most service arrangements.</p>
<p>The OECD will discuss consultation outcomes at a public meeting on 9 November 2026 at the OECD Conference Centre in Paris. Registration details will be published on the OECD website in September 2026.</p>
<p>The public comments are available on the OECD website and can be downloaded <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/events/public-consultations/2026/06/public-consultation-on-taxation-revisions-to-chapter-vii-of-the-oecd-transfer-pricing-guidelines.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">here</a>.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/oecd-consults-revised-transfer-pricing-guidance-for-intra-group-services/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, in June 2026, the OECD opened a public consultation on proposed updates to Chapter VII of its Transfer Pricing Guidelines concerning intra-group services, which ended on 22 July 2026.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has released Issue No. 2026-08, urging eligible foreign filers to register for a Foreign Filer Transmitter Control Code (TCC) ahead of the 2027 filing season on 19 August 2026. The registration provides credentials for electronically filing Forms 1042-S, applicable Forms 1099, and other information returns through the International Data...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has released <a href="https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USIRS/bulletins/425baac" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Issue No. 2026-08</a>, urging eligible foreign filers to register for a Foreign Filer Transmitter Control Code (TCC) ahead of the 2027 filing season on 19 August 2026.</p>
<p>The registration provides credentials for electronically filing Forms 1042-S, applicable Forms 1099, and other information returns through the International Data Exchange System (IDES).</p>
<p>The IRS first announced the Foreign Filer TCC registration solution in <a href="https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USIRS/bulletins/415b2f2" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Issue No. 2026-06</a>, published on 4 May 2026.</p>
<p>The Foreign Filer TCC Registration System allows certain foreign filers to obtain the credentials required to electronically transmit Forms 1042-S, applicable Forms 1099, and other information returns through the International Data Exchange System (IDES). Eligible filers are encouraged to register early and complete the necessary steps before the 2027 filing season begins.</p>
<p>The Filing Information Returns Electronically (FIRE) system is scheduled to be retired this calendar year, with the Information Returns Intake System (IRIS) becoming the electronic filing platform for information returns previously submitted through FIRE.</p>
<p>IRIS access requirements may prevent some foreign filers from accessing the system because their authorised users do not have a US taxpayer identification number, such as an SSN or ITIN. To address this, the IRS introduced the Foreign Filer TCC Registration System, enabling eligible foreign filers to obtain the GIIN and TCC credentials required for IDES enrollment and electronic submission of Forms 1042-S, applicable Forms 1099, and other information returns.</p>
<p><strong>Access requirements</strong></p>
<p>Access to the Foreign Filer TCC Registration System requires users to sign in through Login.gov or ID.me. Users who do not already have an account with one of these providers can create an account when accessing the Foreign Filer TCC Registration System.</p>
<p>The email address associated with the Foreign Filer TCC account must match the email address for the responsible officer or point of contact on the Login.gov or ID.me account.</p>
<p>Filers are encouraged to establish their secure access credentials early to help avoid delays when completing the registration process.</p>
<p><strong>Foreign filer TCC registration process</strong></p>
<p>Users of the Foreign Filer TCC Registration System are required to:</p>
<ul>
<li>Have or create an account with Login.gov or ID.me;</li>
<li>Create a new Foreign Filer TCC account to obtain a Foreign Filer ID;</li>
<li>Complete the registration process to obtain a TCC GIIN;</li>
<li>Request a TCC after the TCC GIIN is issued; and</li>
<li>Enrol in IDES to transmit information returns electronically.</li>
</ul>
<p>Once a TCC GIIN and TCC are obtained from the Foreign Filer TCC Registration System, users should wait three to six weeks before enrolling with IDES. An Authorised Security Certificate from an approved Certificate Authority is required as part of the IDES enrollment process and can be obtained as soon as the TCC GIIN and TCC are issued. Once enrolled in IDES, authorised users will have access to the applicable information return schema.</p>
<p>Eligible filers should begin these steps as soon as possible rather than waiting until filing season. Completing registration in advance provides time to establish system access, complete the required registration steps, and prepare for electronic filing in 2027 through IDES.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Following the US imposition of a 50% tariff on USD 27.6 billion of Canadian goods effective 22 August, Canada has <a href="https://www.canada.ca/en/department-finance/news/2026/08/canada-announces-targeted-countermeasures-and-substantive-support-for-workers-and-businesses-in-response-to-us-tariffs.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> retaliatory tariffs on around USD 20 billion worth of annual US imports on 25 August 2025 alongside support measures for affected businesses and workers, matching Washington’s latest duties dollar-for-dollar, effective 8 September 2026.</p>
<p>Canada will impose counter-tariffs of 15%, 25% and 50% on roughly 700 US products from 8 September, targeting goods subject to US Section 338 and Section 232 tariffs.  The retaliatory measures cover 27.6 billion in imports from the US, focusing on sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.</p>
<p>The Department of Finance also released backgrounders outlining the <a href="https://www.canada.ca/en/department-finance/news/2026/08/list-of-products-from-the-united-states-subject-to-counter-tariffs-effective-september-8-2026.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">products</a> from the US that will be subject to counter-tariffs, as well as the <a href="https://www.canada.ca/en/department-finance/news/2026/08/support-for-canadian-workers-and-businesses-affected-by-us-tariffs.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">support measures</a> available to Canadian workers and businesses affected by US tariffs.</p>
<p><strong>Support package for affected sectors</strong></p>
<p>Canada&#8217;s federal government announced a USD 7.5 billion support package designed to assist workers and businesses experiencing tariff-related disruption. This new funding builds on approximately USD 25 billion in assistance measures previously deployed since US tariffs began taking effect.</p>
<p><strong>Business liquidity and capital support</strong></p>
<p>The government committed CAD 1.5 billion through its Regional Tariff Response Initiative, channelled via regional development agencies to reach small and medium-sized enterprises. The funding aims to address immediate cash constraints caused by tariff impacts.</p>
<p>The Business Development Bank of Canada introduced a CAD 500 million liquidity stream through its Pivot to Grow programme, targeting businesses experiencing short-term cash-flow disruptions.</p>
<p>To broaden access, the government lowered the minimum revenue threshold for applicants to CAD 1 million, expanding eligibility beyond previously qualified firms. Additional flexibilities were added to the Large Enterprise Tariff Loan facility, administered through the Canada Enterprise Emergency Funding Corporation.</p>
<p>A new USD 2 billion Canada Strong Diversification Fund targets shovel-ready capital projects, prioritising maintenance and infrastructure that supports long-term operational resilience. Regional development agencies will handle project intake and coordination with this initiative.</p>
<p><strong>Worker transition and retention</strong></p>
<p>The government allocated USD 3.5 billion toward rapid response support for both workers and employers. This includes expanded Employment Insurance flexibilities to provide income support for affected workers, alongside new workplace-based training programs and upgrades to JobBank.gc.ca to facilitate workforce transitions. A new Worker Retention and Retraining Programme enables employers to retain staff during this period by offsetting the costs of maintaining employment and upskilling initiatives.</p>
<p>The latest escalation <a href="https://regfollower.com/canada-suspends-us-trade-negotiations-retaliates-with-matching-tariffs/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">follows</a> Canada’s suspension of US trade negotiations on 21 August 2026 after rejecting last-minute US trade terms as unfair. The US subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on around USD 20 billion of Canadian goods, prompting Canada to announce retaliatory measures.  The Trump administration has further escalated the dispute by <a href="https://regfollower.com/us-trump-administration-escalates-tariff-threat-on-canadian-automotive-sector/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">planning</a> 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, trucks and automotive parts from 1 January 2027.</p>
